en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Guide (Nettippakaraṇa-ṭīkā) in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
Commentary on the Introduction to the Book:
At the commencement of the commentary, the homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of making known the origin and the purity of the basis of the Dhamma to be commented upon.

Furthermore, that is for the purpose of generating great respect among the wise toward the commentaries on the Dhamma, so that they may properly acquire the qualities of learning, retention, and so forth.

It is for the purpose of accomplishing all benefit and happiness through right practice. Alternatively, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem in this commentary is performed because it is auspicious, because it is the preliminary duty in all undertakings, because it is the conduct rightly practiced by the wise, and because others in the future will follow one’s example upon seeing it.
Alternatively, the making of homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of generating a specific merit consisting in the worship of those worthy of worship.
This is for the purpose of augmenting the power of the karma that caused him to obtain his own present prosperity;
for the purpose of preventing its contraction in the interim; and for the purpose of completing this commentary without interruption by means of both [the homage and the undertaking].
And it is precisely this purpose that is intended here by the Teacher. For he will say: "The merit born of the salutation... [and so on]... of him..."
“By means of splendor. For the worship of the Three Refuges is a preeminent excellence of merit, possessing immeasurable power through its realization as an unsurpassed field of merit.

Thus, even amidst the manifold obstacles inherent in worldly existence, it is capable of destroying all defilements that serve as the basis for those obstacles, and it wards off calamities such as fear. As it has been said:
“And for one who worships those worthy of worship, whether they be Buddhas or their disciples,” and likewise:
“Monks, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost; and for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.”
Likewise:
"The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises 'the Buddha'—
that rapture alone is better than even the whole of Jambudīpa."
“‘The Dhamma’... [and so on] ... ‘The Saṅgha’... [and so on] ... is an island. And likewise:
“Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.”
Likewise:
“In the forest or at the foot of a tree...
[and so on]... there will be no fear, nor trepidation, nor horripilation. And:

In this context, in order to demonstrate the possession of preeminent qualities in the Triple Gem which he wishes to worship, he spoke three verses beginning with "the Greatly Compassionate One" (*mahākāruṇika*). For it is through the possession of preeminent qualities that one becomes worthy of worship;
and worship rendered to those worthy of worship accomplishes the intended purpose. Therein, [he speaks] of that [Triple Gem] whose eulogy he wishes to perform.
That *Netti* is specifically based on the teaching of the *Anuloma* [Sutta], and it elucidates the manifestation of its various modes of occurrence.
For the teaching of the Suttanta is not dominated by compassion as the teaching of the Vinaya is, nor is it dominated by wisdom as the teaching of the Abhidhamma is;
rather, it is dominated by both compassion and wisdom. Thus, it is the elucidation of the distinction of that teaching which is dominated by both.
In order to offer praise to the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), it is said, beginning with “the compassionate Lord” (Mahākāruṇikaṃ nāthaṃ), because all other jewels are rooted in him.
Therein, *kirati* means compassion (*karuṇā*); the meaning is that it scatters away or removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, *kiṇāti* means compassion;
the meaning is that when there is suffering in others, it strikes at or afflicts the [selfish] heart. Or, it is that which causes trembling (*kampanaṃ karoti*).
*Karuṇā* means that when there is suffering in others, it causes distress in the hearts of the virtuous. Alternatively, *ka* refers to happiness (*sukha*);

it obstructs that, hence it is *karuṇā*. For its characteristic is the desire to remove the suffering of others; because those who possess compassion are indifferent to their own happiness, it obstructs—that is, hinders—their happiness. It is called *karuṇā* because it is extended toward those who are suffering.
Or, he is compassionate because he is devoted to compassion; thus he is "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*), just as one is called a "doorkeeper" (*dovārika*).

For just as a man who earns his living in dependence on a door is called a "doorkeeper"—even though he may be engaged elsewhere than at the doorway—because his conduct does not overstep the door, so too the Blessed One, even though he may be engaged elsewhere through loving-kindness and other qualities, [is called compassionate] because he dwells in compassion.
He is called "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*) because he is devoted to compassion through its practice that never transcends [his own nature].
Indeed, from the time of his Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) until his Great Parinibbāna, the Lords of the World remain solely for the benefit and welfare of the world.

He is a "Great Compassionate One" (*mahākāruṇika*) because he is great in compassion. Although the Blessed One possesses greatness by virtue of other qualities as well, [the title is used] due to the presence of the word "compassionate."
Because it has been so stated, the greatness here should be understood as being by way of compassion alone, just as in the expression “one who is a great grammarian.
And having established it thus, by this phrase “the Greatly Compassionate One,” the Teacher’s great compassion is expressed by means of a reference to the person.
Another method: he is called *kāruṇika* because he is worthy of performing compassion, of feeling compassion, and of the manifestation of compassion, by way of accomplishing the welfare [of others].
For the Blessed One, through his omniscience, knows the welfare of beings and the means to that welfare without exception;
and therein he is untiring, desirous of their benefit, and a teacher—qualities which others do not possess in such a way.

Alternatively, he is "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*) because compassion (*karuṇā*), the act of feeling compassion, virtue, nature, and essential character belong to him. For the Blessed One does not have a nature of hardness or impact like earth, touch, and so forth.
“Compassion as its intrinsic nature” means that compassion is its very essence. The rest is exactly as before.

Alternatively, it is called “great compassion” (*mahākaruṇā*) because it is great due to its vast object, its great power, and its great fruit. For the Blessed One’s compassion extends toward all sentient beings without exception;
and when it does so, it proceeds in a way not shared by others; and it [extends] toward the various categories such as those pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), and so forth.

He brings about the greatest possible welfare and happiness for beings in an absolute sense; because he is devoted to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he is called "the Greatly Compassionate One" (*Mahākāruṇika*).

The rest of all this should be understood according to the method already explained. Furthermore, the grammatical derivation of the words here should be understood as being like that of the word *Sumāgadhā* and others.
"He protects" (*nāthati*) thus he is a "protector" (*nātha*); the meaning is that he hopes for and aspires to the welfare and happiness of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

And here, this hoping for welfare and happiness should be understood as occurring through the mode of loving-kindness (*mettā*), not through the mode of compassion (*karuṇā*), because it was stated by means of the first term [of the pair].

Alternatively, he is a "protector" because he "torments" (*nāthati*)—that is, afflicts—the calamity of the defilements residing in those to be trained; or, "he is a protector" because he "entreats" (*nāthati*), that is, makes a request.

The meaning is as follows: For the Blessed One, having requested from beings their respective practice for their welfare by saying, "It is good, monks, that a bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon his own perfection," and so forth, exhorts them toward those practices, being impelled by great compassion.
Alternatively, he is endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind, or he "rules over" (īsati) and overcomes all beings through qualities such as virtue and the rest.
The Blessed One, the supreme lord, is called the "Protector" (nātha); [he is] that Protector.
That which is to be known is the "knowable" (ñeyya): all conditioned things and the unconditioned, distinguished by the divisions of the past and so forth.
It is an ocean (sāgara) in the sense of being a gathering place; it causes those who have fallen into it to sink and submerge due to its own vastness and depth.

The meaning [of *saṃ*] is as follows. Here, the prefix *saṃ-* should be understood according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*), as in such terms as *sābhāvo* (one's own nature) and *sārāgo* (one's own passion). Alternatively, it means "in the sense of making an agreement" (*saṅgaraṇaṭṭhena*).

That is to say, by virtue of its fixed nature, it is as if one were making an agreement or a convention with the world, thinking: "This is my boundary; I shall not transgress this time-limit. Thus, it is called *saṅgaraṇa*.
It is called the ocean (*sāgara*) because it causes water to flow out and stream away from all sides.
For at the time of the world’s dissolution, the great ocean flows hither and thither, turning the entire world-system into a single flood. However, the worldly people say:
"It is called the ocean because it was dug by the sons of King Sāgara; it is the eastern region of the sea."
"Because of its connection with that [ocean], the entire ocean is spoken of in that way by way of conventional usage.
It is called the "Sāgara" because it resembles the ocean; since the knowable itself is like an ocean, it is the "ocean of the knowable" (*ñeyyasāgara*).

And here, the similarity should be understood through its vastness, its difficulty of crossing, its profundity, and its beginninglessness. Yet, this is an inferior simile. For the knowable alone possesses an exceptional vastness, as it pervades immeasurable world-systems.
The state of being difficult to cross, profound, and having a course of existence without a beginning point belongs only to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),
and not to the other [knowledge], because that is limited in scope, can be traversed in a brief moment even by outsiders who are free from passion,

and is finite in its depth and duration. One who has gone to the further shore— the limit— of the ocean of the knowable is called "one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable" (*ñeyyasāgarapāragū*).

To him who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of the knowable (*ñeyya*). Here, "going" refers specifically to the going of knowledge (*ñāṇagamana*), and not the other kind, because of the inclusion of the "knowable. That knowledge is twofold, distinguished by way of comprehension (*sammasana*) and penetration (*paṭivedha*), and likewise by way of cause and fruit.
Therein, [it begins] with "Alas, this world has fallen into hardship," and so forth, solely by way of compassion.

Having thus applied himself, as he comprehended the formations within their manifold modes and spheres, the Blessed One’s knowledge of comprehension plunged into the ocean of the knowable by way of thirty-six hundred thousand approaches and reached its further shore and limit;

this is what is called the "Great Vajira-knowledge. Furthermore, the knowledge of penetration has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints has the knowledge of penetration as its proximate cause.

The knowledge of omniscience is what is called "Great Enlightenment" (mahābodhi). Its crossing to the further shore should be understood both in terms of the accomplishment of its task and its capacity for that end.
Likewise, the aforementioned knowledge of comprehension (sammasanañāṇa) is the cause, while the other is the fruit.

Alternatively, with the knowledge of comprehension as the accompaniment, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) is the cause, and the knowledge of omniscience is the fruit, because it is the nature of its benefit.

I pay homage, I bow down, or I praise [him]. "Possessing subtle, profound, and manifold methods" means that this teaching has methods that are subtle in their gentleness (*saṇha*), profound in their unfathomability for those who have not accumulated the requisites of knowledge (*ñāṇa-sambhāra*), and manifold because they are distinguished by various divisions such as the unity (*ekatta*) and so forth, as well as the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* and other categories.
Thus, it is one whose teaching possesses subtle, profound, and manifold methods.
It is "method" (*naya*) because it leads; that is, the course of the text. And this [course] is subtle in meaning according to the manner in which it was spoken;

it is profound in both meaning and phrasing; and it is diverse due to its manifold nature, such as its occurrence in brief and detailed forms, or in accordance with [the sequence of] exposition and so forth.
For instance, it is [treated] by way of original rules and subsequent permissions, and by way of the categories of defilement, mundane, supramundane, and their mixture, and so on.

The modes of the Pāḷi are manifold, by way of the inclusion of the aggregates such as the wholesome and so forth, the inclusion of the [four] truths, the establishment of the liberations from the conventional, and so forth, as well as the triads beginning with the roots of the wholesome, and the Paṭṭhāna, and so forth.
In that regard, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two ways: by way of his own attainment of welfare and by way of his practice for the welfare of others.

Among these, the accomplishment of one's own welfare is to be understood from the attainment of unobstructed knowledge and from the absolute abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies;
the practice for the welfare of others is to be understood from the teaching of the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering by one whose mind is indifferent to gain,
honor, and the like, and from the arrival of the time for the maturation of the knowledge of his constant aspiration for the welfare of even those who oppose him.
And this [compassion] should be understood here as being twofold: by way of application (*payoga*) and by way of disposition (*āsaya*).

Thus, the practice for the benefit of others (*parahitappaṭipatti*) and the accomplishment of one's own welfare (*attahitasampatti*), each with the aforementioned divisions, are revealed. How so? By the term "Greatly Compassionate" (*mahākāruṇika*), it is shown by way of disposition;
by the phrase "subtle... teaching," it is shown by way of application; and by the term "Protector" (*nātha*), it is shown by both ways regarding the Blessed One.

The practice for the benefit of others is revealed by the phrase "because it illuminates the function of compassion," while the phrase "one who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of the knowable" reveals the attainment of one's own welfare in its highest excellence and the function of supreme knowledge.
Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in three ways: by way of cause, by way of fruit, and by way of benefit. Therein—
The cause is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and that is shown by its own form in the first word [of the verse]. The fruit is fourfold:

perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*), perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*), perfection of power (*ānubhāvasampadā*), and perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāyasampadā*). Among these, the primary ones—perfection of knowledge and perfection of abandonment—are revealed by the phrase "one who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of the knowable" (*ñeyyasāgarapāragu*).
For when the primary is shown, the other is also [implied] due to their inseparable nature (*avinābhāvato*).
The dyad has indeed been shown; for the glory of the Dhamma-body never exists apart from the power and the perfection of the physical body of the Buddhas.

It should be understood that the assistance—consisting of the teaching of the Dhamma of liberation by way of the three vehicles, without making anything external to what is immediate—is revealed by the two phrases: "The Protector... [and] the subtle... teaching."
In this context, by the term “possessing great compassion,” he shows the root of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
For the Blessed One, his mind impelled by great compassion, made the aspiration to lift sentient beings out of the mire of *saṃsāra*;

having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramitā*) in due order, he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment. By the phrase “one who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of the knowable,”...
By this, he shows perfect enlightenment together with the preliminary practice.
For path-knowledge has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge has path-knowledge as its proximate cause; this is what is called "perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, the aforementioned knowledge of comprehension, together with the perfection of wisdom, constitutes its preliminary practice. Indeed, by the power of that [practice],...
The Middle Way—free from the two extremes of dullness and agitation, of exertion and indulgence in sensual pleasure, and of eternalism and annihilationism;
reaching the pinnacle of excellence and having attained the perfection of development—is fully realized.

By the word "Protector" (*nātha*), he demonstrates the fruit of Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), as it reveals his status as the leader of the three worlds. For indeed, [this fruit] is preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful...
The Blessed One is the supreme among all beings because he is intent upon providing benefit and happiness without remainder; because of his unsurpassed perfection of practice;
because of his state of being of ultimate service to the generation including gods and humans; because of his possession of immeasurable and incomparable distinctions of nature and qualities;
and because he serves as the object of unsurpassed veneration for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems.
And he is called the "Protector. By the phrase "skillful... teaching," etc., he shows the purpose of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
For the Blessed One aspired to perfect enlightenment for the sake of ferrying sentient beings across the great flood of saṃsāra;
and that ferrying of sentient beings is accomplished through the excellence of the aforementioned teaching, because it is inseparable from it. By this, [the author shows] the Blessed One’s...
An extraordinary practice for the benefit of others is demonstrated, while the others represent the attainment of one’s own welfare; thus, by means of both,

he illuminates the Blessed One’s status as the fourth among the four types of persons— those practicing for their own welfare and so forth— and thereby illuminates his state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings,
his state of being the supreme object of veneration, and his having become a true field for the act of paying homage.

And here, just as the Great Compassion of the Blessed One is shown by the phrase "the one of great compassion" (*mahākāruṇika*), so too is his Great Wisdom shown by the phrase "the one who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of the knowable" (*ñeyyasāgarapāragū*).

Among these two, by the mention of compassion, the Blessed One’s perfection of all mundane qualities is shown, because it illustrates his uncommon qualities that have attained the state of the sublime (*mahaggata*) among mundane things;
and by the mention of wisdom, [his perfection of supramundane qualities is shown], because it illustrates the knowledge of the path which is the basis for omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
The perfection of all supramundane qualities. The fourth meaning, established by the inclusion of both [compassion and wisdom], is revealed by the word *nātha* (Protector).
By the mention of compassion, he shows the Blessed One’s approach to be free from defilements; by the mention of wisdom, he shows his departure [from the world].
Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, he shows the Blessed One’s activity to be in accordance with worldly convention, because it falls within the domain of worldly discourse.

By the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), [the text] shows the dwelling in the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*); by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), it shows unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Truths, and the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*catu-paṭisambhidā*).

For, through the failure to understand the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena, one oversteps conventional designations (*samaññā*) and engages in the contemplation of beings and so forth. Thus, by the mention of compassion, he demonstrates the abiding in the meditative attainment of great compassion;
by the mention of wisdom, he demonstrates the unobstructed knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths, and the knowledge of the four analytical insights.
The knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence. By the inclusion of "compassion," the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is included;

thus, there are the remaining unique knowledges, the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the unshakable knowledges regarding the eight assemblies, the ten powers, the fourteen Buddha-knowledges, the sixteen modes of knowledge, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
By means of "bases of knowledge" (*ñāṇavatthu*) and so forth, he demonstrates the range of knowledge through the many classifications of wisdom (*paññā*).
Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is the perfection of conduct; by the mention of wisdom, the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā*).

By the mention of compassion, there is lordship over sentient beings; by the mention of wisdom, lordship over the Dhamma. By the mention of compassion, there is the state of being a protector of the world; by the mention of wisdom...

The state of being one’s own refuge. Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is the quality of acting for the welfare of others; by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), there is gratitude. By the mention of compassion, there is the absence of self-affliction;
by the mention of wisdom, there is the absence of self-torment. Or else, by the mention of compassion, there is the accomplishment of the qualities that make a Buddha;
by the mention of wisdom, there is the accomplishment of the state of Buddhahood itself. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, there is the deliverance of others; by the mention of wisdom...
It is itself a deliverance. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, the state of having a mind that favors all beings is shown;

by the mention of wisdom, the state of having a mind detached from all phenomena is shown. Furthermore, among all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion is the beginning because it is the primary cause, and wisdom is the end because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing the beginning and the end, all the qualities of a Buddha [are indicated].
...are shown. Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*) preceded by the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) is shown;
for virtue has compassion as its source, since it proceeds from the abstention from killing and so forth, and that [compassion] is associated with the first three jhānas.

By the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) is shown. And virtue is the beginning of all the qualities of a Buddha, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end.
"Conclusion": In this way, all the Buddha-qualities are shown to be beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, because they are shown by way of method (*nayato*).
For this indeed is the means for showing the Buddha-qualities without remainder, namely, grasping them by way of method;
otherwise, who indeed would be capable of showing the Blessed One’s qualities without remainder, word by word? Therefore he said:
“Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon,
without speaking of anything else, that eon might come to an end after a very long time,

yet the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted. For this very reason, even the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, when questioned regarding the delimitation of the Buddha’s qualities, rejected [the attempt to define them] by saying, “Certainly not, Bhante,” and added, “However, Bhante, the logical sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) is known to me.”
Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief by means of all his qualities of omniscience, he now spoke the words beginning with “Vijjācaraṇasampannā” in order to extol the True Dhamma.
In this context, the phrase “having become endowed with knowledge and conduct” is an elliptical expression (*vacanaseso*).

It is called *vijjā* (knowledge) because it finds (*vindati*) the specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) of phenomena; or alternatively, because it pierces (*vijjhanaṭṭhena*) the mass of greed and so forth.
Knowledge (*vijjā*) is to be understood here first according to its etymological meaning as "that which makes known" the Four Noble Truths.

As for its classification, there are three kinds of knowledge according to the method presented in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*, and eight kinds of knowledge according to the method presented in the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* and others.
They are called "conducts" (*caraṇāni*) because one proceeds by means of them; these are the restraints of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) and so forth.

There are fifteen factors; thus, those who are endowed with these *vijjās* (clear knowledges) and these *caraṇas* (conducts), having attained what was to be attained, are "endowed with clear knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*).

By means of which: by means of that phenomenon acting as an instrument (*karaṇa*) and as a cause (*hetu*). Therein, the meaning of "instrument" should be understood with respect to the phenomenon of the Path (*magga*), because it possesses the state of being the most effective factor in accomplishing the act of deliverance; the meaning of "cause" applies to the phenomenon of Nibbāna, because it possesses the state of being the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

For this meaning of "condition" (paccayattha) is the meaning of "cause" (hetvattha). The meaning of cause is indeed applicable even to the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyattidhamma), because it serves as a cause through a successive lineage.
However, both meanings are possible in the case of the Dhamma that is the fruit (phaladhamma). How so?
Because of the statement, “By that faith which has not yet subsided,” the fruit possesses the function of pacifying and abandoning those defilements that have been eradicated by the Path.

In this manner—namely, by way of being conducive to deliverance (*niyyānānuguṇatā*) and having deliverance as its ultimate end (*niyyānapariyosānatā*)—the sense of the instrumental case may apply to the act of deliverance.

Furthermore, because the insight of the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmimagga-vipassanā*) and so forth serve as decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*), the sense of the causal factor (*hetu*) may also apply.

And this being the case, although the Dhamma consisting of the fruit and the scriptures (*phala-pariyatti-dhamma*) is not grasped as the "peak" (*agga*) and so forth in such discourses as the *Aggappasāda Sutta*, it is nevertheless [grasped] in such texts as the *Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna*.

Because they are grasped as having the quality of leading to safety (*saraṇīyabhāva*), their state of being a refuge (*saraṇabhāva*) is set forth in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* just like that of the Path and Nibbāna.
And here, in particular, it should be understood that only those factors of knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇadhamma*) included within the Path are meant;

for these alone, in the primary sense, are the most effective means for the act of deliverance (*niyyānakiriyā*), and not the others. However, the other factors possess the status of being "leading" (*niyyānatthata*)— [End of excerpt]

...the state of leading out. If this is so, why is it said, "having become perfected in knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampannā hutvā*)? For is it not the case that the attainment of the aforementioned perfection of knowledge and conduct occurs at the very same time as the leading out? This is not a contradiction, because what is intended is precisely their simultaneity, just as in the statement: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. Alternatively, regarding the word *sampannā* (perfected): [it refers to the fact that] at the very moment of emerging from the attainment of cessation, one emerges having attained the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* signifies the state of being endowed with the aforementioned knowledge and conduct. Therefore, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having become perfected in knowledge and conduct. Consequently, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having reached," just as in the expression "having reached the age of sixty years. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having reached the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having acquired," just as in the expression "having acquired the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having acquired the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having accomplished," just as in the expression "having accomplished the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having accomplished the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully realized," just as in the expression "having fully realized the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully realized the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully understood," just as in the expression "having fully understood the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully understood the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully mastered," just as in the expression "having fully mastered the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully mastered the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully penetrated," just as in the expression "having fully penetrated the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully penetrated the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully entered," just as in the expression "having fully entered the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully entered the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully attained," just as in the expression "having fully attained the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully attained the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully established," just as in the expression "having fully established the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully established the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully completed," just as in the expression "having fully completed the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully completed the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully fulfilled," just as in the expression "having fully fulfilled the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully fulfilled the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully perfected," just as in the expression "having fully perfected the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully perfected the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully matured," just as in the expression "having fully matured the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully matured the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully developed," just as in the expression "having fully developed the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully developed the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully cultivated," just as in the expression "having fully cultivated the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully cultivated the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully practiced," just as in the expression "having fully practiced the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully practiced the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully trained," just as in the expression "having fully trained in the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully trained in the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully disciplined," just as in the expression "having fully disciplined oneself in the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully disciplined oneself in the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully purified," just as in the expression "having fully purified the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully purified the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully cleansed," just as in the expression "having fully cleansed the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully cleansed the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully refined," just as in the expression "having fully refined the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully refined the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully polished," just as in the expression "having fully polished the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully polished the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully adorned," just as in the expression "having fully adorned oneself with the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Thus, the meaning is that one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation is one who has emerged having fully adorned oneself with the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *sampannā* is used here in the sense of "having fully embellished
The state of being present in the current time is to be understood here, just as it is with the word "arisen" (*uppanna*) in the phrase "arisen phenomena" (*uppannā dhammā*).
By doing so, the construction of the sentence is established even without the use of ellipsis. Furthermore, the word "by which" (*yena*) should be connected to both contexts:
"by which quality they are endowed with true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampannā*), and by which quality they go forth (*niyyanti*)."
"From the world" means from the world of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth; the meaning is "from the cycle of existence" (*vaṭṭa*).
"That" refers to the Dhamma distinguished as the Path, Nibbāna, the Fruit, and the Teaching. "Supreme" means best. For it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing superior to it.
In this context, the Path is defined by such meanings as the cause of deliverance (*niyyāna*), and Nibbāna by such meanings as escape (*nissaraṇa*) and seclusion (*viveka*).

The excellence of the fruit should be understood in the sense of its being the state of a noble one (ariya-santabhāva) and so forth. This meaning is to be clarified by following such sūtra passages as:
"Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them.

It is called *dhamma* because it supports (*dhāreti*) those who practice according to the instruction, preventing them from falling into the states of misery or into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
The Dhamma. Because he has awakened to all phenomena both correctly and personally, he is the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*);
the Blessed One possesses the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience and the universal eye.

Just as all the qualities of a Buddha are attained precisely through the realization of full enlightenment, so too [are they attained] through correct cultivation, development, frequent practice, right practice, and correct reflection.
By means of a thorough teaching of the Dhamma, through establishing it within the mental continuums of those ready to be trained:
"Monks, I shall teach you noble right concentration. Of paths, the eightfold is supreme.
Monks, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be the foremost among them. It is the one-way path..."

“Monks, this is the path for the purification of beings. Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning”—by these opening words and by way of praise, he is honored, esteemed, and venerated; thus, the connection is that he venerates that Dhamma which is venerated by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: through the attainment of which Dhamma, those endowed with true knowledge (*vijjā*) become...

I pay homage to and praise that supreme and excellent ninefold supramundane Dhamma— along with the Dhamma of the scriptures— which is endowed with the [three] trainings, which leads out from all the suffering of saṃsāra, which is the cause for the Noble Ones’ possession of all virtues,
and which is the cause for the complete escape from suffering; a Dhamma which was honored by the Blessed One himself through such methods as right practice.

And here, by the two phrases, "by which they lead out from the world" and "they are endowed with true knowledge and conduct," the state of the Dhamma as something to be developed and the state of it as something to be realized are stated respectively.

Of these, he praises the Dhamma through the first phrase for its perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā*), and through the second for its perfection of liberation (*vimutti*). Likewise, through the first, [he praises it] for the attainment of meditation (*jhāna*), and through the second...
By means of the perfection of the deliverances: either by the perfection of concentration through the first, and the perfection of attainment through the second;
or by the nature of the knowledge of destruction through the first, and the nature of the knowledge of non-arising through the second.

Alternatively, by the first through its resemblance to lightning, and by the second through its resemblance to a thunderbolt; or by the first through the perfection of dispassion, and by the second through the perfection of cessation.
Thus, he praises the Dhamma by means of its quality of leading out with the first [verse], and its quality of escape with the second;

or by means of its quality of being the cause with the first, and its quality of being unconditioned with the second; or by means of its quality of vision with the first, and its quality of seclusion with the second;
or by means of its quality of supremacy with the first, and its quality of immortality with the second. Alternatively, it is because the first verse demonstrates its quality of leading out.
He praises the Dhamma by way of its being well-expounded through the first [quality], and by way of its being directly visible through the second, because it is to be realized.

Likewise, he praises the Dhamma by way of its being timeless through the former, and by way of its being inviting one to come and see through the latter. Or alternatively, he praises the Dhamma by way of its leading onward through the former, and by way of its being personally verifiable through the latter.
By the term “supreme” (*uttama*), he praises the Dhamma for its perfection through the indication that there is no other superior to it;
by the term “worshipped by the Perfectly Enlightened One” (*sammāsambuddhapūjita*), he praises it for its purity. For its worthiness of worship arises from the removal of all defects.
And through its purity comes the perfection of abandonment, while through its perfection comes the perfection of origin. Through the achievement of abandonment...
And there is the fulfillment of cultivation because of the eradication of faults without remainder;
and there is the actualization of the attainment of the source because there is nothing further to be done beyond that. For it is called "supreme" because it is not shared by others.
Likewise, its aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom—along with the preliminary virtue and so forth—are to be cultivated; and along with that which is to be realized...
The aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those beyond training (*asekkha*) are shown by way of the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

Having thus praised the True Dharma (*saddhamma*) in brief through all its qualities of the True Dharma, he now says "endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth" in order to praise the Noble Saṅgha.
Therein, "endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth" means [endowed] with the qualities of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and so on.

"Endowed" means possessed; or, one whose qualities such as virtue are perfected. For it is the Noble Ones (*ariya*), whose opposites have been destroyed through the abandonment of the defilements to be eliminated by their respective paths, that possess virtues such as virtue which are so thoroughly purified that they deserve to be called "perfected," and not ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*).

This is why the Noble Saṅgha is praised with the words "well-practiced" (*suppaṭipanna*) and so forth. Alternatively, "endowed with the qualities of virtue and so on" means possessing the qualities of virtue and so on in their entirety.

For indeed, through the penetration of the Noble Truths, the aggregates of Dhamma—such as virtue and the rest—reach their fulfillment in the noble persons (ariyapuggala), whether they be trainees (sekha) or those beyond training (asekha), each according to its own capacity.
"Established in the paths and fruits" means established in the paths and in the fruits; the meaning is that he is one who stands in the path and one who stands in the fruit.
The word "ya" (who) indicates the Noble Saṅgha in a general sense, while it should be understood that the word "ta" (that) specifies it.
But is it not the case that within the Noble Saṅgha, not all noble persons are those established on the path (maggaṭṭha), nor are all those established in the fruit (phalaṭṭha)? This is true;
however, he spoke thus by designating the whole through its parts, just as one says, "even powder.
For just as the state of evenness found in the individual components of a medicinal powder is attributed to the whole, saying, "even powder," so too is this said here.

Thus, it should be understood that the state of being established in the paths and fruits, which exists among the noble individuals who constitute the members of the Noble Saṅgha, is designated as "the paths and fruits" when referring to the Noble Saṅgha as a collective whole.

Because he is far removed from defilements, because he does not proceed in what is not the right way, because he proceeds in the right way, and because he is a refuge for the world including the devas, [he is called the Saṅgha].

It is "noble" (*ariya*) because it is to be sought after; it is a "Saṅgha" because it is united by the commonality of view and virtue; thus, being both noble and a Saṅgha, it is the "Noble Saṅgha" (*ariyasaṅgha*), [the object of] that Noble Saṅgha.
Alternatively, it is "merit" (*puñña*) because it purifies one's own continuum (*santāna*) by producing the fruit of becoming worthy of worship;
or it is a "field" (*khetta*) because, like a field such as a rice paddy, it protects (*tāyati*) and preserves the sown seed by providing a place for its growth. The field...
It goes forth to the field (*khetta*); it is called a "field of merit" (*puññakkhetta*) because it is a place of growth by virtue of making the merit of sentient beings bear great fruit.
The connection [in the verse] is with the phrase "he pays homage to the unsurpassed.
And here, by the expression "endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth," he shows that the Noble Saṅgha is the Lord’s "born-after son" (*anujātaputta*).

By this, his perfection of origin is illustrated. With the phrase "established in the paths and fruits," he demonstrates the perfection of abandonment and the perfection of knowledge, because it illustrates the abandonment through the cutting off and the subsiding of the defilements, and because it illustrates the attainment of the knowledge of the paths and fruits.
By the term "the Noble Saṅgha," he demonstrates the perfection of origin, because it illustrates the preeminence of all Saṅghas, including those with devas...
And by the phrase "the unsurpassed field of merit," he shows the world's great benefit to it, because it demonstrates his state as the supreme recipient of offerings.
Likewise, the statement "endowed with the virtues of morality and so forth" demonstrates that the Noble Saṅgha is practicing the right, upright, wise, and proper way.

“Established in the paths and fruits”: although there is multiplicity due to the distinction of mental continua, this indicates the state of the four pairs of persons and the eight types of individuals.
“The Noble Saṅgha”: this indicates its status as one worthy of offerings and so forth. “The unsurpassed field of merit”:
this indicates that it is engaged in practice for the welfare and happiness of the world. Likewise, “established in the paths and fruits” refers to the Noble Saṅgha.
This indicates the presence of his taking refuge in the supramundane; by this, his status as a legitimate son of the Blessed One is demonstrated.

By the phrase “endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth,” the aggregates of Dhamma—virtue and the rest—belonging to both those in training (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha), whose defilements have been destroyed and eliminated without remainder, are shown.
By the phrase “the noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit,” their...
This demonstrates the extreme purity of those very specific qualities mentioned above.

By this, it demonstrates his great majesty, his state as the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), his worthiness of homage, and his status as the field for one’s own act of paying homage.
Furthermore, going for refuge is the beginning of all the qualities of disciples; it is the preliminary practice for those in training (*sekkha*).

It should be understood that all the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha— beginning with the aggregate of virtue and so forth in the middle, and ending with the aggregates of virtue and so forth of those beyond training at the conclusion—
are revealed by this verse as being excellent in the beginning,
middle, and end. Thus, having performed a salutation to the Triple Gem by way of a brief recitation of its entire range of qualities through these three verses:
Now, dedicating that act of prostration toward the intended purpose, he spoke the verse beginning with “Vandanājanitaṃ.
Therein, “vandanājanitaṃ” means produced by way of veneration; the sense is that it was generated by way of praising the qualities of the Triple Gem or by way of prostrating oneself.
“Iti” means thus, in such a manner as “O Greatly Compassionate One,” and so forth.
It is a "jewel" (ratana) in the sense of producing delight—the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha—or else the meaning of "jewel" is the state of being honored and so forth.
For it has been said: "That which is honored and of great value, Incomparable, rare to behold, And enjoyed by beings who are no ordinary— Therefore it is called a 'jewel'."

And qualities such as being "honored" (cittīkata-bhāva) are found only in those beginning with the Buddha and are not shared by others; "the Triple Gem" (ratanattaya) refers to the triad of gems, and [the phrase] "in that Triple Gem" refers to that very triad.
The connection is: "having had obstacles destroyed," meaning having become one for whom calamities have been dispelled.
By this, there is a description of the benefit of that merit, both through the perfection of his own faith and through the perfection of the Triple Gem as its field.
This demonstrates the capacity to strike down harms and calamities. "Everywhere" (*sabbattha*) means in all internal and external bases;
that is the meaning. Alternatively, "everywhere" means at all times—that is to say, at the beginning, middle, and end of this commentary.
"Having been" (*hutvā*) is an action in the prior time; of that [action], it is said: "we shall compose an exposition of the meaning."
By this, the connection [is shown]. "Of that" refers to the merit generated by the homage to the Triple Gem. "By its power" means by its majesty or strength.

Having thus shown the purpose of the homage to the Triple Gem, he now says "The stability," etc., in order to show the difficulty of commenting on the meaning because of the profound nature of the *Nettippakaraṇa*. Therein, "stability" means a state.
"Non-disappearance" means occurrence without interruption. "By one who desires" means by one who wishes, who aspires;
it is said that he aspires thus: "O, may this guide of the True Dhamma endure for a long time!
"For a long time" means for a lengthy period, the sense being a period measuring five thousand years. "Of the guide of the True Dhamma" means of that which is designated as the True Dhamma...

*Nettiyā*. For the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) is a "guide" (*netti*) because it leads the noble qualities (*ariyaguṇa*) into the mental continuums of those to be trained; or, the guide of the True Dhamma is the "Guide to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammanetti*).
Regarding this "Guide to the True Dhamma," this meaning has already been investigated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"By the Elder" (*therena*) means by one endowed with the quality of stability. "Requested" (*abhiyācito*) means requested with reverence and respect, or [requested] face-to-face.
"Requested" means having made it a supreme request. "Or requested with reference to" means having made it a weightier request;
what is meant is that he was thus entreated regarding the commentary on the meaning of the *Netti*: "May the Venerable One compose some commentary on the meaning of the *Netti*.
And here, by one endowed with the aspiration who desires the long endurance of the True Dhamma...

By the verse beginning with “ṭhitiṃ ākaṅkhamānena,” he shows that it was not possible for him to refuse the request of his fellow celibate practitioner—who was endowed with stable virtues within the Dispensation and possessed of reverence and respect—or who had approached him face-to-face and made the entreaty.
“Of the Lord Padumuttara” means of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara. “Passato” means by means of the eye of past lives (pubbenivāsacakkhu).
Or rather, by means of the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*), seeing the resolve as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of one's hand.
"Tādinā" means endowed with the state of being such (*tādibhāva*), or being entirely free from agitation; the words "by our Blessed One" are to be supplied.
"Yassa" refers to the Venerable Elder Mahākaccāna. "Ṭhapito" (placed)—

“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus, in analyzing in detail the meaning of what has been stated in brief: that is to say, Mahākaccāna. Thus he was established [in this rank].

Because they are great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*) by virtue of their excellence in qualities such as morality and the like, they are called the Great Disciples; these are Mahākassapa and the others. This venerable one is one among them, thus he is a Great Disciple. Furthermore, because he is supreme due to his possession of specific qualities, he is the “Supreme among Great Disciples” (*mahāsāvakuttama*).

[He is the master] of the states of mastery—such as adverting and the rest—which are preeminent in the jhānas and so forth, and of the supreme mastery over the mind through noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*).

He has attained mastery because he has realized [the Dhamma]. He has "analyzed the analytical knowledges" (pabhinnapaṭisambhido) because of his possession of the analytical knowledge that has reached a distinguished differentiation regarding meanings and so forth.

He was "praised by the Fully Awakened One" because the Blessed One praised him on many occasions, saying, "Bhikkhus, Mahākaccāna is wise; bhikkhus, Mahākaccāna is of great wisdom," and so forth. Therefore it was said: "And extolled by the Teacher."
"...and esteemed by wise fellow-celibates. "Rejoiced" means:
"Excellent, excellent, Kaccāna! It is well indeed, Kaccāna, that you have spoken this exposition of the Dhamma"—thus was he rejoiced.
It is said that on one occasion this Great Elder was dwelling in the Jambuvanasaṇḍa grove.
He spoke this treatise, adorned with methods of analysis and synthesis, to the bhikkhus who were in his presence.
Having spoken, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side;
there, he presented this treatise exactly as it had been spoken to the Blessed One. Upon hearing it, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation with the words, “Excellent, excellent,” and so forth.
"Therefore, Kaccāna, you should remember this exposition of the Dhamma as the 'Guide to the Dhamma' (Dhammanetti)"—thus they say he gave it that name.
Because all expositions of the Dhamma follow the methods of the "Guides" (Nayas), such as the "Guides to the Teaching" (Desanāhāra) and the "Circulars" (Nandiyāvaṭṭa), he said:
"The commentary on the meaning of the ninefold scripture is forever dependent upon the Dispensation."
“By those of profound knowledge” means by those possessing deep wisdom, not by mere faith;
or alternatively, by the Noble Ones (ariya) who possess great wisdom through their profound knowledge. By the phrase beginning with “Even though,” he demonstrates this meaning:

having recognized the profundity of the subject matter of this treatise and the fact that his own knowledge does not extend far enough into its scope, he shows that although he was sinking at the start of the commentary, the excellence of the qualities of the Dispensation (sāsana) and other supporting conditions (upanissaya) encouraged him.

By the phrase “having entered into all five collections,” it is shown that [this work] enters into and remains within all five great collections (mahānikāya) of the *Netti*, and that it serves as their commentary.

In this context, bringing forward the Pāḷi of the *Peṭakopadesa*—such as the passage beginning “What is the gratification and what is the danger?”—and then here providing the analysis of the meaning of the words regarding the modes of teaching (*desanāhāra*) and so forth, is called “correspondence with the *Peṭaka*. “According to one’s strength” means...

By this he demonstrates his lack of pride, indicating: "It is not easy for me to compose a commentary on the *Netti* in every respect and in all its aspects; however, I shall do so according to the power of my own knowledge.
"Suvisuddhaṃ" means thoroughly purified, [free] from the faults of other sectarian tenets that might have been interpolated here and there.
"Unmixed" (asammissa) is the intended meaning. "Uncrowded" (asaṃkiṇṇa) means not crowded even within its own category by the postulation of other word-meanings and so forth;
it is free from such confusion, unconfused, and well-delimited. It is called "determination" (vinicchaya) because it determines [meanings] in various ways.
"Determination of meanings" (atthavinicchaya) is the determination of meanings. Regarding those meanings that constitute knotty points, it acts in the manner of breaking up the hard soil.
It is "one whose discernment of meaning is subtle" (*nipuṇatthavinicchayo*) because it possesses a refined, delicate, and gentle determination of meaning that dispels doubt as it proceeds.
Alternatively, it is "discernment of meaning" (*atthavinicchayo*) because it discerns the meaning; it is the knowledge whose object is the aforementioned meaning.
It is "one whose discernment of meaning is subtle" because its discernment of meaning is clever and skillful; [he teaches] that discernment of meaning which is subtle. "The occasion" (*samayaṃ*).

The established doctrine (*siddhanta*). This is what is meant: the established doctrine of the Mahāvihāravāsins is, according to the method already described, perfectly pure, unconfused, and characterized by subtle and refined analysis.

Without contradicting that established doctrine, and in conformity with it, I shall provide a commentary on the meaning of the *Nettippakaraṇa*, elucidating the very guide to the Dhamma (*dhammanetti*) proven therein.
"Pramādalekhā" refers to careless readings that arose due to negligence during the later period when the texts were committed to writing after having been wiped clean.

"Vajjetvā" means having removed them. "Sammā niyojayanti" means correctly applying the respective canonical texts (Nettipāḷi) as examples in their respective places within the suttas, or else correctly applying those various suttas known as examples within the commentary on the meaning (Atthasaṃvaṇṇanā).

Correctly applying the Pāḷi to each respective characteristic within the *Nettippakaraṇa* treatise; "Upadesa" refers to the basis (*upanisa*) of the *Netti* and the heart-essence (*hadaya*) of the *Netti*.

That which is the object, established without confusion through the analysis of signs (*nimitta*), consisting of the thirty-three types of *Netti*-terms along with the analysis of their characteristics (*paṭṭhāna-vibhāga*)—that [object] he is "elucidating," meaning making manifest. Of that *Netti*...
The connection is: "I shall compose a commentary on the meaning.
Here, by the phrase "being requested," he shows the cause for the commentary on the meaning;
by the phrase "desiring the long endurance of the true guide of the Dhamma," he shows the purpose; and by the phrase "I shall compose a commentary on the meaning," he shows the summarized meaning.

For the meaning of the treatise (*pakaraṇattha*) being commented upon is the summarized meaning (*piṇḍattha*) of the commentary itself. By the words “relying upon that,” etc., the manner of composition is shown.

Now, directing [the audience] to listen to the commentary, he spoke the concluding verse beginning with “Thus is the meaning. Therein, the word “carefully” (*sakkaccaṃ*) should be applied in both places: “of him who analyzes carefully, listen carefully.
The explanation of the introductory discourse to the text is finished.
In the *Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā*:
"The exposition of the treatise being spoken will shine forth for one who has understood the general meaning of the treatise through knowing the meaning of the words;
therefore, a thorough comprehension of the meaning of the *Netti* terms is appropriate at the beginning. For that purpose, he asks: "In this regard, in what sense..."
"Nettī. Regarding that, "therein therein" means: in that which was stated as "we shall provide a commentary on the meaning of that *Netti*";
the sense is: by what meaning is that *Netti*, for which we have promised to provide a commentary on the meaning, called a *Netti*?
Or alternatively, "therein" refers to this statement "of the *Nettippakaraṇa*": by what meaning is that *Netti* which was mentioned [there] called a *Netti*?

The meaning [of *netti*] is as follows. Since the expression “in the sense of leading” (*nayanatthena*) is a term common to the agent, the instrument, and the locus, he first explains the meaning of the word *netti* by way of the agent-instrument (*kattusādhana*), saying “it leads to the noble Dhamma” (*ariyadhammaṃ nayati*). Now, in order to explain it by way of the instrument-locus (*karaṇādhikaraṇasādhana*), he says:
“They lead by means of it,” and so forth.
For it has been said: "Thus it is stated," because the comprehension of the Suttas is dependent precisely upon the instructions of the *Netti*. In the *Peṭaka*:
"Therefore, by one desiring to attain Nibbāna, the meanings should be sought through that which consists of what has been heard (*sutamaya*); therein, this is the successive order for seeking:
the sixteen modes of conveying (*hāra*), the five methods (*naya*), and the eighteen root-terms. [This is] apart from the investigation of the modes of conveying and the methods.
He said, "The exposition of the meaning of the Sutta is dependent upon the *Netti* instruction," because there is no specific difference in the exposition of its meaning.
This point will be made clear later in the miscellaneous discussion (*pakiṇṇakakathā*). To the question, "Since this *Netti* has such a vast scope, from what does it originate?
he replied, "It originates from the Sutta. By this, he demonstrates that the *Netti* possesses the status of an authoritative standard (*pamāṇabhūta*). And this...
This [work] is intended to demonstrate its dependence upon the *Netti* as its support, not to deny its origin from the Elder.
For the Elder, having plunged into the five great collections (*nikāya*), spoke this treatise—which is a commentary upon them—precisely by relying on them;
therefore, this very quality of being a commentary consists in its dependence upon the dhamma that is to be commented upon.

"By way of the division of the treatise" means by way of the classification of the treatise. For the three sections beginning with the "Exposition of the Modes" (*Hāravicāra*) are the divisions of the *Nettippakaraṇa*;

or alternatively, it refers to the chapters that constitute the treatise itself. For these three are indeed the treatises, which is to say, the three topics beginning with the "Exposition of the Modes.
"By way of the determination of the text" means by way of the arrangement of the recitation.

By the passage beginning with “For the entire meaning of the treatise,” he shows that the section on inclusion (saṅgahavāra) possesses a designation according to its actual meaning (*anvatthasaññata*).
The opponent raises an objection regarding a deviation, saying: “But is it not the case that here the *Paṭṭhāna* is not included?

The other [the author] refutes this with the words “This is not so alone,” etc., showing that although it is not included in its literal form (*sarūpato*), it is nevertheless included by way of its meaning (*atthato*). Again, with the words “For thus,” etc.,...
He makes this same point clearer by means of the Pāḷi. The methods of meaning (*atthanaya*) include the *nandi-vaṭṭa* and others.

The triads of formations (*saṅkhārattika*) include the meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth, as well as the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and so forth. Among these, the mutual inclusion of the methods of meaning will be made clear later.
Furthermore, the wholesome volitions belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) constitute the meritorious volitional formation.
Unwholesome volition is the formation of demerit; wholesome volition pertaining to the formless realm is the formation of the imperturbable.
The formation of merit and the formation of demerit, when proceeding through the door of the body, are bodily formations;

those same [formations], when proceeding through the door of speech, are verbal formations; but when proceeding through the door of the mind, all three types are mental formations. Thus, according to their classification, [they are explained] in the first triad.
The very same factors mentioned in the second triad by way of the doors are also mentioned in the first triad; thus, their mutual inclusion should be understood.
"Where" means in which section. "In the *Peṭaka*" means in the *Peṭakopadesa*. "Assembling" means gathering together by way of commentary.
The phrase "due to the diversity of the methods of phrasing" is a statement of the reason for the assembly of many *hāras* within a single discourse (*sutta*).
For thus the grammarians say: "Sounds are composed of manifold potencies.

By the phrase "not by way of their own form," it is shown that the *Paṭṭhāna* is extracted from its meaning even in the sections on Enumeration (*uddesa*) and Exposition (*niddesa*), just as in the section on Compendium (*saṅgaha*).
Since it is already included by the very mention of the root-terms, let it be so for the Enumeration section; however, regarding the Exposition section:
But how so? It should be understood that even there, by the grasping of the method (*naya*), the root-terms (*mūlapada*) are also grasped;
for no application of the method is possible without the root-terms. Others, however, say:

"Like the *hāra* and *naya*, the *Paṭṭhāna* is not a specific type of commentary on the Sutta, but rather merely the specific qualities—such as being conducive to defilement—that are obtainable in this or that Sutta."

"There is no inclusion of the meanings of the terms for that treatise. And having done so, it is said that among the thirty-three term-meanings of the *Netti*, the *Paṭṭhāna* is not included, nor is it even mentioned in the sections on the Enumeration and the Exposition.
To support the point already stated—that "this is understood from the Canon itself"—he says, "For thus... [etc. ...is brought forth," by which...
He shows that the fact of the Blessed One’s expression of approval is likewise consistent with the Canon (pāḷi), just like the fact of the Elder’s speech.
Anticipating the objection that "the introduction (nidāna) was not stated because it was spoken by a disciple," he says:
"It was spoken by a disciple...," showing that the presence or absence of an introduction is not an absolute criterion for determining whether something was spoken by a disciple or by the Buddha.

There is no reason [to conclude otherwise], because both [the presence and absence of a nidāna] are seen in both cases. Therefore, he shows that the fact that the *Netti* was not spoken by a disciple is not established merely by the absence of a nidāna.
Thus he said: "And for that reason alone those [other texts] are not invalid; it should be understood in the same way here as well.
By the very same reason that the absence of a nidāna establishes the status of being an authoritative source (*pamāṇa*), by that same reason the status of this treatise [is established].
He shows that the status of being an authoritative source (*pamāṇabhāva*) is established by the passage beginning with “And what is called the introduction (*nidāna*)...
Now, by the phrase “Or else,” he states the non-deviating reason through the absence of an introductory statement in the *Netti*. Herein, the formal argument is as follows:

an introduction need not be stated for the *Netti* because it is a commentary on the meaning of the Canon (*pāḷi*). For whatever is a commentary on the meaning of the Canon does not require a statement of its own introduction.
This has been seen in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-niddesa* and other such works.

With the words "This is the classification," etc., this is the conclusion: that the classification of the treatise, which was shown starting from the singlefold division up to the eighty-four thousandfold division, should again be understood by way of the initial method.

In that context, by the phrase "by way of the method beginning with 'therein,'" the word "beginning" (ādi) includes: the description of the states to be directly known; the analysis of the states that are the designations and the things to be designated;
the investigation of the states included within the three planes; the purpose of crossing over the four floods; the abandoning of the five kinds of delight and so forth;
the pacification of the six groups of craving; the inclusion within the seven sections beginning with the section on compendium; and the demonstration of the eradication of the eight wrongnesses.
The inclusion of such [terms] should be understood in this way.
1. Commentary on the Section on Inclusion (*Saṅgahavāra*):
The word *yaṃ*, which is an indefinite pronoun, is used here in the sense of the accusative case. The employment of words is for the purpose of making the meaning understood.

The word *attha* (meaning) alone is dependent on its referent; however, when the subsequent word *iti*—which effects a reversal of the referent—is added, it becomes a word whose referent is sound (*saddapadatthaka*).
Thus, he said: "‘Yaṃ’ is an indefinite indication of the accusative case. This same method applies to such expressions as “*loko* is an indication of the agent,” and so forth.
In this way, the meaning of the verse lines beginning with “*yaṃ*” is shown by way of demonstrating the object, the agent, the action, the non-agent, the qualifier, and so on.
Having thus spoken, he now said, "They are 'worlded' (*lokiyanti*) therein," and so forth, in order to show the meaning of the word by way of its constituent parts.

Here, the word *loka* should be understood as referring to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*) by virtue of its contextual power. Therefore, he said, "by way of being a state suitable for the act of worship.
Worship after the disappearance of the Teaching is to be understood through the arising of other Buddhas, such as the present-day [worship] of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones beginning with Vipassī.

Although the passage beginning with “Dīpaṅkara” was spoken by the Blessed One himself within the *Buddhavaṃsa* teaching, he said, “as the Blessed One spoke when he was Sumedha,” referring to how it occurred in his existence as the wise man Sumedha.

“By the sequence of full understanding” means by the order of the full understandings, such as the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*). “The penetration of characteristics” refers to insight (*vipassanā*).

Therefore it was said: “by means of the doors of emptiness (suññatā), etc. And likewise it was stated by the Blessed One regarding the excellence of the Teaching, because it is to be experienced by the wise:

“Let a wise man come—devoid of deceit, free from guile, upright in nature—I shall instruct him; I shall teach him the Dhamma. Practicing according to the instruction, before long he will realize for himself and see for himself.
Here, the word *yaṃ* refers to the Teaching (*sāsana*), while the word *lokapāla*, though referring to the Teacher, is subordinated to the world; thus [it is said] “of that” (*tassā*).

Having considered the objection as to how the Teacher’s domain can be the subject of a secondary description (*paṭiniddesa*), he said: “And here, ‘with the world-protectors’ (*salokapālo*)” and so forth.

Although the word “world-protector” (*lokapāla*) is subordinate, it is worthy of a secondary description as if it were the primary term; for the sequence of words is one thing, while the sequence of meaning is another.

Out of reverence for the Dhamma, the Blessed One, honoring the Dhamma, did not consider his disciples who were like children to be restrained, but rather [honored it] through the attainment of meditative absorptions and the reviewing of the Dhamma.
"He spent seven times seven days" is said [in the text] as "the Blessed One’s... should be illustrated. Therein, by the word "etc.
(ādi), the inclusion of the disciples' hearing of the Dhamma and their welcoming procession and so forth is to be understood.

"Iccassa" means "iti assa"; thus, by this, there is the illumination of the state of being unobstructed in omniscience through the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma that is non-perverted, free from obstacles, and leading to liberation.

The meaning [of the word *tena*] is as follows: by means of the possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the ten powers (*dasabala*)... [and so forth]... are manifested as being inseparable from that.

Regarding the phrase "the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadhamma*) and so forth," here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Truths, the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), the knowledge that delimits the five destinies (*pañcagati*), the knowledge of the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the seven treasures of the noble ones (*ariyadhana*), and the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
The eight types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*), the unshakable knowledges regarding the eight assemblies, the eight liberations (*vimokkha*),

the nine modes of concentration practice, the nine successive dwellings, the ten qualities that make one a protector, the ten abodes of the noble ones (*ariyavāsa*), the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma,
the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutadhamma*), the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha, the fifteen factors of conduct, and the sixteen modes of knowledge practice.
The sixteen applications of mindfulness regarding inhalation and exhalation; the nineteen kinds of knowledge of reviewing; the twenty-four kinds of knowledge of the analysis of conditions;
the forty-four bases of knowledge; the seventy-seven bases of knowledge; the great diamond-like knowledge that traverses the twenty-four hundred thousand million meditative attainments;
and the knowledges proceeding in the manner of teaching the detailed investigation of the *Paṭṭhāna* with its infinite methods—of such qualities as these did the Blessed One [possess].
The inclusion of specific qualities (guṇa-viśeṣa) is to be understood.

Another method: it illuminates the distinction of qualities; and that distinction of qualities is to be known through Great Compassion (mahā-karuṇā) and Great Wisdom (mahā-prajñā), because by means of these the perfection of the Teacher is accomplished.
Therein, the classification of the activity of Great Compassion is [described] as "for those who see in many ways..."
It should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, beginning with: “Great compassion for beings descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Furthermore, the specific manifestations of great wisdom have already been explained. In this regard, through compassion the Blessed One possesses the perfection of conduct (*caraṇasampatti*);
