through wisdom, he possesses the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjāsampatti*). Through compassion, he has mastery over sentient beings (*sattādhipatitā*); through wisdom, he has mastery over the Dhamma (*dhammādhipatitā*). Through compassion...
Being a lord of the world through wisdom; being self-mastered through wisdom. Being a pioneer through compassion; being grateful through wisdom.

Not tormenting others through compassion; not tormenting oneself through wisdom. The accomplishment of the qualities that make one a Buddha through compassion; the accomplishment of the state of Buddhahood through wisdom.
The ferrying across of others through compassion; the ferrying across of oneself through wisdom. A mind of assistance toward all beings through compassion.
"By means of wisdom, the state of having a mind detached from all phenomena is manifested";

thus, it should be understood that there is a complete fulfillment of both the practice for the benefit of others and the attainment of one's own welfare. "In all three stages" refers to the stages of cause, fruit, and assistance to sentient beings.
"Realization" pertains to the teaching of penetration; "attention" pertains to the teaching of practice; and "cultivation through hearing and so forth" [pertains to the teaching of mastery].
The phrase "of the teaching of the scriptures" (pariyatti-sāsana) should be construed with all three [aspects of the Dispensation]. Therefore he said, "accordingly.

Having stated here, by the expression "with careful preaching of the Dhamma," the worship through preaching common to all three kinds of the True Dhamma (saddhamma) referred to as "the Dispensation," he now analyzes and demonstrates that same [worship] by way of the worship through praise, beginning with: "Noble, O bhikkhus... and so forth.
In this context, the word “sakkaccaṃ” (carefully) should also be construed with the word “thomanena” (by means of praise).
Alternatively, the construction of the words here should be understood by way of both types of worship. “Ariyabhāvādayo” refers to the noble, supreme, and preeminent states, and so forth.
“Niyyānādayo” refers to the causes for deliverance, the vision [of the path], and so forth. “Svākkhātatādayo” refers to being well-expounded, visible here and now, and so forth.

Now, in order to show that the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha are also revealed by this verse, the passage beginning with “yasmā pana” (but because... was stated. “From the transcendence of childhood and so forth” means from the transcendence of the state of being a fool, an immature person, and so on.

“Distinction of knowledge” refers to the knowledges consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. “Distinctions of states” refers to the states of what is to be heard, what is to be attended to, and what is to be penetrated.
“Both” refers to the word as phrasing and the word as meaning. “In both ways” is said in the sense of the instrument and the object.
Each [term] should be applied individually. "Because it is to be practiced" means because it is to be known.
The statement beginning with "And this verse... is the opinion of some. For others say, "This verse was spoken by the Elder himself.
Indeed, even a teaching of the Dhamma directed toward oneself sometimes occurs, as in: "Monks, one endowed with the ten powers... [and so forth].

“The Tathāgata is confident through the four grounds of self-confidence,” and so forth. By doing it in this way, the statement beginning with “Which are the sixteen modes of conveying (hāra)? is justified.

“By means of the very same headings of meaning as stated above” means by the extraction of the meanings designated as the root-terms. “It will follow later” means it will appear at the conclusion of the section on exposition (niddesa) with the words “and the three methods (naya) are not lacking,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “it is said,” he says “he speaks” because it is a designation of the object (kamma-niddesa) in the sense of the agent (kattar). Alternatively, “it is said” is a designation of both the object and the agent (kamma-kattar).

This is the meaning here: if both the strings (*hāra*) and the methods (*naya*) are encompassed—that is, if they are grasped in every respect by the commentator—it is called a "thread" (*sutta*), because it explains the thread itself. By this, he shows that the commentary on the thread is easily accomplished through mastery of the strings and methods.
"By another mode" means by a manner different from what was previously stated as "the Dispensation" (*sāsana*), namely, as "the teaching" (*desanā*) and "that which is taught" (*desita*).

"Having determined" means having ascertained its absolute cognizability. Cognizability (*viññeyyatā*) is the act of knowing found in the words that are cognizable within the distinguished teachings and what is taught.
Since the teachings and what is taught exist solely for the purpose of being known, knowing is primary; thus, in order to specify that very thing, he said: "Therein" means "in that knowing."

Regarding the phrase *etthāha*: the challenger speaks thus with reference to this statement of meaning, namely, "the ninefold teaching and the nine kinds of discourses" (*navaaṅgasāsana-navavidhasuttanta*).
His intention is this: there ought to be a demarcation by means of nine distinct factors that are free from mutual confusion;

and if that were so, then since the Geyya-factor and the others would lack the essential nature of a discourse (*sutta*), the statement that there are "nine kinds of discourses" would be contradicted. Now...
The *geyya* and other factors have the nature of *sutta*. This being so, there would be no separate *sutta*-factor called "sutta";
such being the case, it would follow that the Dispensation consists of eight factors. Therefore he said, "But how... and so forth. By the words "And whatever...

and so on, he shows that if even a few among the *geyya* and other factors were of the nature of *sutta*, the aforementioned fault would not be avoided, let alone if all of them were. "In the compilations" (*saṅgahesu*) means...
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For the current commentaries are called "compendiums" (*saṅgaha*) because they are a summary of the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).

As for what is called "discourse" (*sutta*), it may be either with verses (*sagāthaka*) or without verses (*niggāthaka*); thus, by means of these two factors alone, both are made into a single factor.
Consequently, there is no separate factor of "discourse," because there exists no discourse apart from those two. Therefore, it was said:
“...it would not even be a *sutta*. Furthermore, he says “even somehow it might be,” referring to the general rule (*sāmaññavidhi*) that will be explained.
Showing that this is still a fault even in that case, he says: “of the *Maṅgalasutta* and so forth.
“The cause for its being that” means the cause for its being a limb of *geyya*. The connection is: “the cause for the *Veyyākaraṇa* being that.”

The objector, disregarding the statement "in the absence of a verse," and taking only the bare statement "an answer to a question is an explanation," challenges [the position] with the words "this being so," and so forth.
However, the other [respondent], showing that the rule for what is not an occasion (anokāsa) is stronger than the rule for an occasion (okāsa),
and demonstrating that here it is precisely the explanation devoid of a verse that is intended, says "he does not incur [an offense]," and so forth.

It avoids [the opposite]. "In that way" means for that very reason; the meaning is: even when there is the application of other signs of perception, it is solely due to the powerful nature of the perception of open space.
The commentary on the Section on Compendium is finished.
2. Explanation of the Section on Enumeration (Uddesavāra-vaṇṇanā) 1.
"By way of analysis" means by way of an analysis according to their specific forms. That by which what has not been seen is illuminated is "the illumination of the unseen" (*adiṭṭhajotanā*).
That by which what has been seen is brought into harmony is "the correlation of the seen" (*diṭṭhasaṃsandanā*); and here, "correlation" refers to the making of a determination by means of discussion.
“Doubt is cut by this,” thus it is *vimaticchedanā* (the cutting off of doubt). “An inquiry for consent” (*anumatipucchā*) means an inquiry regarding consent.
For when one asks, “What do you think of that? one is inquiring as to what your consent (*anumati*) is. “Desire to speak” (*kathetukamyatā*) means [the desire] to speak.

Regarding the word *hāra*, it is used according to the functions of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the agent (*kattū*), the state (*bhāva*), and the object (*kamma*), as in the phrase “by these they are carried away,” and so forth.
Having stated the meaning, the phrase beginning with “like necklaces” (*hārā viya*) was spoken in order to show it by way of an analogous application.

Furthermore, just as the words *gantha* and so forth are established in the sense of composing a work and so on, he said “they carry away” (*hārayanti*) and so forth to demonstrate the establishment of the word *hāra* in the sense of making a necklace and so forth.
By the phrase “because of carrying away and because of delighting,” he shows that these specific types of commentary are both captivating (*manoharā*) and delightful (*manoramā*).

"Reasoning that establishes through proof" (*upapattisādhanayutti*) is the cause as a characteristic (*lakkhaṇahetu*). "By the method already stated" refers to following the method explained in the Mode of Conveying the Teaching (*desanāhāra*), beginning with the words: "But are not other [modes] also accompanied by reasoning?

It is stated that a compound of different referents (*aññapadatthasamāsa*) is permissible even for words with different grammatical bases when there is a "grouping of four" therein, just as in the case of *urasiloma* ("hair on the chest") and so forth.
"The rest" refers to such things as: "a synonym is indeed a synonym" (*vevacanaṃ eva vevacanaṃ*).

"Entering into" means they are immersed. "Being concentrated" means they are maintained. "Without conceptual differentiation" means without the conceptualization of the existence of distinct referents for words, such as "birth is a universal," "distinction is a universal," or "relation is a universal.

"By way of the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) and so forth" means by way of the proximate cause, synonyms, cultivation, and abandoning. "Some" refers to those who speak with reference to the proximate cause, requisites, turning back, transformation, description, and penetration.

2. Relation (*sambandha*) means the connection through the state of cause and fruit. For those phenomena that have become thus, their establishment within a single continuum is the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*).
Distinction (*vibhāga*) is the state of having distinct intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) even while they possess the state of cause and fruit; for the cause is indeed one thing and the fruit another.
Absence of activity (*byāpāra*) is the state of being effortless (*nirīhatā*). For it does not occur to the cause and the fruit in this way: "I am producing this," or "By this, I..."
"Reborn. The nature of being a conventional reality (*sammutisabhāva*) consists in the conformity of conditions to the things produced by those conditions, which arises from appropriate fruits;

it is a mere designation established by worldly convention based on aggregates and so forth. The nature of ultimate reality (*paramatthasabhāva*) consists in the characteristics of earth, contact, and so forth, such as hardness and touching.
This, then, is the summary here: that in which, when broken, or when other factors are excluded, there is no such cognition produced by the mind—this [is the conventional].
Conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) is, for example, as it pertains to a jar or water together with its constituent parts; by way of contrast, ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) is the opposite.
"For the penetration of ultimate truth" means for the attainment of Nibbāna.

"Internal" (*anto*) means inside. "By way of the principal factor" means by way of being the root. In such passages as "Delight (*nandī*) is the root of suffering," craving is called "delight. In such passages as "He courses in delight regarding battle," it refers to joy; thus he says, "of craving or of joy."

3. "By way of difference in kind" means by way of the distinction between the wholesome (*kusala*) and the unwholesome (*akusala*). Regarding the word "are joined" (*yujjanti*), it should be understood that the sense of cause (*hetu*) is inherent here;
thus he says "they are joined" (*yojīyanti*). By what are they joined? The intention is: "by the commentators.

Alternatively, "are joined" means they are "connected"; the meaning is that because they possess a common application with those [wholesome and unwholesome states], they are included by the very mention of them, owing to their being of the same class (*tadekaṭṭhabhāva*).

In this context, the instrumental case in "by nine terms" (*navahi padehi*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*), whereas in the previous instance it was used in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, the reading is "ete kho. Here, the particle *kho* should be understood as either a filler (*padapūraṇatā*) or for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇattha*).
"These very ones" means these very things—craving and so forth—and not anything other than these. "Only eighteen, neither more nor less" refers to the former [set].
In the first [alternative], there is an absence of intermediate root-terms; in the second, their neither deficiency nor excess is illustrated.
The commentary on the section of the summary (uddesavāra) is finished.
3. Commentary on the section of the exposition (niddesavāra).

4. In the section on exposition (*niddesa*), "in common" (*sāmaññato*) means generally; "specifically" (*visesenā*) means individually. "Word-meaning" (*padattha*) is the meaning of the term (*saddattha*).

"Characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Sequence" (*kama*) is the serial order. "To this extent" (*ettāvata*) refers to the state of having such a measure. "Cause and so forth" (*hetvādi*) refers to the methods (*naya*) of cause, fruit, plane, proximate cause, similar, and dissimilar characteristics.
Furthermore, specifically, it is connected with the word "characteristic."
**Summary of the Explanation** 1.
Regarding the phrase "That which, monks... (*yaṃ, bhikkhave*): here, *yaṃ* is in the nominative singular;

and since it stands in grammatical apposition with the two terms "pleasure" (*sukha*) and "mental joy" (*somanassa*), it is stated that "it is enjoyed, thus it is gratification (*assāda*); [namely] pleasure and mental joy. This refers to feelings such as pleasure and the like.
“Even so, a desirable object,” he says, because even such things as pleasant forms are to be relished by one who is not free from lust.

Alternatively, “it is relished by means of this, thus it is *assāda* (relishing), namely craving. By this [explanation], he shows that the word “yaṃ” is a particle used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Herein, this is the meaning:
by whatever cause pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon the five aggregates of clinging through their state of being relishable, [that is the cause].

“This gratification, known as craving, is the cause for the act of gratifying. Having established this, he says, “Thus the perversions also,” because this meaning is possible even within the perversions due to their nature of delighting in what is seen and so forth.
By the word “also” (*pi*) in the phrase “even the undesirable” (*aniṭṭham-pi*), it should be connected with “the desirable” (*iṭṭham-pi*);
for all contaminated phenomena (*sāsavā dhammā*) without exception are included here by the mention of the object. Thus he says, “of all...”
"Of the formations belonging to the three planes.

Regarding the phrase "of painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings," here only those feelings that have the nature of suffering are included as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant," because an undesirable object is intended;
it does not refer to those having the nature of pleasure. With reference to this, it was said: "That which, venerable sir..."
“Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling was called ‘peaceful’ and ‘sublime happiness’ by the Blessed One.

By the phrase “because of the existence of a figurative expression for happiness,” he shows that even through the mere fact of being desirable, there can arise for sentient beings a sense of gratification in an object.
“Disadvantage” (*ādīnava*) is so called because it is an outflow of fault (*doṣa*); this should be understood as functioning through oppression. Thus he says: “The disadvantage is suffering...”

“Feeling, or the three kinds of suffering. Having thus shown the meaning of its faultiness as a disadvantage (*ādīnava*), the phrase beginning with “Alternatively” (*atha vā*) is now stated to show its meaning as wretchedness (*kapaṇa*).
“Because of which” (*yato*) means because it has the nature of being both faulty and wretched; this is what is meant. “Emergence” (*nissaraṇa*) means seclusion (*vivitti*);

the meaning is the seclusion from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). “By way of a general designation” (*sāmañña-niddesena*) means by way of the commonality of being expressible by the term “emergence.”

“Of the former” means of the gratification, the danger, and so forth. Regarding the phrase “and the means,” etc., he says “and of the latter” because the word *ca* (and) is used merely for the sake of completing the meter; the meaning is “of the fruit, etc. “Of the various types included therein” refers to the specific qualities comprised within the Noble Path.

Regarding “of the sense-sphere existence, etc.,” by the word “etc.,” not only the fine-material and immaterial existences are included, but also the percipient existence and so forth, as well as the single-aggregate existence and so forth. Therefore, he said: “of each of the three existences.”
"The Blessed One’s teaching is solely for the purpose of final Nibbāna through non-clinging"—with this in mind, he says: "But is it not... [etc. ...accomplished?

By the words "It has already been stated," he raises the objection regarding the fault of tautology. The other, acknowledging this by saying "That is true," then resolves it with the words "And yet...
and so forth. By the phrase "by way of succession," he implies that it is not like internal wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
This shows that the voice of another is the proximate cause for the realization of the Dhamma, because the Dhamma is to be personally experienced.
For it is said: "The Tathāgatas are the proclaimers; those who practice will be liberated; those who meditate are freed from the bonds of Māra.
The cause for that realization would be the cause for realizing the Noble Path. To the question "What, then, is that? he says: "It is the cause for the state of attainment."
By this, he speaks of the perfection of merit that serves as the cause for one’s final existence.
“Having uprooted the view of a self, thus one may cross over death”—this establishes the attainment of the fruit through the preliminary practice of the Noble Path.
For by whatever method the uprooting of the view of a self occurs, there is likewise the crossing over of death.

Thus it is revealed by the word "even so. Regarding the eradication of the view of self and the crossing over to the deathless, there is simply nothing more to be said about their status as the fruit.
However, because the verse beginning with "The Dhamma indeed... speaks of mundane meritorious fruit, he says, "This is the fruit.
That which is to be produced is the fruit; that which produces it is the means. This is the analysis here.
Therefore he said, “By this method,” and so forth. “Perfection of the physical basis” (*upadhisampatti*) means the beauty of one’s personal existence (*attabhāva*).

“Purification” refers here to purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*); thus he said, “In this case too... should be understood. With the words “But because,” and so forth, he makes that same meaning even clearer through another statement.
Those [passages] cited literally: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu [knows] the arising and...”
In such passages as, "One understands, as they really are, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape," these [terms] are mentioned.
They are also mentioned by way of partial inclusion in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, there is much suffering, much despair;
herein the danger is greater; this is the escape from formations, namely, Nibbāna."

They have not been presented in their literal form, as they are in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* and other such discourses. "By way of meaning" means by way of the meanings such as "to be enjoyed" (*assādetabba*) and so forth.
"Not elaborated upon" means not explained in detail. 2.

By the phrase "this same method," the remainder of the statement being examined is indicated through the device of extension (*atidesa*). He uses the suffix *-ta* in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāvattha*), saying: "it has been answered."
"Answer. The intention is that what is found in the Sutta is not [repeated] in the Commentary by way of a commentary on the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*).
Here, "sequence" (*pubbāpara*) refers to conformity with the question; this distinguishes it from the fourfold sequence (*catubyūha-pubbāpara*).

"Connection of the question" (*pucchānusandhi*) means the linking of the answer with the question. In the Commentary, however, it refers to the subsequent teaching occurring as a result of the preceding teaching which served as the occasion for the question.
The connection is stated as the "connection following the question" (*pucchānusandhi*). "In relation to what precedes" means in relation to the words of the question and the response.

Alternatively, by the phrase "of the sutta," it should be understood that the inclusion of the word [“sutta”] also encompasses the remaining categories of the method of investigation (*vicayahāra*), setting aside the question, the response, and the verse-chorus (*anugīti*). In this interpretation, the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse should be regarded as serving merely to complete the meter.
When asked, “Is the eye impermanent? the categorical response, “Yes, the eye is indeed impermanent,” is an answer by way of a single alternative (*ekamsavyākaraṇa*).
When asked, “Should the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) be developed, and should it be realized? the analytical response, “That which is included in the path should be developed;
that which is included in the fruit should be realized,” is an answer by way of analysis (*vibhajjabyākaraṇa*). [The same applies when asked about] the faculty of final knowledge...

When asked, "What is wholesome?"—after counter-questioning, "Is the meaning of 'wholesome' the meaning of 'blameless,' or is it the meaning of 'having a pleasant result'?"—the reply given is an answer by way of counter-question (*paṭipucchābyākaraṇa*).
When it is stated, "The self is eternal, or is it non-eternal?", the failure to give a reply, saying "This has not been declared," and so forth, is setting aside (*ṭhapanā*). [And when asked:
"But are these 'wholesome' and 'dhammas' synonymous, or do they have different meanings?"

This question is with remainder (*sāvasesa*). However, the fact that the answer has a remainder should be understood in terms of the teaching according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

That which lacks a supporting reason (*appaṭihīraka*) is surpassed; that which possesses a supporting reason (*sappāṭihīraka*) is unsurpassed (*niruttara*). The rest is easily understood from the exposition of the "method of investigation" (*vicayahāra*).
And here, the gratification (*assāda*) and so forth should be understood as applying to the causes (*hetu*) as well, starting from "the gratification" up to "the cause of command" (*āṇattihetu*).
Therein, in brief, gratification (assāda) is characterized by pleasure and its conditions; this should be illustrated specifically by the attainment of heavenly realms, for that is its excellence.
However, the remaining forms of worldly success (bhava-sampatti) found here should be understood as following upon that.

Its cause consists of the bases of meritorious action consisting in giving and morality. Disadvantage (ādīnava) is characterized by suffering and its conditions, namely the suffering inherent in change (vipariṇāma-dukkha) and the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha).
By way of its obstruction, the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is also included herein. Specifically, however, it should be understood as the "sphere" (*okāsa*) of sensual desires (*kāma*);
this is to be clarified by means of the basis for defilement (*saṃkilesavatthu*), its transient manifestation, and so forth.

Its cause consists of the ten unwholesome courses of action (*akusalakammapatha*). Renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is the escape; its cause is the preliminary practice (*pubbhāgappaṭipadā*) appropriate and conducive thereto, as the case may be.
The fruit is precisely the fruit of the teaching; its cause is the teaching itself. The means is precisely the aforementioned means;
its cause is the four wheels. The command is the instruction; its causes are the world’s being ablaze with the fire of passion and so forth, and the Teacher’s application of great compassion.
Likewise, among the four noble truths, there is gratification through the truth of origin, danger through the truth of suffering, and escape through the truths of the path and cessation.
The path or the means is the *upāya*; the instruction thereof is the *āṇatti*; the fruit is the *anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*.
Thus, investigation (*vicaya*) should be understood as the act of discerning through the Buddha’s uniquely exalted teaching of the Dhamma, together with its progressive exposition.
The connection between a word and its meaning is the cause (*hetu*), for that is the motive for its occurrence; the desire to know is the cause of the question.
And there is the desire to know. For among the four [types of questions], such as those for the demonstration of the unseen, the former is the desire to know, while for the other, it is the latter.
The answer is the cause of the question. In this way, the same should be stated for the remaining [questions] as appropriate. 3.

Regarding the examination of the suitability or unsuitability of the phrasing and the meaning: by the mention of "phrasing" (*byañjana*), the word (*pada*) is included; by the mention of "meaning" (*attha*), [the sentence is included].

The gratifications and so forth are included along with the questions and so on. Indeed, the very meanings of the mode of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*), when accompanied by distinctions such as what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, constitute the meanings of the modes of connection (*yutti-hāra*) and the rest.
Likewise, those same [meanings], distinguished by the relationship between the basis and that which is based upon it, constitute the meaning of the mode of footing (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*).

Those same [meanings], distinguished by the state of being the characteristic and that which is characterized, and further determined, constitute the meaning of the mode of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*). And those same [meanings], distinguished by the elucidation of etymological derivations and so forth, [constitute the meaning of the mode of derivation].
The Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra) is distinguished by way of similar states and dissimilar states; the Turning (āvaṭṭa-hāra) is distinguished by its turning [of the meaning];
the Analysis (vibhatti-hāra) is distinguished by the classification of planes and so forth; the Reversal (parivattana-hāra) is distinguished by its reversal of opposites;
the Synonym (vevacana-hāra) is distinguished by its synonyms and alternative expressions; and the Source (pabhava-hāra) is distinguished by its demonstration of origins and so forth.

The Mode of Conveying Description is distinguished by its entry through the doors of the aggregates and so forth; the Mode of Conveying Entry is distinguished by its entry via the specific approaches of the aggregates and so forth;

the Mode of Conveying Purification is distinguished by its cleansing of the formulation of questions regarding words and their meanings; the Mode of Conveying Determination is distinguished by its determination of generalities and particularities;

the Mode of Conveying Requisites is distinguished by its equipment with the factors of conditionality; and the Mode of Conveying Coordination is distinguished by its determination of what is to be abandoned and what is to be developed.

Regarding the terms: by stating "the phoneme’s being its own intrinsic expression (*sabhāvaniruttitā*), and the meaning’s not contradicting the discourses (*sutta*) and so forth, its state of being logical (*yuttabhāva*)," he illuminates that the lack of intrinsic expression and the contradiction with the discourses and so forth constitute the state of being illogical (*ayuttabhāva*).
By this, he shows the cause for what is logical and what is illogical.

4. Regarding "appropriate attention and so forth" (*yonisomanasikārādi*), by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he includes the common factors such as hearing the true Dhamma and reliance upon a person of integrity (*sappurisa*).
And it includes the uncommon [factors] such as the object to be given and the recipient. "As appropriate" means in accordance with that particular state (dhamma).
Regarding the phrase "as far as all states," here "all" refers to a partial all (*padesasabba*), not an absolute all (*sabbasabba*).
For this word "all," just as in the first alternative it has a partial scope by way of the states mentioned in the Sutta, so too in the second alternative...
By means of the extraction [of factors] through their respective bases and the bases of those bases, there is a grasping of the phenomena delimited by each specific context;

thus, it has only a partial scope and does not have the entire range of phenomena as its object. The Mode of Conveying Bases (padaṭṭhāna-hāra) is characterized by the extraction of a causal succession, such as:

"Whatever are the bases of the phenomena occurring in the Sutta, and whatever [are the bases] of those... On the other hand, the Mode of Conveying Requisites (parikkhāra-hāra) [concerns] the phenomena occurring in the Sutta...

The characteristic of this [term] is the manifestation of the specific distinctions among the various conditions and their respective causal relations; thus, even though it shares the nature of investigating causes, this is the distinction between the modes of "proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhāna*), "function" (*hāra*), and "requisite" (*parikkhāra*). 5.

Just as in expressions such as "co-referential and identical in word," the term *samāna* has the meaning of "one," so too, in the sense of having a single flavor (*ekarasa*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
In the phrase "of a single arising" (*ekuppādā*) and so forth, the word "single" (*eka*) has the sense of "identical"; thus he says "of identical characteristics" (*samānalakkhaṇā*).

In the expression "by way of commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇanāvasena*), the suffix *-ana* has the sense of the object; the meaning is "by way of being that which is to be commented upon. "Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇā*) means "distinguishing marks.
In such passages as "those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, through non-attention to diverse perceptions," it refers to concomitance.

They are to be understood as follows: first, by inclusion through the mention of perception (*saññā*), for phenomena accompanied by perception are included therein by that very mention of perception. Second, by having a common function (*samānakicca*), as in the passage, “Giving binds one to friends,” and so forth;

for here, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality are also included because they share the same function of binding one to friends, owing to their status as bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
Third, by having a common cause (*samānahetu*), as in the passage, “With contact as condition, feeling [arises],” and so forth.
For just as contact is a condition for feeling by way of being co-nascent and so forth, so too it is a condition for perception and the others;
thus, because they share the same cause, they are mentioned together. For it has been said:
"volition born of the contact of the mind-consciousness element appropriate thereto," and "touched, one perceives; touched, one wills," and so on. Likewise: "with craving as condition, clinging."
Examples such as these should be cited. In passages such as “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” the fact that they share a common fruit should be understood.
For just as volitional formations are the fruit of ignorance, so too are craving, clinging, and the rest; thus, they too are implicitly included therein. Therefore he said:
“In the previous kamma-process existence, delusion is ignorance, the exertion is volitional formations, and the attachment is craving; the approaching is...”

“Grasping. When it is said, “One relishes and delights in form; with that as its object, lust arises,” the associated states such as feeling and so forth are already implied, because they share the same object. For there is no arising of that [lust] without them.
By the phrase “and so forth,” the word “etcetera” (ādi) here includes the force of context, treatise, grammatical gender, proximity to other words, and capability.

The inclusion is to be understood. For even by way of meaning and so forth, a selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is possible in the Sutta regarding things not explicitly stated, just as it is for those that are stated.

"In the manner already mentioned" refers to the manner stated in the Pāḷi as "having a single characteristic in the sense of being a murderer," and so forth, and in the Aṭṭhakathā as "coexistence," and so forth.

6. "Analysis" (*nibbacana*) refers to an etymological derivation (*niddhāraṇa*), such as "contact (*phassa*) is so called in the sense of touching (*phusana*)," and that applies only to a word, not to a sentence; thus he says "analysis of words.
Here, both the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) and the cause (*nidāna*) are to be analyzed by way of the literal expression (*byañjana*) alone.

Since there is nothing further to be said regarding the connections between the preceding and following parts of the etymology, he says: "specifically, by way of the door of the literal expression alone."
“the search for the goal. The motive is the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) and so forth. 7. Regarding the phrase “in the proximate cause” (*padaṭṭhāne*):

this is stated for the purpose of showing that one should select the factors that serve as the causes for the factors mentioned in the Sutta and then apply them by way of similarity and dissimilarity; it is not according to the sequence of the text itself. Therefore, regarding the determination of the proximate cause...
Thus it is established that [the term] is indeed appropriate even without a formal turning back (*āvaṭṭana*).

Alternatively, the "basis of the word" (*padaṭṭhāna*) is the locus for the occurrence of the sound of the word, which is the meaning of the word (*padattha*). In this latter view, regarding the statement, “‘Exert yourselves!

Strive! is the basis of energy (*vīriya*)”, that meaning expressed by the verbal root *ārambha* and so forth is the locus for the occurrence of the word *vīriya*, and is what is denoted by the word *vīriya*.
"Meaning" (attha) is to be understood in this sense. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "The rest" refers to that which is other than what has been mentioned by name;
furthermore, that may either be its opposite or something else. Therefore, he says: "or by not including those that are dissimilar.
"Applying it to the commentary" means by means of the explanation of the meaning, which consists in the determination of the aforementioned dissimilar phenomena.

Connecting it with the text (pāḷi), he said: "The teaching. Regarding the phrase "in the opposite cases," this should be understood as a mere illustration, since the turning [of the mind] is also intended by way of similar factors.
"By way of name" means by way of a common name. However, in the text, [it refers to] "beings fixed in falsehood and those who are unfixed."

Because it has been stated that "the defilements to be abandoned by vision are common to beings," it is said: "by way of the names such as 'to be abandoned by vision,' etc. "By way of the basis" means by way of the continuity of beings (*sattasantāna*). For that [continuity] is intended here as the "basis" (*vatthu*) because it is the locus for the occurrence of phenomena.
Hence he says: "For the worldling and the stream-enterer, sensual lust and ill will are common," and so forth.
“By way of the reverse of what was stated” means by way of name and basis, due to their exclusivity.
For the state of being established in each respective path and fruit, the capacity for those capable, and the incapacity for those incapable, are unique (asādhāraṇā). 9.
Regarding the word “developed” (bhāvite), this is a characteristic mark of the act of developing; there is no intention here to express time, hence he says, “to be developed.”
"Meaning" (*attha*): here, "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means "repetition" (*āsevanā*); furthermore, the word "wholesome" (*kusala*) should be understood as having the sense of "blameless" (*anavajja*).

"From the opposite side" (*paṭipakkhato*) means from the contrary side. By way of a dissimilar example, it is established through contrast (*byatireka*), for this [definition] is grounded in the intended phenomenon.
"Of the meaning of the word" (*padatthassa*) means of the meaning expressed by the word, or of the phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*).
“Placement” (nikkhepa) is the teaching; “origin” (pabhava) is the arising. 12.
By the phrase “the inclusion of even those not mentioned,” he shows that the word *ca* has the sense of a collective inclusion (*avutta-samuccaya*). 13.
By the phrase “those set forth in verse,” he shows that the question should be understood as it appears in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), and not otherwise. Therefore he said:
“‘Expounded by the Buddha and others’: this refers to the meaning that has been undertaken; thus he states the scope for the clarification of that undertaking.
And here, since the clarification of the phrasing is also accomplished by means of the meaning alone, he says again ‘of that meaning.
Alternatively, ‘it has been answered’ refers to the answer; for through the clarification of the answer, there is the clarification of the question.”
"Pañha" refers to a question. "In a verse" (*gāthāyaṃ*) is an elliptical expression; by this it is meant that [the question applies] both in a verse and in the *sutta*, *geyya*, and so forth.

"With reference to which" (*yamārabbha*) means with reference to that virtue (*sīla*) and so on which was taught in the verses and other texts; the meaning is "in regard to that subject. "Was asked" (*pucchitā*) means one who asks, thinking:
"What here is the purity of words? What is the purity of the question? What is the purity of the subject?"
The construction is as follows: having thus posed the question, she proceeds to examine what is pure and what is impure.

Regarding the phrase "it should not be conceptualized": just as in the world people conceptualize or imagine a universal (*sāmañña*) such as "birth is a universal," "division is a universal," or "relation is a universal"—and likewise imagine the particular (*visesa*) which is the opposite of that—so too, it should not be conceptualized in this manner.

The meaning is as follows: when a particular time receives the designation "tomorrow" (*sve*), upon the passing of that day it is designated as "today" (*ajja*), and upon the further passing of that day it is designated as "yesterday" (*hiyyo*); thus, these specific times are of an unstable nature.
Regarding direction as well, [it is said]: "In relation to one limit there is the eastern direction, but in relation to another [limit] there is what is called the western direction," and so forth.

The state of having an unstable nature should be understood. "In view of birth and so forth" means in view of the specific sufferings of birth and so forth. "In view of the truth" means in view of the commonality of being a truth.
Although that which is called "craving" is a common term when considered in view of craving for sense-pleasures and so forth, it becomes a specific term when considered in view of the truth;
it is with reference to such cases that he said, "This same method applies to the origin and the rest as well."
16. “In this” means in this word of the Buddha. Therefore he said, “of that which is comprised within the three trainings,” and so forth.

“According to the literal expression” means as it was stated, understood from the sound, and determined; it does not mean understood through other means of knowledge such as context, chapter, gender, or the proximity of other words.
“Shown according to the meaning” is said with reference to those suttas where only cultivation (bhāvanā) is mentioned, and not abandonment (pahāna).
Commentary on the Summary of Methods (Nayasaṅkhepavaṇṇanā) 17.
[The compound] *saṃkilesapakkho* means "that which has defilement as its side," because it has craving and ignorance acting as its instruments (*karaṇa*).

The construction is: "the characteristic of the method for that meaning of the sutta which belongs to the side of defilement. The connection is with "of the meaning of the sutta belonging to the side of purification" (*vodānapakkhassa*).

The method of grasping that accords with the path—the aspects of comprehension such as the fact that suffering and so forth are to be fully understood—is the method of grasping by means of insight (vipassanā) that is powerful and leads to emergence.

If this is so, one asks: "In what way is it a method? To which he replies: "But of that... and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "the terminology of method," he shows that what is designated as the "method" is the basis for the method.
18. “By way of being subject to sublation, etc. means by way of being subject to sublation, non-origination, non-existence, and non-emancipation.

“By way of the absence of change” means by way of the absence of being non-sublatable, not non-originated, not non-existent, and not non-emancipated. “By way of having the true nature” means by way of having that very nature as its essence. “By way of non-deceptiveness” means by way of not deceiving regarding the state of possessing the noble nature and so forth; the meaning is that it is unerring.

19. *Saṃkiliṭṭhadhammā* means phenomena possessed of defilement (*saṃkilesa*). *Saddhammanayakovidā* means those skilled in the methods of the True Dhamma, such as the method of the Truths and Dependent Origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), or those skilled in the methods of unity (*ekatta*) and so forth.

20. *Atthavissajjanesu* refers both to the answering of questions formulated in the Suttas, such as "These phenomena are wholesome" (*ime dhammā kusalā*), and to the explanatory commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) on their meaning.
By the term "purifying" (*vodāniyā*), it is shown that here "wholesome" (*kusala*) refers to blameless phenomena (*anavajjadhammā*).
This shows that [the intended meaning] is not a result of pleasure. The construction is: "one should examine with the mind for the purpose of applying each respective method of meaning. 21.
If it is of the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*), how can there be no other meaning for it? He says, beginning with "by which," etc., regarding the phenomena that have become the directions.
Because it consists of the states of surveying, examining, and bringing together, the method is termed "conventional" (*vohāra*) and "functional" (*kamma*);
it is not a "referential" (*attha*) method like the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* and others. Thus, it is called the "method of convention" (*vohāranaya*) and the "method of function" (*kammanaya*).
Commentary on the Twelve Terms.
23. "When the word is not finished" means that at the time of pronunciation, the word is incomplete; the sense is that it is unfinished.
For the designation "word" (pada) would apply only when it is finished, not when it consists of mere "syllables" (akkhara)—this is the intended meaning.

Because it is a synonym for "word," it is figuratively (pariyāyena) like something moving or shifting according to its meaning; however, a phoneme (vaṇṇa) is not a synonym in this way. Thus he says, "figuratively."

Regarding the phrase "because it is indestructible" (*akkharaṇato*), this is said with reference to the specific phonemes such as the letter *a* and so forth, and not to the generality of phonemes (*vaṇṇasāmañña*).
For indeed, the synonym for that [generality] is stated as "they call it a phoneme" (*akkharanti*).

Having explained the meaning of the word *akkhara*, he says "In what sense is it a phoneme? (*kenaṭṭhena vaṇṇo*) and so forth, in order to explain the word *vaṇṇa* as well by way of that same context.

In this context, having in mind the objection that "it is by means of a word or a sentence that the meaning is described, not by means of a syllable," he says, "For it is the description itself," and so forth. "By way of being words, etc. means by way of being words and sentences.
"According to their connection" means according to convention (saṅketa). [The commentary explains: "The word 'this' denotes this meaning; this meaning is what is to be expressed by this word."
The relationship between words and their meanings is the state of being a designator and a designated object, corresponding to the conventional linguistic agreement as it has been grasped.

Alternatively, that which is the mutual inseparability (avinābhāva) between words and their meanings is the connection (sambandha). Corresponding to that [connection], a single-syllable noun-phrase consists of the particle *mā* and so forth, as in the examples "mā evaṃ maññāsi" and others.
"Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri; for they maintain that the teaching of the Abhidhamma is a "teaching by means of the mind."
For this reason, the teacher Rāhula said: "Because it is not expressed by mind or speech, that which is purified compassion is designated as 'syllable' (akkhara) due to its non-articulation.

"Substance-preeminent" (satvappadhāna) means substance-preeminent. For in a noun (*nāmapada*), the substance has a manifested form while the action has an unmanifested form, as in the word "contact" (*phassa*).
In a verb (*ākhyātapada*), however, the action has a manifested form while the substance has an unmanifested form, as in...
“‘Touches’ (phusati): by this, their predominance in the act of touching is stated. It is the cause for grasping a specific action, because it clarifies a specific action;

that is, it is the reason for understanding a specific action, since it illuminates a particular kind of activity. For example, in the phrase ‘one who has been long away’ (cirappavāsi), the prefix *pa-* illuminates the state of being distinguished from the act of dwelling.
[This is also seen] in such passages as ‘attend thus with the mind, do not attend thus with the mind,’ and so forth.”
The word *evaṃ* indicates a particular action; in such cases as “of such virtue, of such nature,” it indicates a particular being.
The intention is that this applies to the remaining particles as well. Therefore he said: “...the particle indicating action...
This was stated in brief; but what is that? He says: “expressed by a word. Or alternatively, it was stated in brief.
That which is said to be "indicated by syllables" (akkharehi saṅkāsito) is that which is expressed by words (padābhihitaṃ), spoken by words (padehi kathitaṃ), and declared by words (padehi pakāsito).

Regarding both of these, if a sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words, what constitutes its limit? They say that as far as the completion of the intended meaning extends, so far it is a single sentence;
many varieties of this are described here. What is the use of those [descriptions]? [A sentence consists of] a verb (*sākhyātaṃ*) together with indeclinables (*sābyayaṃ*).

A "sentence" (vākya) should be understood as that which possesses both an agent (sakāraka) and a qualification (savisesaṇa). Anticipating the objection, "But surely meaning is also manifested by a single word," he says:

"Even when only a word is heard," and so forth. Alternatively, "etymological explanation expressed through modes" (ākārābhihitanibbacana) refers to the etymological analysis stated within the various divisions of sentences. They say that the term "abhihita" (expressed) is what has come down in the Pāḷi text.

The detailed exposition of the etymologies begins with: “It seeks Nibbāna, or it is sought by those seeking Nibbāna, or it goes while slaying the defilements; thus it is the ‘path’ (magga),” and so forth.
He states this meaning as “the exposition (niddesa) because it is a statement of its definition,” explaining that “it is an exposition because it teaches the matter exhaustively.
Or, [the word] “by means of words” (padehi) refers to those which constitute the components of a sentence, when being analyzed from the sentence.
Or [it is] by means of words such as verbs (*ākhyāta*). Therefore he said, "the analysis of a sentence" (*vākyassa vibhāgo*), and likewise he said, "when it is not yet finished," and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that the "form" (*ākāra*) is the analysis of syllables (*akkharavibhāga*) by way of base, suffix, elision, augment, and so on; the "etymology" (*nibbacana*) is the analysis of words (*padavibhāga*) according to the method of derivation (*niruttinaya*);
and the "explanation" (*niddesa*) is the analysis of sentences (*vākyavibhāga*). For phonemes, words, and sentences are both unanalyzed and analyzed.
They say there are "six grammatical cases. "The sixth statement" means the sixth case-ending (*pada*). It should be formulated as follows:
"Syllable, word, phrase, form, likewise etymology, and designation—this is the sixth statement," according to the verse;
or else, by way of commentary, the meaning is that the term *ākāra* (form) should be made the fourth. All verbal usage is [established] through these divisions.
Since there is no other mode [of expression] than these very syllables, phrases, and sentences which have been analyzed, he said, "Those which are these," and so forth.
To show that the word *kāsana* has the sense of an object (*kamma*), it was stated, "It is made known" (*kāsīyati*), and so forth.

While the making known (*saṅkāsanā*) and the revealing (*pakāsanā*) of the meaning may indeed occur by means of phrases, and a commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) is intended to have the phrases as its limit, how then does it occur by means of syllables?
He said: “While the syllables are being heard,” and so forth. “The apprehension of the meaning of the words” means the comprehension of the meaning expressed by the words.

By stating, “He makes it known through the syllables,” and so on, the author indicates that the aforementioned meaning is established by one who speaks of the act of syllable-production as being the manifestation (*saṅkāsanabhūta*) and the act of grasping (*ugghaṭanakiriya*); thus he said, “For in this way,” and so forth.

“Vibhajanuttānīkammapaññatti” (the designation of the act of analyzing and making clear) is a *dvanda* compound, meaning a collective expression of unity (*ekattaniddesa*). “By both” refers to this pair: “vivaraṇā” (explanation) and “vibhajanā” (analysis).
Regarding “by these,” the particle *eva* is indicated as being elided; thus he says, “by these alone. By the phrase “saṅkāsanā... pe ...
abhāvato” (from making known... up to... non-existence), the result of the restriction is shown to be that the intended meaning is neither deficient nor excessive.
It shows [this]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in "the method of concise exposition, etc.," it includes the methods of detailed exposition (*vipañcananaya*).
"Correctly joined" (*sammā yutto*) means correctly, that is, without error, and completely joined—that is, connected. For it has been said: "without deficiency.
Indeed, the entire meaning of the scripture (*pāḷi*) is comprehensively included through the words and the methods of meaning. Therefore he says: "For all... and so forth.
26. But why are the root-terms and the word-bases not included here? Because there is no other meaning for the words.
For this method is shown by the fact that the root-terms are called "word-bases" merely because they are the source from which the methods (nayā) arise. Therefore it was said:
"There is no meaning of the guide's words (nettipadattha) apart from these."

"By means of the *Netti* as the instrumental cause": the "guiding principles" (*hāras*) are to be explained by way of the commentary on the meaning of the Sutta; that is to say, these guiding principles are to be expanded upon according to the method of commenting on the Sutta's meaning.

"This very one": this is the sequence of commentary. By whatever sequence they were taught in the *Netti*, by that same sequence they should be applied here by way of commenting on the meaning of the Sutta.
"Thus established": because it is already established by the very order of the teaching. "This is the undertaking": "The sixteen guiding principles come first."
Thus the undertaking proceeds. "This meaning" refers to this meaning being stated, which is characterized by a fixed rule.

If the methods of exposition (*hāranaya*) were to be applied to the Sutta solely according to the order in which they were taught, would that order be independent of a reason, or rather dependent upon a reason?
And what is the case here? First, if the sequence of the methods of exposition were independent of a reason—
When many meanings are being stated, they must necessarily be stated in some particular order. This being the case, [the sequence] could be applied to the Sutta in any order whatsoever;
if that were so, the fixed rule would be purposeless. Alternatively, if it depends on a reason, what is that reason?
The other [author], without seeking a further reason, intends to show that in this context, the meaning itself is what should be sought.
Having said, "This inquiry does not settle anywhere in a sequential order," and stating,

"But we do not intend to frustrate the wishes of Devānampiya," he establishes the reason for the teaching at the very beginning of the "Food of the Teaching" (desanāhāra) by investigating the purpose, starting with the words "Moreover" (apica). In that context,
the basis for the teaching of the Dhamma consists of the benefits (assāda), the dangers (ādīnava), and the escape (nissaraṇa).

“Body” is the instruction. By its very nature and essence. Even without an explicit extraction (*niddhāraṇa*), because there is no state of being established [otherwise] and because of the state of being a support.
With the words “For he will say,” etc., he makes the meaning as stated more evident. This same method applies to the others as well.

“Immediately after the investigation” means immediately after the mode of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*). The same method applies to the remaining ones as well. “For thus” refers to the analysis of the mode of characteristic (*lakkhaṇa-hāra-vibhaṅga*).

The inclusion of even those [terms] not explicitly mentioned is stated because they possess a single characteristic by virtue of their nature being determined through a succession of reasons regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate.

"Of those determined by way of meaning" refers to the textual teachings (pāḷidhamma) brought into the sutta currently being commented upon, which have been extracted from other suttas according to their meaning— such as the extraction of the subject matter (atthuddhāra),
the sequence of preceding and following passages, and so forth— and which are obtained here both by way of the word and by way of other means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

Because it must be investigated, he says "without remainder. "Of the meaning" (atthassa) means of the referential meaning; "of the phenomenon" (dhammassa) means of the phenomenon as intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
"He directs that [name] here and there" means that he applies that name to each respective meaning and phenomenon, and designates it by saying, "This has such-and-such a name.
By the two terms "of the meaning" and "of the phenomenon," the meaning and the phenomenon are treated in their general sense.
And because it is grasped without remainder, he says "the exhaustive inclusion" (*anavasesapariyādāna*); for this reason it is stated, "in each respective instance.

"In that way" means that just as the exhaustive inclusion—which illuminates the understanding of the meaning without remainder—was formulated in the *Catubyūha-pāḷi*, so too, in the phrase "he enters the womb again and again," the meanings obtained through the mode of occurrence are the "correct practice" (*sammāpaṭipatti*).
The word *tathā* has the sense of a conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
"By that very [means]" is because it serves as the method for turning toward other similar and dissimilar phenomena in order to correlate them with another sutta.

"Since" is because it serves as the method for analyzing common and other characteristics in order to turn toward similar and dissimilar phenomena. "In the case of those whose nature has been analyzed" means...
In their analyzed nature by way of being counterparts.

"Those phenomena" refers to phenomena that have been turned back from their opposites. Since the analysis of the conventional does not grasp the distinctions of designations, he said: "The analysis of the conventional... and easy understanding. The answer is the clearing up of the question;
the explanation of the meaning of the teaching is the clearing up of the undertaking. The investigation of both is [the analysis].
Since this [insight] arises only for one who is not deluded regarding the elements and so forth, he says: "The elements, bases... pe... should be accomplished.
It should be understood that this very same meaning is also expressed by the presentation of the canonical text beginning with "the pure undertaking.

He speaks with reference to the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) as "the mode of the cause" (*kāraṇākāra*). "The mode of teaching" (*desanākāra*) is a synonym for it when analyzed in detail. Having extracted [this meaning],...

"Being spoken of" means being extracted and set forth; this is the intended sense. "For the sake of awakening to the reality of the Sutta's meaning" means for the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths by way of understanding the meaning of the words of the Sutta.
The instruction on the threefold method of meaning is called "employed according to the three types of those to be trained," because it is indeed applied to the three types of those to be trained.
"In the convergence of conditions, one applies the meaning that attains the fruit of that instruction; thus it is said.

"In that very same sequence" means in the sequence of teaching for those [types of persons], such as those who understand by a brief summary (ugghaṭitaññū) and so forth. "Those" refers to the three methods of meaning (atthanaya).
"For them" refers to those such as the ugghaṭitaññū and the rest. Just as the concise, medium, and detailed modes of exposition are beneficial for the three types of persons, so too—
Of those methods of meaning (*atthanaya*). "Of that" means of the method of meaning. "Therein" means in each respective plane.

"Origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) means the causal source (*nidāna*). "In many ways" refers to the method of grammar (*saddanaya*) and the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), thus being of manifold kinds. "Word-meaning" (*padattha*) means the meaning of the term (*saddattha*).
Regarding "prescription" (*vidhi*) and "restatement" (*anuvāda*): here this is the statement of prescription and this is the restatement; such is the distinction to be understood.

"Should be composed" means it should be maintained. "The connection should be brought forth accordingly" means that the commentary should be brought forth in accordance with the sequence of connection by which the subsequent teaching proceeded in the Sutta. "The purpose" is the fruit.
"The summarized meaning" is the concise meaning. "The connection" refers to the connections such as the connection of inquiry and so forth. "The introduction" is the illustration.
"Moving" (*cālana*) means challenging (*codanā*). Its manifestation is the rebuttal (*parihāra*).

"Analytical discourse" (*bhedakathā*) is the explanation that proceeds by breaking down the components of words such as "nature" (*pakati*), for example: "They play (*dibbanti*), therefore they are called 'gods' (*devā*).

"Discourse on reality" (*tatvakathā*) is the explanation of the meaning of a word, for example: "'Buddha' refers to that Blessed One who is self-become and teacherless. "Synonymous expression" (*pariyāyavacana*)...

The inclusion of synonyms is as in the expression, “wisdom is understanding. They are included in the modes of conveying meaning (hāra) such as investigation, the fourfold array, permutation, and partial inclusion, as well as in the mode of conveying synonyms;
thus it is said, “these are here included in several modes of conveying meaning.

A phenomenon (dhamma) is so called because it bears its own fruit; thus the nature of a cause as a phenomenon should be understood. Even indicative causes (ñāpaka-hetu) are [causes] in the sense of being instruments for producing knowledge.
Having included it within the category of the "agent" (*kāraka*), he said: "The agent is twofold: the producer and the accomplisher.
Then, showing that the cause is precisely that which produces the eye-seed and so forth, he said: "Again... it is threefold," and so on.

The non-greed and other factors mentioned in the passage beginning with "Three wholesome roots," as well as greed and the others, are called "causes as causes" (*hetu-hetu*). [As it is said: "Bhikkhus, the four great elements are a cause..."
The "condition-reason" (*paccayahetu*) is that which is stated in such passages as, “the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of form.
Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called the "predominant reason" (*uttamahetu*) with respect to its own result.

The eye and so forth, or the seed and so forth, are called the "specific reason" (*asādhāraṇahetu*) for eye-consciousness, sprouts, and so forth. Although wholesome and unwholesome states are indeed conditions, they are mentioned [separately] in order to show their status as the specific causes for desirable and undesirable results.

The separate mention [of these two] should be understood as being for the purpose of showing that sound and the paths [of communication] function as causes by way of making known and conveying [respectively].
The uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇahetu*) of a sprout and so forth is the "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāgahetu*) because it is a cause belonging to the same class, such as a seed.

The common cause is the "non-homogeneous cause" (*asabhāgahetu*) because it belongs to a different class, such as water, soil, and so forth. That which is bound to the faculties and exists within the continuum is the "internal cause" (*ajjhattikahetu*).
The other is the external cause (*bāhirahetu*). Some, however, say: "That which belongs to one's own continuum is the internal cause (*ajjhattikahetu*);
the other is the external cause. The embracing cause is the supporting cause. The successive cause is the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).
Although *nibbāna* is not subject to production, there is still the state of being attained through the attainment of the abandoning of the origin and the cessation of the origin.
Just as the state of being a cause for the path with respect to Nibbāna is established through figurative usage, so too is the state of being a fruit for Nibbāna with respect to the path;
thus he said, "the designation of 'fruit' is applicable.
The factors of the path belong to the stage of one who is practicing; the factors of the fruit belong to the stage of one who has practiced.
"By function" means by their own essential nature. "By characteristic" means by way of their specific defining marks. "By commonality" means by way of their shared state.

By this, their having a common cause, a common fruit, and a common object is included. Regarding that, whatever needs to be said has already been stated below in the commentary on the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra*).

Furthermore, in this context, the classification of the method (nayavibhāga) should also be understood by way of association, dissociation, contradiction, category, gender, proximity to another word, capacity, and so forth. Therein, first, the classification of the method by way of association is as follows:
“Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that changes so rapidly as the mind. [This is said] regarding the mind.
The term "quickly changing" includes the mental factors as well, because they are associated with that [consciousness], since elsewhere their association with consciousness is demonstrated.

Alternatively, it says "possessing perception. For by the statement that they are accompanied by perception, their possession of feeling, volition, and so forth is also demonstrated through association.

By way of dissociation: they are called "rootless" (*ahetuka*). For since phenomena associated with roots are called "with-roots" (*sahetuka*), it is understood that those phenomena which are the opposite of these are called "rootless" by way of dissociation. Alternatively, they are called "without perception" (*asaññino*).
For it is understood that what is intended here is the occurrence of phenomena dissociated from perception, not the mere absence of perception.
By way of contradiction: when it is said, "the eighth person" or "the faith-follower," the abandonment of the three fetters within that continuity is understood;
likewise, when it is said, "or, with a residue remaining, non-returning," the abandonment of the five lower fetters is understood;
and when it is said, "final knowledge in this very life," the abandonment of all fetters without remainder is understood.

From the point of view of classification (*pakaraṇa*): “unexplained phenomena” (*abyākatā dhammā*). For it is understood from this context that they are not spoken of as being either wholesome or unwholesome. And: “For acquisitions (*upadhī*) are a source of sorrow for a man. It is understood here that external phenomena are intended by the term “acquisitions.

From the point of view of characteristic mark (*liṅga*): “It is affected by cold, and it is affected by heat,” and so forth. For by the inclusion of cold and so on as a characteristic mark, the nature of matter (*rūpa*) belongs only to those phenomena that are of the nature of primary elements and derived matter, and not to anything else.

Due to the proximity of another word: “tranquillity of the body (kāyapassaddhi), the body-base (kāyāyatana). For, because of such statements as “that which belongs to the aggregate of feeling,” the first term *kāya* denotes a collection; the other, due to the proximity of the word *āyatana*, denotes the sensitive matter (*pasāda*).

Due to the force of the context: “All, monks, is aflame; all tremble at the rod,” and likewise, “He dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness…. For here, even though the word *sabba* [is present],...
Because it denotes beings without exception, yet expresses a meaning that is dependent [on a specific context], the word *sabba* (all) is used here in a partial sense;

the word *loka* (world) also denotes beings, for the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) have beings as their object. Likewise, in the phrase "having killed mother and father," the expression is used in its entirety because of the negation [of such acts] and because of the proclamation of the extreme gravity of the kamma of matricide and patricide.
And here, by the mention of their approval, it is understood that certain evil-natured things similar to a mother and father are included for the sake of those to be trained. But who are they?
They are craving (*taṇhā*) and conceit (*māna*). For craving is the mother of beings; thus it is said: "Craving gives birth to man.
Conceit stands in the place of the father, for by depending on it, one grasps at a self-exaltation, thinking, "I am [the son] of so-and-so..."
“...or the son of a royal minister,” and so forth. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “capacity and so forth,” the local custom and other such factors are included.

“By way of determining the meaning of the terms found in each respective discourse” means by way of determining the meaning of the terms such as “satisfaction” (*assāda*) and so on, which are actually present in those various suttas.

“According to the characteristic” (*yathālakkhaṇaṃ*) means according to whichever characteristic [is applicable], or in accordance with the characteristic. [This refers to] cause, fruit, and so forth.
The intention is that [the factors] should be applied after having been examined according to those [individuals].

Now, in order to show which factors such as cause and fruit should be sought with particular emphasis in each method (*hāra*), he says, "But specifically... and so forth. That is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the section of the detailed exposition (*niddesavāra*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Section of Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāravaṇṇanā) 1. Commentary on the Analysis of the Nutriments of Teaching (Desanāhāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 5.
"Anvatthasaññataṃ" means the state of having a name that conforms to its meaning; the meaning is that this designation "nutriment of teaching" is *anvatthā*, that is, it conforms to the meaning.
“Avuttameva” means precisely that which has not been previously commented upon. The passage beginning with “‘Dhammaṃ vo’” was stated in order to show the connection of those words;

for the *Nettippakaraṇa* is the characteristic commentary on the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Piṭakas, and it is already included within the Sutta passages that comprise the Dhamma of the scriptures, since they have been taken as the subject matter to be commented upon.
Therefore he said: “By means of the nutriment of teaching... he shows.
Those aspects such as gratification (assāda) which have the characteristic of being analyzed by the nutriment of teaching are presented in the verse;
and here too, in order to analyze them by way of examples through the passage beginning “gratification, danger,” etc., the section starting with “In this context, what is gratification? is commenced.

Regarding the phrase "therein, therein": in the verse beginning with "the gratification and the danger," what is the gratification (*assāda*) that is mentioned? Alternatively, the meaning is: "In the enumeration of gratification and danger given here by the words 'gratification and danger,' etc., what is the gratification?

This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Of the two types of gratification—which are distinguished by their status as object and subject, and characterized by the relationship between the objective field and the perceiver—[what is the first?]
Two verses were cited for the purpose of illustration; likewise, two verses each were cited for the purpose of illustrating the two kinds of disadvantage—
namely, that characterized by the transformation of sensual pleasures and that characterized by the suffering of saṃsāra—
as well as for the purpose of illustrating the two kinds of escape— namely, the Noble Path and Nibbāna.

Regarding the statement, "Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma": here, for one who lives by Dhamma, there arises a protection that is preeminent through the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.

With the intention that even for those in a state of prosperity, a miserable rebirth is undesirable due to the suffering inherent in change and conditioned formations (*vipariṇāma-saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*), he says, "without taking recourse to the escape [from existence]. For he will likewise say: "In comparison with Nibbāna..."
“All rebirths are miserable states.

The term *avekkhassu* (you should look) is an injunction (*vidhāna*). However, the mode of occurrence, the object, and the agent of that looking are stated by the three words “suññato,” “lokaṃ,” and “mogharājā”;
thus he said: “Suññato... [etc. ...āṇatti. In that context, regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārānaṃ*)—
Emptiness (suññatā) may exist by virtue of the nature of non-self (anattasabhāvatā) and by virtue of being empty of a self (attasuññatā).

Since they are not subject to one's mastery and are devoid of the essence of a self, they are non-self; and since they are void, hollow, and empty of a self, [the text] shows both of these by means of the phrase beginning with "not being subject to mastery" (avasavattitā), and so forth.
"Thus one may cross over death" means that through such practice one may become a crosser of death. This is said of one who acts after having made this supposition.

He says, "The fruit of that... [etc.]... is the fruit," because the teaching on the preliminary practice for crossing over death bears exceedingly abundant fruit as it is being realized through direct experience. 6.

"By way of illustration" means by way of example. Therein, by the phrase "by way of the classification of individuals," he shows that the Blessed One’s specific mode of teaching regarding gratification and so forth is prompted by individuals such as those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and others.

"Merely grasped" means merely taken as an object by the stream of mind-door consciousness following along the ear-door. "Of the mode of eternalism, etc. refers to the mode of eternalism or annihilationism.
For these two are to be set aside during the teaching of the Dhamma, not during the stage of conformity-patience (*anulomikakhanti*) or the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*).
For within this tetrad, there is a commonality of underlying disposition. Indeed, it has been said:
“Eternalism and annihilationism, Conformable patience, And knowledge as it truly is— This is what is termed ‘disposition.
“For the purpose of shaking” means for the purpose of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).

“For the purpose of following others” means for the purpose of eradication (*samucchedana*). “One who knows [the truth] upon being struck [by a brief teaching]” is one who gains knowledge through a concise instruction (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
The grammatical derivation of the word should be understood through the application of the *mūlavibhuja* rule and others.

He says "slowly, gradually" because *vipañcitaṃ* is a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka), as in such expressions as "the moon and sun move unevenly. The discernment of the escape, the disadvantage, and the escape-and-advantage constitutes that which is capable of training the three types of those to be trained.
"Four" refers to these four: gratification (*assāda*), danger (*ādīnava*), both gratification and danger, and gratification and escape (*nissaraṇa*).
If the analysis of escape is capable of training those to be trained, why is a fifth not included? To this he says: "Because of the mention of danger.
For if this method were stated with reference to one who gains knowledge through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*), it would be sufficient by means of escape alone.

Now, should the one who gains knowledge through elaboration (vipañcitaññū) or the one who is led to understanding (neyya) be told of the danger (ādīnava), the escape (nissaraṇa), and the gratification (assāda), or both the danger and the escape?
Because [the teaching] does not proceed in that manner for them, they are not included. Therefore he said, "Because of the non-statement of the danger," and so forth.

As for "teaching" (desanā), which was taken in its general sense, he specifies it as "a portion of a sutta or a verse. And here, the phrase "not grasping the mere word" (padaparama-aggahaṇaṃ) is used.
Because the escape [from suffering] together with its means has not been touched upon.
By the term "wholesome" (kalyāṇa), a desirable result is intended; by "evil" (pāpaka), an undesirable result is intended. Thus he said: "This is the gratification, this is the danger.
Or, considering that gains and so forth are the fruits of merit, he said "this is the gratification" in accordance with that.
It has been said. By way of the opposite of that, the disadvantage of non-gain and so forth should be understood.

"Sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) refers to both sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) together with the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*). "In manifold forms" (*virūparūpena*) means in an unseemly manner. "Crushing" (*mathenti*) means they trample upon [the mind].

"I have gone forth" (*pabbajitomhi*) means I have entered into the life of renunciation. "Infallible" (*apaṇṇaka*) means not subject to failure. "The state of a recluse" (*sāmañña*) means the condition of being a *samaṇa*.
The state of having calmed evil (samitapāpabhāva) alone is better—that is, more excellent.

In this context, “For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful” refers to the gratification (assāda); “They agitate the mind in various forms” refers to the danger (ādīnava); and “The ascetic life is unerring” refers to the escape (nissaraṇa). Thus he said: “This... [and] the escape.
Because the fruits and so forth were presented in the Canon both as single units and as triads, he stated: “Also by way of dyads.”

Regarding the two modes of practice— the pleasant mode of practice and the painful mode of practice— it is said that "the division according to the mode of practice arises from the mode of practice" because each of these two modes is further divided into two by way of sluggish or quick direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). For one who has performed the preliminary duties,
the first application of attention (*pathamasamannāhāra*) is the initial mental engagement occurring with respect to the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, such as "earth," and so on.
“Access” means access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*). Concentration is also called “the way” (*paṭipadā*) because it is that which is to be practiced.
It is called “direct knowledge” (*abhiññā*) in the sense that it is a wisdom superior to the preceding [lower] wisdom.
