“Defilements” refers to the types of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and the defilements associated with them. “Manifestation of the factors” means the acquisition of the jhāna-factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
"Adhering" means establishing [the mind]. "Grasping at the material and immaterial" means grasping the material and immaterial phenomena by delimiting them through their characteristics and so forth.

Since the manifestation of the Path for one who has grasped the material and immaterial might be sluggish due to the difficulty in accomplishing the tasks such as the definition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*), it should not be said that the state of being a "difficult progress" (*dukkhā-paṭipadā*) is due solely to the difficulty of grasping the material and immaterial.

Why? Because the path manifests even when insight—accompanied by the faculties that have been successfully established in such a way—is weak, due to the weakness of the defilements that are adverse to the determination of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, even though those [faculties] were easily established.

"Having discerned the material and immaterial" means having discerned them without difficulty; there is nothing at all to be said regarding what is discerned with difficulty. The same applies to the remaining cases. "Determining mind-and-body": [means...]
While establishing that "this is merely name-and-form; there is no other such thing as a 'being' (satta) and so forth," one asks:

which of these stages is appropriate here? For among the stages of suppression—such as "once," "twice," or "many hundreds of times"—the stages of suppression occurring once or twice are indeed the "pleasant path" (sukhā paṭipadā), but beyond that, it is not a pleasant path.
Therefore, from the third instance of suppression onwards, the practice should be understood as painful.

Furthermore, the practice should be understood as painful because of the difficulty involved in suppressing three times the defilements of insight that arise during the contemplation of rise and fall at the conclusion of the comprehension by groups.
Herein, the practice is called "painful" because of its sluggishness.
Even when this [present practice] is difficult, the fact that the previous practices were difficult is explained by the same method as before.
However, for one for whom there is ease in all respects, it should be understood that their practice is the "supremely excellent easy practice" (*paramukkaṃsagatā sukhā paṭipadā*).
Just as the practice is "difficult and slow in direct knowledge" (*dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*) due to the difficulty of discerning name-and-form and the slowness in the manifestation of the path.
Having explained [the first], he says, "By this... it should be understood," showing that the fourth is to be known by way of its opposite, the second and third by way of their combination.
It is stated that they "belong to the side of insight" because the intended meaning is the emergence from the suffering of saṃsāra.
Regarding the phrase "by way of cause, means, and fruit": herein, being of a craving-temperament and having dull wisdom are the causes for the first path;
being of a craving-temperament and having keen wisdom are the causes for the second; being of a view-temperament and having dull wisdom are the causes for the third;
and being of a view-temperament and having keen wisdom are the causes for the fourth. As for the means, they are respectively the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, energy, and wisdom.

The foundations of mindfulness, jhānas, right efforts, and truths are the supporting conditions (*upanissaya*). The fruit is the departure from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
"By way of concentration" means by way of the application of development through the gateway of concentration. For this very reason he said, "insight preceded by serenity.
"Here" refers to this *Nettippakaraṇa*. He will say: "The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the fruit of the trainee."
“And ‘the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the transcending of the sensual element. Here, “he” refers to the non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
“By that” means by the counteragent (*paṭipakkha*). “From that” means from the counteragent.

Having formed a compound of the terms “liberation of mind” (*cetovimutti*) by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the phrase beginning with “or alternatively” (*atha vā*) was stated in order to express them as having different referents (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*). Again, by the phrase beginning with “or of the mind” (*cetaso vā*), etc.
He shows the compound of the terms for "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) by way of their external referents (*aññapadatthavasena*).
He says "as far as possible" because a construction with the word *ceto* (mind) in the sense of "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) is not possible.
The word *hā-* has the sense of "going"; and since "going" here is intended in the sense of "knowledge-going," he says, "to be abandoned means to be made to go. "To be led" means to be made known.

7. This is the analysis of persons (*puggalavibhāga*). "By way of the analysis of knowledge" means by way of the classification of knowledge such as that consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya*) and so forth.

"Generation" means production. "Therein" refers to the vessel of the teaching, which consists of the analysis of persons beginning with "one who understands through a condensed statement" (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
"In the teaching" means in the Sutta. "To show that" means to show that analysis of persons. "How, then, is this Mode of Conveying (*hāra*)..."
Some read "sambhavati.
"Sā" (it) refers to the wisdom that investigates the aforementioned categories of phenomena. "By way of context" means by way of the context such as "the Teacher teaches the Dhamma," and so forth.

"By way of capability" means by way of the state of being capable of training disciples who are to be trained, such as those who understand through brief exposition (*ugghaṭitaññū*). It is the "retention of the Dhamma of the scriptures."
In this case as well, one should supply and connect the phrase "either by way of subject matter (adhikāra) or by way of capacity (sāmatthiya).
It can be connected according to the method already stated: "By way of the first alternative, it possesses the synonyms of investigation (vīmaṃsā) and so forth;
by way of the second alternative, it possesses the divisions of investigation and so forth; 'consisting of reflection' (cintāmayī) means produced by reflection which serves as its cause," and so on.
He said: "The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Regarding the phrase "in the knowledges consisting of hearing and reflection" (*sutacintāmayañāṇesu*): it should be understood as a *ekadesasarūpekaśeṣa* (a collective singular formed from a part of a group), meaning both in the knowledge consisting of hearing (*sutamayañāṇa*) and in the knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayañāṇa*).
For it is precisely by being established in the knowledge consisting of reflection that the Great Bodhisattvas [attain] their final existence.

They undertake insight meditation (*vipassanā*), while others do so through the knowledge consisting of hearing and reflection (*sutamaya-ñāṇa* and *cintāmaya-ñāṇa*). "By them" means by those who recite [the text] in that manner.

"In the manner stated" refers to the method explained in the discourse on the path (*paṭipadākathā*) beginning with, "He comprehends derived form (*upādārūpa*), he comprehends the formless (*arūpa*)," and so forth. 8.
The intention is that "the voice of another" (*parato ghoso*) is its condition. And "by means of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) arisen within oneself."

It should be understood that this turns [the meaning] a second time by way of repetition (*āvuttinayena*). By this, the arising of knowledge consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa*) for disciples (*sāvaka*) is included.

Or rather, it is the arising of knowledge for disciples alone that is intended here, because of the statement concerning the classification of those who understand through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth.

In this alternative, the method of "one remaining" (*ekasesanaya*) mentioned previously should also be seen as rejected. [The verse continues: “Of the awakening from one’s disposition and application...”

By the phrase "because they have been brought to completion," it is shown that the statement "these two kinds of wisdom exist" was made with reference to the wisdoms consisting of hearing and reflection (*sutamaya-ñāṇa* and *cintāmaya-ñāṇa*), which are included within the latter two wheels and are comprised of prior causes.

Furthermore, their existence should be understood as being unassailed by opposing factors. This is because they are neither neglected nor contrived; this applies even to the wisdom consisting of hearing when it has already been previously established.

"By means of the analysis of knowledge regarding the teaching and the way of practice" means by means of the analysis of teachings such as the teaching on escape (*nissaraṇa*), the analysis of ways of practice such as the painful way of practice (*dukkhā-paṭipadā*), and the analysis of types of knowledge such as knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).

"By the remaining assembly" means by that which is included within the assemblies of khattiyas and householders. "Of eight" refers to these eight: the assembly of khattiyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of recluses, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmas.
"He makes capable" means he makes it capable, that is, he establishes its connection.
The connection is: "having illuminated that very state consisting of twelve factors. Regarding "of its meaning":

because the sixfold exposition (chachakkapariyāya) encompasses all the teachings of the scriptures (pariyatti), and because both that exposition and its meaning are included within the Sutta on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta), it is said:
"clarifying all... [etc.]... by way of analysis. This refers to the literal words (byañjanapada) by virtue of their being the objects [of that meaning].
He says, “the relationship of those... [to] the state of being related,” with reference to the connection between the word-meanings as objects (*visaya*).

Letters (*akkhara*) are the constituents of a word (*padāvayava*). The meaning of a word (*padattha*) is a constituent of the meaning of a word. “Of the grasping of the word-meaning” means of the comprehension of the word-meaning.
“The establishment of a distinction” means the arising of a distinction. “In a difference of sentences” means in a particular sentence. “Satisfying the mind” means pleasing the mind.
The "whetting" (*tejana*) of the sharpening of the intellect (*buddhi*) means making it sharp by means of wisdom (*paññā*).
Furthermore, the fact that [the teaching] has various sentences as its object is established, because the explaining of the meaning is accomplished even through phrases (*pada*) and so forth.

For if there were only the scope of a single sentence, there might be a restriction that the explaining of the meaning of phrases and so on occurs only in relation to syllables (*akkhara*) and the like, respectively. By this—namely, by the sense that the meaning of phrases has various sentences as its object.
“Points for concise and detailed exposition” (*ugghaṭanādi-atthānī*) means the bases for concise, detailed, and mental application exposition.

To show that the word *upaṭṭhita* has the sense of a locus—that which is established there—it is said “the place of establishment” (*upaṭṭhānaṭṭhāna*), just as in the case of the term “well-trodden” (*padakkanta*).
Therefore he says, “This is their...,” and so forth. [The phrase] “by way of practice, teaching, and penetration” (*paṭipatti-desanā-gamanehi*).
By means of the teaching on the progress of practice and its attainment: starting from old age and death with the words, “Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; it is born...

[and so on] unto old age and death,” the Lord of the World—having applied insight by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) to cut through the great thicket of defilements, like one setting an axe upon a whetstone—wielded the axe of knowledge to sever the dense jungle of the afflictions.

Radiating light for the sake of attaining Buddhahood because the perfection of causes had reached maturity, causing the embryo of insight (*vipassanā-gabbha*) to be conceived for the realization of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*),
he entered various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) from time to time; and by means of the insight into phenomena as they arise one after another (*anupada-dhamma-vipassanā*),
he comprehended the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*) in their manifold aspects and bases, and thus exercised that knowledge which proceeds through three hundred and sixty million modes.

They call that "the Great Vajira-knowledge" (*mahāvajirañāṇa*). In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it appears as "the Great Vajira-knowledge that moves through four hundred and twenty-four million attainments" (*samāpatti*);
this is said with reference to the knowledge that precedes and follows the attainments employed on a daily basis.
But that which he will later describe as "the Vajira-knowledge that shatters the net of delusion" refers to the path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) together with insight (*vipassanā*).
It should be understood. To show that "this holy life" (etaṃ brahmacariyaṃ) refers to the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya), he said, "of Brahmā," and so forth.

In the word "desanāya" (by the teaching), this is an instrumental case used in the sense of the instrument. Regarding the word "niyutto" (joined), showing that the sense of cause is inherent here, he said, "having extracted [it], it is joined.
The commentary on the analysis of the nutriment of teaching is finished.
2. Commentary on the Analysis of the String of Investigation (Vicayahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 11.

The investigation of words (*padavicaya*) should be carried out based on differences in sound, such as genus (*jāti*), gender (*liṅga*), tense (*kāla*), grammatical derivation (*sādhana*), case-inflection (*vibhatti*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and so forth.
Demonstrating that when this is performed, it is well-executed only when done according to the natural linguistic usage (*yathāsabhāvanirutti*), [the author] says: "This is a noun-word (*nāmapada*)."
... [and so on] ... Having said, "This is the investigation of the word from the perspective of its sound," he spoke the passage beginning with "But as for that...

*Vattabbatthasaṃvaṇṇanā* (elucidation of the meaning to be expressed) is the explanation that proceeds by first stating the distinctions of the meaning conveyed by each respective word and then unfolding it through synonyms.
*Viciyamānassa suttapadassa* refers to a sutta-word occurring in the form of a question. "Also the words of other suttas... [and so forth].
They say that [these] proceed by way of questions alone, and thus "not every word of the Sutta" is included.

An *atthuddhāra* (extraction of meanings) is the extraction of many possible meanings from a single word. A *paduddhāra* (extraction of words), however, is the extraction of many possible words for a single meaning.
For indeed, all [words and meanings] are obtainable when the Sutta being commented upon is fully considered.
Regarding the phrase *padatthe*: the construction is that he brings together and investigates the ninefold Sutta—meaning the Sutta consisting of nine types, such as the Sutta, Geyya, and so forth.

Alternatively, by means of this method characterized by investigation, expressed as “all ninefold Suttas,” he investigates all nine types of Suttas, including the Sutta, Geyya, and the rest. Therefore, he said, “the Sutta, Geyya, and so forth.”
The fifty-six verses beginning with “*Kosalānaṃ purā rammā*” are the narrative verses (*vatthugāthā*).
However, the nineteen verses beginning with “*Pārāyanamanugāyissan*” are the versified recitations (*anugītigāthā*). As for the name given to it:

this name “*Pārāyana*” was assigned because these teachings are to be traversed to the further shore; therefore he said, “Because these teachings are to be traversed to the further shore, this discourse on the Dhamma is called ‘*Pārāyana*’ indeed.”

“An expression. The construction is as follows: at the time of teaching this analysis of the "Investigation" method (*vicayahāra-vibhaṅga*), the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke thus, having brought it into operation within his own intellect as it was revolving there.

It is "to be answered categorically" (*ekaṃsabyākaraṇīya*) because it belongs to that which is to be answered categorically; or alternatively, it is "to be answered categorically" because it is to be explained with certainty.
The meaning is: "fit for a categorical (ekamsa) answer. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.

"To be set aside" (ṭhapanīya) means it is not to be answered because it must be set aside. He says "the cutting off of doubt" with the intention that the questioner, having encountered uncertainty regarding a matter that is by its nature prohibitive due to familiarity with other systems, asks the question.
However, [it is said] because he does not know that the matter is by its very nature prohibitive.
“He asks out of a desire to know” means that there may also be a question for the purpose of clarifying what has not been seen; for he will say later:
“by one who does not know the world’s obstructions and so forth.
“Grasping a single subject-matter” is because of the apprehension of a single referent meaning.

The faculties that ripen liberation (*vimuttiparipācaka-indriyāni*) are the qualities beginning with faith (*saddhā*) belonging to one who stands on the side of turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭapakkhe*). But why is there an inclusion of these even among the noble ones (*ariya*) within the world of the faculties?

To this he says: "By way of the states included [within the mundane]" (*pariyāpannadhammavasenā*), and so forth. By way of the four factors—namely, the dark fortnight, the fourteenth day, the dense forest thicket, and the covering of the cloud-mass at midnight—he is endowed with the four factors.
"Vivicchā" means doubt (*vicikicchā*). Therefore he says: "Caused by doubt" (*vicikicchāhetū*). Regarding the phrase "Suffering is his great terror": here...
Showing that the word “of him” (*assa*) mentioned [in the previous verse] should be connected by bringing it forward from the phrase “I declare craving to be its smearing,” he said:

“Craving is the smearing of this world. By means of the phrases beginning with “of all beings” and “in every way,” he demonstrates through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*) the preeminent nature of ignorance as an obscuration. “The virtuous shine even from afar...”
It should be understood that even by means of these two verses beginning with “The impassioned does not know the goal,” the investigation of the *anugīti* (repeated verses) is shown.

“Those of the fine-material sphere” (*rūpāvacara*) refers to beings of the fine-material sphere. The connection is: “a statement of the cause for liberation from the suffering of change” (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*).

Liberation is from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*); that suffering of the round is [liberated] by way of grasping the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) through the complete exhaustion of them without remainder.
“Having a single basis” means having a single object or foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

Because two meanings—namely, *nivāraṇa* (obstructing) and *samuccheda* (cutting off)—as well as *vikkhambhana* (suppressing) and *pidhāna* (covering)—have been questioned, it was said, “in order to show that they have multiple bases. Therefore he said: “The restraint known as *nivāraṇa*...
[and so on] ...they are covered and cut off. The meaning of this is: “the suppression known as *nivāraṇa*...”
“Tell me of restraint (saṃvara) and concealment (pidhāna).

By the term “cleansing” (vodāna), the purification by suppression (vikkhambhana-visuddhi) of the taints is intended; by the term “emergence” (vuṭṭhāna), the purification by eradication (samuccheda-visuddhi) is intended.
Thus he said: “In order to reveal that the question has two types of referents, the words beginning with ‘even so’ (eva) were spoken. Likewise:
And he said: "It purifies... [and so on] ...the Noble Path.
Since the streams of views, conceit, and ignorance are also followers of the stream of craving, he said: "mostly by way of inclination.
"By way of proximity" means by way of proximity as a support. "From all" means from every door, from the eye up to the mind. "In every aspect" means...
In such ways as through craving, wrong adherence, and conceit.
"That very mindfulness" refers to that same mindfulness which was described in the preliminary stage as having the function of suppressing the streams [of defilements].
"At the moment of the Path, I call it the restraint and the closing of the streams. For mindfulness, at the moment of the Path, is indeed that which closes them.
They follow after wisdom; here, the function of wisdom alone is predominant, which is why it is said: "by wisdom these two are closed.
Regarding the phrase "by the closing of restraint" (*saṃvarapidhānānaṃ*), the word *saṃvara* here denotes warding off.
In whichever noble path has not yet been attained, whatever formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) is liable to arise—
When each respective [consciousness] is attained, that very consciousness ceases through non-arising and cessation together with the name-and-form associated with itself;
thus it is said: "by the cessation of this and that consciousness, together with...
For here, "cessation" is intended in the sense of "cessation through non-arising," since the Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna) is what is intended. It is linked [to the next section].
"By this" refers to the connection; here, it refers to the matter being asked about.
"Together with the object" means that in this context, the truths themselves are the object.

The truth of origination has the nature of what is to be abandoned, while its object is the truth of suffering. [As it is said: "Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that lead to fetters..."
For it is said: "Craving increases. The Truth of the Path has the nature of abandoning, and the Truth of Cessation is its object;

thus he said, "Together with the object... among the Truths. Although it was begun here [in the Visuddhimagga] that "the origin is abandoned in two planes," it is also stated that "by vision, three fetters are abandoned; by cultivation, seven fetters are abandoned."
However, since only an explanation of the classification is required, he says: "In order to show the classification of what is to be abandoned by way of the classification of what abandons.
It is stated that sensual lust and ill will are abandoned without remainder by the third path, while the others are abandoned by the fourth path;
thus he says, "but the others without remainder. Therein means: in the three realms of existence, distinguished as the round of kamma, its result, and the round of becoming.
"By way of fetters" means by way of always yoking, by way of binding.

Although it is one and the same in its nature as the knowledge of the supreme fruit, it receives two names by way of the conventional designation "fruit," due to the reviewing knowledge which has as its object the destruction and non-arising of those very fetters.
Explaining the meaning of how the attainment of the name "joyful" occurs through this designation for the object, he said: "In the destruction... [etc. ...by way of the designation."
13. "By the inclusion itself" means by the inclusion of the five material faculties with contact as the fifth. "By way of association, etc.

refers both to their being related through conditions such as co-nascence and immediacy, and to their being related as support and object. By the term "associated," it is intended here that there is a state of being conjoined and non-distinct;
thus he says, "with reference to the state of being grasped without differentiation."

Regarding how one arouses the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), it is said: "And here, by the inclusion of mindfulness (*sati*), the abandoning of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) is intended. For the abandoning of obsessions is not possible through concentration alone. It is called *padhāna* because one exerts oneself (*padahati*) by means of it;
it is energy (*vīriya*). "Those" refers to the formations of energy (*vīriyasaṅkhāra*).

"With a single flavor" means that just as the faculties have a single flavor, so too they proceed with a state of single flavor, proceeding in such a way that they are remembered. Precisely through such a proceeding, [it is] well...
“‘It carries the wind-energy’ is said to be ‘gladdening’ (sampahaṃsanā) in the sense of carrying the energy that has approached it, because it is to be intended thus by the yogin.
Therefore he said: ‘In this way for me... [etc. ...by way of being the cause.
The first meaning of the word *iddhi* was stated as the agent (*kattū*), the second as the instrument (*karaṇa*); the word *pāda* has one meaning as the instrument.”
Thus it is. The psychic powers (*iddhi*) are said to be those to be attained, yet they do not actually succeed.

Furthermore, since the powers to be attained cannot stand in grammatical apposition with the "foot" which is the means of attaining them, how can it be rightly said that "by the first meaning, psychic power itself is the foot"?
Likewise, the psychic power consisting of wisdom—which is to be accomplished by performing the act of psychic power—is [to be accomplished] by performing the act of attainment.

If it is asked: "Since the two grammatical instruments cannot have a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatā*), how can it be said that 'the basis of success (*iddhipāda*) is by means of the second sense'?
It is possible, because the basis of success is the state of being the means for the instrument of success in the portion that is being successfully accomplished.
Alternatively, "by the first sense it is the basis of success; by the second sense, success itself is the basis, thus it is the 'basis of success' (*iddhipādo*)."

Thus it is by way of application. How so? Here, by the principle of proximity, the word *paṭhama* (first) is intended to mean the immediately preceding one, and the word *dutiya* (second) refers to the one prior to that.

From the statement, “If a bhikkhu, making desire his dominant influence, attains concentration,” and so forth, [the phrase] “he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with the volitional formation of striving and concentration through desire” should also be understood as *chandādhipati-samādhi* (concentration dominated by desire), following the elision of the word *adhipati*.

It is understood that the compound is stated by way of [the word] *samāsa*. However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated by way of showing the meaning of the word *adhipati* as "concentration caused by desire (*chanda*) or predominant in desire (*chanda*). Therefore, here too, concentration with desire as its dominant factor (*chandādhipati*) should be understood as "concentration of desire" (*chandasamādhi*).
Showing that desire by way of the head of faith (*saddhā*), according to the method already described, he says: "Predominance of faith... (*saddhādhipateyyā*)...
"one-pointedness of mind" is what was stated. Or else, "this is the striving" refers to energy (*vīriya*).

Having spoken of it in the singular along with its associated term "energy," and because all four kinds of energy are intended, it is said "these are formations" (*ime saṅkhārā*) by way of distinguishing the states to be produced.

Thus, the compound should be understood as "formations that constitute striving. Furthermore, here [the word "formations"] is used for the purpose of excluding conditioned formations (*saṅkhatasaṅkhāra*) and so forth.
The term *padhāna* (exertion) is used [here]. Alternatively, it is called *saṅkhāra* because it conditions various specific qualities; thus, it refers to all energy (*vīriya*).

In this context, the inclusion of the word *padhāna* is for the purpose of excluding anything other than that which accomplishes the four functions; the meaning is that they are "exertions" in the sense of being preeminent or supreme.

In the description of the basis of psychic power consisting of energy, the word *vīriya* appears twice in the phrase: "endowed with the volitional formation of exertion consisting of energy-concentration."
It has been brought forward. Therein, the first [term] is a qualification of concentration: "concentration dominated by energy" (*vīriyādhipati samādhi*) is "energy-concentration" (*vīriya-samādhi*).
The second is for the purpose of showing the factors of possession; for in all cases, there are only two factors of possession:

concentration and the volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*). Desire and the others are qualifications of concentration, whereas the volitional formation of striving is [indicated] by the word "striving" itself.
It is distinguished by zeal and so forth; thus, here the predominance of energy (*vīriya*) is not stated as the "determination factor" (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*).
Furthermore, since energy remains as something that has already distinguished concentration, it is expressed by the term "determination factor" in the sense of being a factor of possession;
therefore, neither is the possession of two types of energy stated. However, because it is distinguished by zeal and so forth...
The volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) and the remaining factors are associated with that very same distinguished concentration (*samādhi*).

Therefore, they are called "the four bases of psychic power" (*cattāro iddhipādā*) by way of the distinctions of concentration. And the state of being a distinction occurs for desire and the others through their respective modes of attending (*appaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, in the expression "desire-concentration... base of psychic power," the sense of support (*nissaya-attha*) is also intended.
By the word "foot" (pāda) in the sense of a means (upāya), the status of desire and the other factors as "bases of psychic power" (iddhipāda) is stated.

For thus, in the Abhidhamma, in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*, the status of desire and the others as bases of psychic power is stated by the passage beginning, "The four bases of psychic power: the basis of psychic power consisting of desire," and so forth.
And in the *Pañhāpucchaka*, although it begins with, "The four bases of psychic power: here a bhikkhu [possesses] concentration through desire," it again [speaks of] desire and the others alone.

The state of being wholesome and so forth has been analyzed. Indeed, the demonstration of the basis-foundation (nissaya-iddhipāda) was made precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the means-foundation (upāya-iddhipāda);
otherwise, there would not even be a fourfold division. This is how the determination of the meaning here should be understood according to the text (pāḷi).
Having stated that [the first three] are based on seclusion consisting in partiality, eradication, and escape, [the fourth] is based on seclusion consisting in tranquility (paṭippassaddhi-viveka).

The absence of words [in the sutta]—“he develops the concentration of desire... pe ... the basis of psychic power”—is because the bases of psychic power that are to be developed have already been stated.
For the bases of psychic power included within the fruit are those to be realized by one who has developed the bases of psychic power.
The word *vossagga* has both the sense of relinquishment and the sense of leaping forward; thus, the twofold nature of relinquishment has been stated. According to what was said above...

"In what manner" means in the manner of its eradication by way of substitution (tadaṅga) and in the manner of being inclined toward and taking that as its object. "While transforming" refers to the moment of insight (vipassanā).

"By means of preliminary wisdom" refers to the wisdom of access (upacāra-paññā) occurring in the cognitive processes (vīthi) of either a single adverting consciousness or multiple adverting consciousnesses. "By means of acquired wisdom" refers to absorption wisdom (appanā-paññā).
Again, "by means of preliminary wisdom" refers to the wisdom of access through multiple adverting consciousnesses and the wisdom of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-paññā).
"By means of conventional wisdom (*upacāra-paññā*)" means by means of the conventional wisdom that occurs either in a single moment or throughout all [of its stages].

"The analysis of questions and answers" means the analysis of the answers to the questions as they have been stated. "In accordance with the method already described" means following the method stated below regarding the illumination of what was not seen and the cutting off of doubt.

15. "In the trainee (*sekkha*) and the one beyond training (*asekha*)" refers to noble persons who are trainees and noble persons who are those beyond training. "Abandonment preceded by insight" means the abandonment of defilements occurring after making insight the forerunner; the meaning is "the clear realization of abandonment."

Having shown the canonical text (pāḷi) as “What is impermanent, suffering, and non-self,” he then shows that they recite the statement here as “In what is impermanent, suffering, and non-self” in this way.

“The remaining defiled and purified phenomena” refers to the defiled phenomena remaining after greed, as well as all purified phenomena. “By means of non-existence” means by way of non-becoming or by making [them] non-existent.
“Exertion and striving” (*payogaparakkama*): intense application is *payoga*; exertion itself is *parakkama*; thus, *payogaparakkama* is the mind.
"He throws up" means that, not allowing himself to fall into the side of indolence, he proceeds as if throwing himself upward toward the side of the wholesome.

"Exertion of striving" (*padhānavīriya*) is the supreme energy in the sense of the non-arising of unwholesome states. "Should be applied" means they should be applied by way of the passage beginning with "practicing, he exerts effort.

"Unarisen" refers to those that have reached a state where they cannot be spoken of—namely, those that have not yet attained their plane, whose objects have not been grasped, which have not been suppressed, and which have not been eradicated.

16. Because it is stated, “The faculties of the eighth person,” the phrase “faith and the rest in the first path,” etc., was said. Furthermore, the mention of the “faculties” (indriya) in the Pāḷi should be regarded as merely illustrative.

Since the contemplation of the foul is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body, he said, “By the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, sensual thought is well-restrained.
He spoke thus to show that when concentration arises, it arises only after having restrained even sensual thought.

He says, “by means of the foundation for the happiness of blamelessness,” and so forth. By the passage beginning with “one who has initiated energy regarding wholesome states,” he shows that the desire for energy (*vīriyacchanda*), which arises from the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*), nourishes patience (*khanti*).

Just as the cultivation of helpful qualities occurs through the practice of wisdom (*paññā*), so too does the avoidance of unhelpful qualities; thus he says, “of concentration and so forth,” and so on.

17. To show that the teaching based on all phenomena (*sabbadhammādhiṭṭhāna*) was spoken in order to analyze it by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), he said: "In order to show ‘of all phenomena’... pe ... [the words] beginning with ‘the world,’ etc. Standing upon sublime states (*mahaggatadhamma*) means the very attainment of them.
The same applies to the remaining cases. "While they are increasing" means while they are being brought to maturity in such a way that they ripen liberation.

“Full understanding through seeing” (*dassana-pariññā*) is the thorough knowledge of material and immaterial phenomena by way of their specific characteristics and their conditions. Therefore, he said, “full understanding through knowing” (*ñāta-pariññā*).
Here, “full understanding through developing” (*bhāvanā-pariññā*) is intended as the manifestation of the three characteristics together with the destruction of their opposites;

thus he said, “full understanding through developing... and full understanding. Full understanding for the purpose of seeing is “full understanding through seeing”; [that] for the purpose of developing—
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as "full understanding" (*pariññā*) being "full understanding through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-pariññā*).

"Contact with hardness, etc. means contact with that which is hard, and so forth. "Having fully known" (*abhijānitvā*) means having known by means of higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) or wisdom (*paññā*); the meaning is "for one who stands [in that state], because of having fully known. "Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the fruit (*phala*). "Method" (*naya*) refers to the method already stated. Some also read "that which is unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*).

"Skilled in the four methods" means proficient in the set of four methods such as unity (*ekatta*) and diversity (*nānatta*). "Skilled in the application of teaching" means proficient in the procedure for teaching the Dhamma.
The intention is that they should be made concordant by way of comparison. They should be brought together [with the thought]: "This teaching is thus correlated with this teaching.
"Devoid of meaning" means having an inappropriate meaning. "Having unrelated meanings" means having word-meanings that are not mutually connected. One might raise the objection:
"Is not the investigation of the *Paṭṭhāna* a distinct mode of inquiry, unmixed with the *Hāras*, just like the investigation of the *Nayas*? [Thus] one should take this to mind.

Having done so, he says: "But because... and so forth. "Placed here" means placed here within this *Suttavicaya* (Investigation of the Suttas) due to its nature as an investigation into the meaning of the suttas;

or rather, it should be understood that by this very demonstration of the fact that the *Paṭṭhāna* is included within the *Hāra* (Modes of Conveying), the absence of any distinct meaning for the *Paṭṭhāna* apart from the meaning of its constituent terms is shown, just as in the case of the root-terms (*mūlapada*).

"Of this sutta" is said with reference to the sutta being commented upon. "In which word" is said with reference to the verse being commented upon. "By means of its analysis" refers to analysis by way of questioning and so forth, and analysis by way of gratification and so forth.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Investigation is finished.
3. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Connection (Yuttihāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)

18. Thus, in order to demonstrate the investigation of what is appropriate and inappropriate—namely, the abandoning of meanings that should not be grasped and the grasping of those that should be grasped—it is said:
“The meanings of the Sutta, when grasped in a manner other than they truly are, are the objects [of error],” just as in the case of: “Release the left, [grasp] the right.”
"Take it. For when the meaning of the Sutta has been distinguished from the words of the Sutta by means of what is to be rejected, that which is to be taken remains as a residue.
Thus he will say: "The teaching that 'for one dwelling in loving-kindness, ill-will will persist by obsessing the mind' is not tenable;
the teaching that 'ill-will is abandoned and comes to an end' is tenable."

Having distinguished [the teaching] from what is not its true nature by means of a reasoned analysis (yuttiniddhāraṇa), he speaks of the causes for grasping a phenomenon according to its true nature, saying "Buddha and so forth" and so on, with the meaning:
"Those to whom great authority is to be referred are 'great authorities' (mahāpadesā). "Foundations" (patiṭṭhānāni) means the means of establishing [the teaching].
"In the others" refers to the authority of the Saṅgha and so forth. For it is precisely the primary meaning [of the term *apadesa*] that applies here.

The intention here is that what has come down in the Pāḷi is the "Great Authority" (*mahāpadesa*) as the reason for determination. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "crossing over by means of the Sutta, etc.," crossing over by means of the *Aṇu-sutta* and so forth is also included.

For, in determining whether something is "Dhamma" or not, the crossing over by means of the Sutta and the pointing out of the Vinaya are the reasons for determining a text brought forward by anyone as "Dhamma.
Conversely, the failure to cross over by means of the Sutta and the failure to point out the Vinaya are the reasons for determining it as "non-Dhamma" (*adhamma*).

"If it is thus": if the criterion for determining whether something is "Dhamma" or "non-Dhamma" is whether or not it accords with the Sutta and Vinaya regarding a given matter as it truly is—this being the meaning of "if it is so"—then those by whom the Dhamma is handed down and made known are called "those who hand it down" (sampadāyino).
They are the proclaimers.

It is called *vinaya* because by means of it lust and the other [defilements] are removed; thus, it is the cause. Therefore he said: “the sign for the pacification of lust and so forth. But what is that?

It consists of the teachings such as the foundations of mindfulness (*sati-paṭṭhāna*), the methods of serenity (*samatha*), and insight (*vipassanā*). These are what will later be referred to as “the forty-three factors conducive to enlightenment.

The great authorities of the *Vinaya* are called “conformable to what is allowable” (*anuloma-kappiya*) because they conform to what is permissible. Due to their similarity to those, the great authorities of the *Suttanta* are also conventionally termed in the commentaries “conformable to what is allowable. Hence it was said: “that which is called ‘conformable to what is allowable.’”

Although the miscellaneous teachings of the Blessed One delivered on various occasions constitute the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), it is called the "Teacher’s Tradition" (*Ācariyavāda*) because, after the compilers of the Dhamma had recited the Buddha-word contained in the Three Piṭakas, they established it as a formal oral tradition in accordance with the explanation of its meaning.
Therefore it is said: "The Teacher’s Tradition is the *Aṭṭhakathā*. There were also three councils (*saṅgīti*).
Indeed, the path of discourse consisting of the commentary on the meaning of the Buddha’s word was established later by the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi in the Sinhala language.

This is the Theravāda according to their own judgment. By the phrase "only that which is consistent should be accepted," he shows that meanings should be extracted from the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa) in such a way that they harmonize with the Canon (pāḷi). Regarding the reading resulting from negligence...

Since there may sometimes be a lack of correspondence between the teacher’s doctrine and the Canon, he said, "Only that which accords with the Sutta should be accepted," showing that such [inconsistent] doctrine must not be taken up.
"It is consistent with the four great authorities" means it does not contradict the four great authorities. Now, regarding the manner of that non-contradiction:
In order to show this, the passage beginning with “yena yena” was stated. Here, the very act of crossing over by means of the suttas and so forth is the reason.
And because that [crossing] has many modes, it is expressed as “pakārena” (in various ways). The connection is: that which is to be grasped by way of commentary within the sutta being commented upon.
“Ābhatena” means brought forward. “Suttato” means from another sutta. This is the meaning here: by some occasion, from another sutta...

When a sutta is being commented upon—by means of a textual passage extracted and brought forward, such as for the purpose of crossing over the sutta, and by way of the various modes of reasoning that do not contradict the four great authorities (mahāpadesa)—the various meanings should be grasped according to the method of commentary. Therefore he said: "By that... [etc. ...it should be done.
In that context, "the application of the mode of reasoning should be done" means that this mode of reasoning should be applied by way of determining the logical consistency.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "The application of all the modes [of interpretation] should be made by means of this mode [of interpretation], namely, the Mode of Reasoning (yuttihāra);
having sought the reasoning according to the method that will be explained hereafter, one should apply all the modes by means of that reasoning.

For the Mode of Reasoning is the characteristic mark for the seeking of reasoning; thus he said: "The examination of what is reasonable and unreasonable regarding the ground and the range of all the modes."
“By this reasoning, it should be investigated through various causes.
19. Alternatively, the construction is: “all the terms express a single meaning. 20.

“Alteration in that which is subject to aging”: whatever alteration or change of state belongs to that which is enduring, this is called aging (*jarā*). Momentary death is momentary cessation. Death by total cutting off is the final nirvana of the aggregates for those whose taints are exhausted.
"Kevalassa" means unmixed with aging. "Aging is one thing, death is another"—this is the reason given because "only death, as it was asserted, has been seen.
"As among the gods" is a similar example; however, the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) and so forth are dissimilar examples.
Having grasped the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), these should be applied accordingly.
“By that” means by aging and death.
By the phrase “having the nature of decaying and breaking up,” he joins craving with aging and death as being non-different.
Although it is established that “craving is one thing, aging is another, and death is yet another”—with reference to which it was said: “No...”

Regarding the passage beginning with "idaṃ," although it is thus, the objection is raised for the sake of avoiding what is possible; in order to show the fault that has arisen therein, he says, "If...
[etc. ...he shows," presenting the words as they occur in the Pāḷi: "If... [etc. ...he shows. The meaning is "existence" (bhāva). "Of these" refers to craving, aging, and death.
Some read: “By this reasoning, it should be investigated through mutual causes”;

the intention is that it should also be investigated from the perspective of the phrasing (*byañjana*), meaning that in one place it is [stated] according to the meaning (*attha*) and in another place also according to the phrasing.

To show that very same thing from the perspective of the phrasing in another way, the text says: “Or ‘an arrow’,” and so forth. “Of these” refers to the arrows and the means of their removal. Regarding the perversion of desire (*icchā-vipariyāsa*):

"In the non-attainment of what is desired, or in the presence of lack of confidence. This too is a demonstration, because it shows the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of another meaning intended [by the opponent].
"In the reversal of aging-and-death" means when aging-and-death is absent. For it is not the case that craving does not exist when the intended aging-and-death is absent.
"Stated in two ways" means stated in two modes, or stated twice. "That which is this... [as far as] "...by way of making it an object."
Or, they are called "expressing"; thus it should be understood that the "misapprehension of action" (kriyā-parāmasana) is to be applied [here].
"The distinction" (visesa) refers to the distinction characterized as the nature of these desires and cravings (icchā-taṇhā). There is also a textual reading: "by two names.
Even if this is so, although there is indeed some mere differentiation of desires and cravings according to the specific objects and the aforementioned specific states, [it remains as such].
The meaning is as follows. Showing that there is no difference in terms of intrinsic nature (sabhāva), he said, "Nevertheless" (tathāpi).

"They desire" (icchanti) means they long for. "Craving" (taṇhā) is the state of wishing to manifest. "In the sense of burning" (santāpanaṭṭhena) means by way of consuming. "In the sense of drawing toward" (ākaḍḍhanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of carrying away.
"Moistened" (saritāni) means wet with passion (rāga). "Glossy" (siniddhāni) means through the joy associated with that [passion].
*Siniddhitāni*. *Visattikā*: expanded (*vitthatā*) by way of pervading (*byāpana*) among the phenomena of the three planes, such as form and so forth.
*Visaṭā*: this is merely a synonym for the preceding term, spoken by changing the letter *ta* to *ṭa*. *Visālā*: extensive (*vipulā*). *Visakkati*: it moves about; it endures (*sahati*).
For one who is lustful endures even when struck with the foot, which is the object of that lust. "Moving away" (*osakkanaṃ*).
They say it is "quivering" or "sticking. It is deceptive because it grasps what is impermanent and so forth as permanent and so forth.
"It diverts" means that by showing the advantages of sense pleasures in various ways, it draws back and contracts the mind from its engagement directed toward renunciation.
Alternatively, "visaṃ" means suffering; the meaning is that it carries away or bears that [suffering]. Of that which produces suffering...
Because it is the cause of karma, it has poison as its root (*visamūlā*); or, because painful feelings and so forth are its root, it is "poison-rooted" (*visamūlā*);

because it is the origin of suffering, it has poison as its fruit (*visaphalā*). By means of this [craving], there is only the consumption of suffering such as form and so on, not of the Deathless; thus it is "the consumption of poison" (*visaparibhogā*).
In all these cases, the derivation of the words should be understood according to their etymological analysis (*nirukti*). Furthermore, regarding that which is here...
The primary meaning [is that of craving]; to demonstrate this, it is stated again: "Or else, twentyfold," and so forth. *Sinehanaṃ* means the act of endearing.

"In the sense of binding" means in the sense of fettering (*saṃyojana*). "In the sense of longing" means in the sense of desiring. "In the sense of delighting" means in the sense of relishing, or in the sense of welcoming.

21. *Anabhirati* means dissatisfaction. *Ñāṇanibbidā* means the contemplation of disenchantment. And the construction is to be understood as: "And just as the application regarding suffering... was stated for the [five] aggregates."

[The four types of practice are: easy practice with slow direct knowledge, easy practice with quick direct knowledge, difficult practice with slow [direct knowledge], and difficult practice with quick direct knowledge.

By the passage beginning with "one of lustful temperament," he shows this meaning: for one who is capable of attaining distinction through a difficult practice, a teaching of the Dhamma administered as if it were suitable for one accustomed to an easy practice does not bring about distinction; therefore, that [teaching] is not appropriate.

It should be understood that the text says, "Vipassanā... [etc.]... teaching," in order to show this meaning: for one whose temperament is characterized by passion (*rāgacarita*), if instruction on insight (*vipassanā*) is given from the very beginning without first clarifying the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, as well as the benefits of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), it will not bring about distinction because the underlying disposition has not been purified. This applies to the remaining phrases as well.

Just as the inconsistency of the teaching in the Pāḷi was stated by way of the divisions of those of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) in the passage beginning with "of one of a lustful temperament," so too, according to this method, even in the remaining sections—such as the divisions of those of a hating temperament (*dosacarita*) and so forth—one should determine and state the meaning as it applies, even though it is not explicitly stated in the Pāḷi, such as: "One should teach the foul (*asubha*) to a person of a hating temperament. Why?
However, bearing in mind the objection that the exclusion of what is illogical has already been performed through the method of the "fitting" (yuttihāra), he says, “And here,” and so forth.

The same method applies to the remaining cases as well; that is, this very same approach is to be used when seeking the illogicality among the remaining determinations made by way of the temperament of defilements (dosacarita) and so on.
There is also a textual reading, *anulomappahānaṃ*, which has the same meaning.
By the phrase “as far as the range of knowledge extends,” he demonstrates the vast scope of the Mode of Conveying Logical Reasoning (*yuttihāra*).

Why, then, is this mode of such great scope? Because it consists in the investigation of logical reasoning, and because the Dhamma to be expounded is endowed with specific qualities such as proficiency in various methods;
demonstrating this, he asks, “For what reason? (taṃ kissa hetu).

"In the latter part" means in the subsequent portion. Because it states that the state of abiding in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*) has not been lost, "non-application" (*ayoga*) is mentioned. Therefore he said, "mindful" (*sato*). "Precisely for the reason stated above" means precisely because they are opposites.

Since the conceit of views (*diṭṭhimāna*) is something to be abandoned, those who feel revulsion toward applied thought (*vitakka*) by seeing its danger do not take even the factors of the access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*) near the second jhāna as objects of thought, let alone the factors of the second jhāna itself.
He said, “In this context, the word ‘accompanied’ (sahagata) has the sense of making something an object,” according to the intended meaning (adhippāya).

Having thus demonstrated the investigation of what is logical and what is illogical regarding the characteristic of the ‘Jewel of Reasoning’ (yuttihāra) from the perspective of scripture (āgama), he now says “Furthermore, in this case...
and so forth, in order to demonstrate that same [characteristic] through reasoning (yutti) that follows scripture by analyzing faults by way of their virtues. That [passage] is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the Analysis of the String of Reasoning is finished.
4. Commentary on the Analysis of the String of Footings (Padaṭṭhānahāra): 22.
"Of those and those" is an exhaustive inclusion; by this, it refers both to those phenomena that are stated in the Sutta and to those which belong to them.
It is the cause; this is what is meant by "of all those. To show the meaning of "the non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena," the passage beginning with "But where [is that]? was stated.
"Of a lovable kind" means having a nature that is endearing. "Wrong practice" refers to the transgression of negligence and wrong adherence.
Or: even though the volition of killing has arisen only once, it is a cause for the arising of hatred because it gives birth to enmity;
likewise, even though an offense of negligence or a wrong adherence has arisen only once, it is a cause for the arising of delusion.

Showing that this must be deduced by way of reasoning even if not explicitly stated in the text, he said: "The meaning should be understood by this very method... pe ... of hatred. [This refers to] the characteristic of grasping the sign as an object.
Color and shape are the "sign" (nimitta); the secondary characteristics (anubyañjana) have the characteristic of grasping the meaning [of those signs].

Thus it is said: "having the characteristic of grasping the sign and the secondary characteristics. In this context, the "sign" refers to the signs of a woman or a man. The "secondary characteristics" refer to the hands, feet, smiles, speech, and so forth.

That which has contact as its condition is "conditioned by contact" (phassapaccayā); the state of being that is "the state of being conditioned by contact" (phassapaccayatā). That by which one relishes is "relishing" (assāda); it is craving (taṇhā).
The "bases" are the phenomena to be known; thus it was said: "Non-deviation from the bases is the penetration of the true nature of the object.
To show the right practice intended here, it is stated: "the perfection of virtue and concentration.

In the Canon, the perception of foulness is defined by the mention of the livid and the festering, either by way of illustrating a single aspect or by way of what is suitable for one who is attached to color and fragrance.
Having stated that [disenchantment] is the proximate cause for that [disgust], the passage beginning with "disenchantment" was spoken to demonstrate that disenchantment.

Therein, in order to distinguish it from agitation (*paritassanā*), it is qualified by the word "by means of knowledge. Likewise, "occurring in such a manner" means occurring in the mode of disenchantment.

For Rucā, the daughter of King Videha, who emerged through wise reflection, there arose the knowledge of recollecting past births (*jātissara-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*).
It was the cause, and not reliance upon an unworthy person; it was the fault of that very king’s general, Bījakāla, who emerged from his state with improper reflection.
Demonstrating this point, he said: “And of this... [the example] should be cited.

“That” refers to the confidence (pasāda). “Distinction of state” (avatthāviseso) refers to the differentiation of states characterized by the unperturbed nature of the associated mental factors (sampayuttadhamma).
“Gone to the sense bases” (*āyatanagata*) means gone to the [proper] place; the meaning is that it has become the object of the Three Jewels.

By the words “the body,” etc., he shows the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) as established by its own intrinsic nature, independent of any particular state. And in this passage of the Canon, those phenomena whose proximate causes were previously determined—those phenomena [are now indicated].
It should be understood that the passage beginning with "Another method" is commenced in order to show those phenomena which serve as their proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*).

It should be understood that the attention to gratification (*assādamanasikāra*) has been described as having the characteristic of improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) for the purpose of providing a mere illustration;
or else, it was stated for the purpose of showing that, for the most part, the improper attention of sentient beings arises through the influence of greed (*lobha*).
Thus it was said. *Upapatti* itself is *opapaccaya*; the state of that is *opapaccayika*. Therefore, he said, "by way of the state of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
"Determined state" means the determined state of matter (*rūpa*), due to its function of having specific objects such as seeing and so forth.
"Limbs of existence" means the causes of existence. In the second [case], "limbs" means parts; or alternatively, the round of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*) should be connected by way of being a causal limb.
"Of the meditation subject" means the cultivation, the increase, of meditation. "Among those" refers to being knowledgeable about the watering places (*titthaññutā*) and so forth.
"Also by properly attending upon a good friend" means that through the hearing of the Dhamma obtained by depending on him, there arises joy connected with the Dhamma;

thus, being knowledgeable about the watering places is the proximate cause for being knowledgeable about the watering place [of the Dhamma]. In this way, when there is liberation, there is the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"It is its proximate cause" means that this sense is evident; thus he said, "Of the preceding...

it is indeed easy to understand. "Together with the resolution" means together with the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*). For the full understanding through knowledge is the basis for the full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*).
The rest is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Footings is finished. 5.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra).
23. It was stated: “He asks about the domain of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics. When it is asked, “But what is its domain? [the answer is: those things that possess common characteristics.
Regarding the "unspoken teachings": when body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) has been undertaken, the contemplations of feeling (*vedanānupassanā*) and so forth are accomplished with ease;
thus, by that statement, it is shown that mindfulness directed toward feelings and the rest have already been spoken of.

Since they share a single characteristic by way of being foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the means of accomplishing the foundation of mindfulness of body-contemplation are the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, supported by faith.
This was stated by applying the same principle to the others as well. This meaning will appear later in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself.

In this manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining descriptions of the single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇatā-niddesa*) as well. "Later" refers to the commentary on the *Catubyūha-hāra*.

"Unmixed" means that although feeling and the other [aggregates] are also dependent upon this [body] and rebirth-linking occurs here, the meaning is that [the contemplation] is not mixed with those [other aggregates], even when the occasion for contemplating feeling and so forth in relation to the body arises.

In order to prevent the grasping of a whole, the clinging to a conventional designation, and the adherence to a substantial core, he said, "Thus it is not in the body," and so forth, in order to analyze the body into its limbs and members, those [limbs] into hair and so forth, and hair and so forth into the primary and derived material elements.

Even those who maintain the existence of a whole perform a grasping of a whole with respect to a collection of parts such as a palace or a city; for they think that what is called a "city" is some [single entity].
However, since some might pursue the conventional designation (samaññā) thinking "there is an object," the example of a city was given regarding the pursuit of such designations as "woman" or "man.
[The text asks: "Is there anyone else, such as a 'being' (satta), whom one sees as a woman or a man?
[It replies: "Is it not true that there is no seeing of a woman or a man with the eye? [It continues: "True, there is none; yet one says, 'I see a woman,' or 'I see a man.'"
However, it is said "that which one sees" by way of conventional usage regarding what is currently occurring.
Or, that which one sees through wrong seeing—that is not the visible base (rūpāyatana) as seen; the meaning is that it is not the visible base, or rather, it is not that [visible base].
Alternatively, that aggregate consisting of the primary elements and the derived matter, such as the sheath and so forth, is not "seen"; or else, it is not the "seen" as previously described.

The meaning is "it exists. "What is seen, that he does not see" means that whatever is seen—the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) or the collection of primary elements and derived matter consisting of hair and so forth—he does not see that according to its true nature by means of the eye of wisdom; this is the meaning.

"He does not contemplate other phenomena" means he does not contemplate other intrinsic natures; it is said that he does not contemplate any aspect other than [the aspect of] the foul (*asubha*), and so on.
Regarding "the earth-element body" (*pathavīkāya*): he calls it a "body" (*kāya*) because it is a collection of earth-phenomena such as head-hairs and so forth;

or alternatively, he calls it a "body" by taking the characteristic earth-element itself—which is divided into many varieties and pervades the entire body—as a collective whole existing in a sequential order from front to back. This is also the case elsewhere.
"Of that which is reckoned as a collection of modes" means of the synonym for the aggregate of modes such as impermanence and so forth.
"Defilements in the three realms of existence" means defilements having the three realms of existence as their object. "Beneficial in all respects" means:

(1) desirable benefits when the mind is either sluggish or agitated in any situation; or (2) those factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) which are to be developed and are necessary for one who possesses a mind that is either sluggish or agitated.
"Universal" (sabbatthika). "Internal contraction" (anto-saṅkoca) means shrinking inward; the meaning is laziness (kosajja). 24. "In those that have been grasped":
by the mention of "cultivation" (bhāvanā), they are meant to be grasped; the meaning is "in those that have been cultivated," or else "in those grasped by the word.
However, because the mention of cultivation is for the purpose of illustrating the grasping by the word, the mention of cultivation is primary here in relation to the grasping by the word.

To show this point by means of the designation of their identical characteristics— that it is impossible for one in whom the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānā) have been developed not also to have developed the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā),

such as the right efforts (sammappadhānā) and so forth— the Pāḷi states: "When the four foundations of mindfulness are being developed, the four right efforts reach fulfillment through development," and so on.
The perversions are abandoned because they are the direct opposites [of the truths]. From the statement, “With the arising of nutriment there is the arising of the body;
with the arising of contact there is the arising of feelings; with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness;

with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form,” one understands through the full comprehension of the physical body and so forth that edible food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which constitute the origin of the body and the rest—are the nutriments for the body and so forth.
Showing that they are fully understood through the abandoning of their opposites, he said, "The four nutriments," and so forth.
"In all instances" refers to such passages as, "one becomes non-clinging through clingings.
In that context, because the five strands of sensual pleasure are especially obtained in the body, the body is specifically [the object] of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).

Feeling is the basis for the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), because through the relishing of pleasant feeling, one becomes indifferent to the next world and gives rise to the misconception that "there is no giving" and so forth.

Mind is the basis for the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), because through the grasping at permanence in the mind, there arises the misconception that "purity comes about through one's own virtue and so forth. And it is the actual [basis] for the clinging to self-theory (*attavādupādāna*) by means of the delimitation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
For one who does not see according to reality, the thought "there is a self" constitutes the basis for the clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*); therefore it is said:
"When the four foundations of mindfulness are cultivated, one becomes free from clinging through the various forms of clinging.

Furthermore, in the manner already stated, the body is the basis for the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*), and the craving for existence (*bhavāsava*) arises by way of grasping at pleasure within the realms of existence.
"There is [feeling]" refers to feeling as the bond of becoming (*bhavayoga*). Because of the grasping at a solid continuity, there is the adherence to a self in the mind;

thus, "mind" refers to the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*). Because the analysis of phenomena is difficult to achieve, and because it is hard to penetrate that phenomena are merely phenomena, there is delusion;

thus, "phenomena" refers to the bond of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*). Therefore, by means of the development of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catusatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya*), [these bonds are abandoned].

In those [states], their dissociation from the yokes (*yoga*) is stated because of the accomplishment of their abandonment. By this very fact, their state of being "without taints" (*anāsava*) through the taints (*āsava*), and their having "crossed over" the floods (*ogha*), are also extolled;

for it is precisely lust for sensual pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and the rest that constitute the nature of the yoke of sensual pleasure (*kāmayoga*), the taint of sensual pleasure (*kāmāsava*), the flood of sensual pleasure (*kāmaugha*), and so forth.

In the manner already stated, the body is the basis for the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*); [likewise,] "the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) toward painful feeling..."

“...clings”: feelings that consist of the suffering of suffering (*dukkha-dukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-dukkha*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*) are specifically the basis for the bodily tie of ill-will (*byāpāda-kāya-gantha*).
Because of the adherence to the mind as permanent, there arises the misapprehension (*parāmāsa*) of eternalism such as “Purification comes through virtue,” and so forth;

thus, the mind is the basis for the tie of clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbata-parāmāsa*). Due to the absence of vision regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) together with its conditions, [there arises] what is termed the view of existence and non-existence (*bhava-vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
The phrase "this adherence to 'this is the truth'" should be connected with "the phenomena are its basis," namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.
According to the method already stated, specifically, the body is the basis for the shaft of lust; feeling is the basis for the shaft of hatred;

and as it is said, "by way of grasping at permanence, the mind regards the self-adherence as a self and views it as superior and so forth," the mind is the basis for the shaft of conceit; and according to the method already stated, the phenomena [are the basis for the shaft of views].
"The basis for the arrow of delusion" should be connected with the four foundations of mindfulness.

For when the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena have been fully understood through the practice of contemplation of the body and so forth, the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations are fully understood;
and when the mind is fully understood, perception is likewise fully understood. Therefore, [the text speaks of] the "stations of consciousness."
It is said: “And they come to full understanding of it.
Likewise, because one who is specifically concerned with the body falls into the bias of desire (*chandāgati*), the body is the basis (*vatthu*) for the bias of desire.

In the same manner described above, feeling is the sign (*nimitta*) of ill-will (*byāpāda*); thus, feeling is the basis for the bias of hatred (*dosāgati*). Through the grasping of a solid mass (*ghana*) as a continuity (*santati*), in a mind such as that possessed of lust (*sarāga*), etc., [the mind becomes the basis for the bias of delusion].
“Delusion occurs” means that the mind follows the wrong course through delusion; “fear occurs” means that fear arises through a lack of understanding of the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva).
Thus, by the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, there is the abandoning of following the wrong course regarding phenomena as objects. Therefore, he said:
“And by not following the wrong course, one does not go on a wrong course.”
The phrase “by way of unwholesome mental joy” is stated on the grounds that this meaning is also possible.

However, because of the statement, “The underlying tendency to lust underlies pleasant feeling,” it should be understood that by the inclusion of pleasant feeling, the truth of the origin (samudayasacca) is taught through its underlying tendency therein.
Likewise, the Noble Truth of Suffering is taught by the inclusion of the suffering of suffering (dukkhadukkha).
The Noble Truth of suffering has been explained as being preeminent; thus it is stated in the Pāḷi: “The Noble Truth of suffering has been taught.
Whatever needs to be said regarding association and so forth has already been stated in the commentary on the section of the Niddesa below.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra) is concluded.

6. Commentary on the Analysis of the Catubyūha String (Catubyūhahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 25. Regarding the phrase "of the strings" (*hārānaṃ*): this is a genitive case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*). The construction is as follows: "Among the strings, this Catubyūha string is distinguished because it consists specifically in the analysis of the phrasing of the Sutta. Therefore, it is said: "It shows... the phrasing... and so forth. The word "by which" (*yāya*) refers to the etymological interpretation (*nirutti*).
"As appropriate" (*yathārahaṃ*) means that whatever etymological derivation is suitable to be stated for the Sutta being commented upon, that is provided in accordance with worldly convention alone.
Having fulfilled the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*), one subsequently attains the realization of truth (*saccābhisamaya*); thus it is said, “conventional reality...
[etc]... comes to be. Alternatively, the connection is this: by means of grasping various designations (*paññatti*), there occurs the grasping of the ultimate reality (*paramattha*).

That which was stated here as “between both” refers to the continuity of material form (*rūpa-santāna*) not bound to the faculties (*anindriyabaddha*). This is in the section on the Mode of Entry (*otaraṇahāra*).

In order to show that this was stated with reference to phenomena such as contact (phassa) that arise at the doors [of sense], the meaning “in between both” is explained as “among those phenomena arisen together with contact. However, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā say: “The word ‘antarena,’ moreover, indicates an alternative interpretation.
Therefore, the meaning here is as follows: neither this world, nor the world beyond.
"Now, 'between both' (ubhayamantarena)": another interpretation is that the phrase "between both" indicates the absence of an alternative option.
Its meaning is this: the meditator does not meditate depending on this world, nor does he meditate depending on the world beyond;
rather, there is no other place between these two.

Furthermore, those who— having wrongly grasped the meaning of these scriptural passages, namely “one who attains Nibbāna in the interval” (antarāparinibbāyī) and “one who seeks existence” (sambhavesī)—
claim that there is indeed an intermediate state (antarābhava), must also consider this:

they attain Parinibbāna by reaching the Supreme Path and the complete extinction of all defilements in the middle of their lifespan, without having exceeded the midpoint of their life-span, in various places such as the Aviha heaven.
The meaning of the first sutta passage is: "one who attains parinibbāna in the interval" (antarāparinibbāyī) is not one who has become [an intermediate being] in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
And as for the latter [passage], those who have already become [liberated] and will not become again—namely, those whose taints are exhausted—are called "become" (bhūtā) by the preceding words.

Because they are the opposite of that, those who seek becoming (sambhava) are called "seekers of becoming" (sambhavesino). They are trainees (sekkhā) because the fetter of becoming (bhava-saṃyojana) has not yet been abandoned.

And as for ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*): among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*) and those born from a womb (*jalābuja*) are called "seeking existence" (*sambhavesī*) as long as they have not broken out of the eggshell or the amniotic sac;
once they have emerged from the eggshell or the amniotic sac, they are called "beings" (*bhūta*).

Those born of moisture (*saṃsedaja*) and those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) are called "seeking existence" during the first moment of consciousness, and from the second moment of consciousness onward...

"Beings" (bhūta) refers to those who have already come into existence. Alternatively, the meaning is that as long as they are born with a particular posture (*iriyāpatha*) and have not yet reached another, they are "seeking birth" (*sambhavesī*);
beyond that, they are "beings. Therefore, it must be rejected [to say] that such beings do not exist.

For when there is a meaning that is straightforward and conforms to the Canon (*pāḷi*), what is the use of postulating an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) whose functional capacity remains undetermined?

As for those who say: "The uninterrupted manifestation of phenomena proceeding as a continuum in different locations is observed—as in the case of the non-conscious continuum of rice and so forth—so too must there be such uninterrupted manifestation in different locations within the conscious continuum as well.
And this principle is consistent only if an intermediate state (antarābhava) exists, not otherwise."

They speak of logical consistency (*yutti*). For one who possesses psychic power (*iddhimant*) and has attained mastery over the mind (*cetovasippatta*), when resolving upon a body that follows the mind, logical consistency must be stated regarding his arrival here from the Brahma-world in an instant, or his departure from here to the Brahma-world.

If the occurrence of phenomena in disconnected locations is not accepted anywhere at all, then even if there were such a thing as the "domain of psychic power" (*iddhivisaya*), [it would be untenable].
“...is inconceivable. This is the same here as well, because of the statement, “the ripening of kamma is inconceivable”; therefore, that [position] is merely their own opinion.

For phenomena that possess intrinsic nature have an inconceivable nature; they manifest in some cases in a delimited location due to specific conditions, and in other cases in an undelimited location.
