Thus, by means of the sound from the mouth and so forth, [a reflection appears] in another location, such as the region of a mirror or a mountain.
Reflections, echoes, and so forth are seen to arise as conditionally produced phenomena; therefore, one should not apply every [principle] to every [case].

This is the summary here. For a detailed treatment, however, the investigation of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), beginning with the proof of the reflection's status as an illustration, should be taken from the commentary on the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*.
Others, however, say: "‘Here’ refers to sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava); ‘there’ refers to formless existence (arūpabhava); and ‘in between the two’ refers to fine-material existence (rūpabhava).
They also say: "'Here' refers to conditioned phenomena (paccayadhamma); ‘there’ refers to dependently arisen phenomena (paccayuppannadhamma);

and ‘in between the two’ refers to conceptualized phenomena (paṇṇattidhamma). None of this is found in any of the commentaries; therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.

"Remaining matter" refers to the characteristic types of matter together with the water element and the space element, and it is stated with reference to nutritive essence (*ojā*), because non-faculty-bound matter is intended here.
That consciousness of that one whose taints are destroyed does not know, nor is it known by, these [elements], because it is said to be "meditating. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Catubyūha-hāra is finished.
7. Commentary on the Analysis of the Āvaṭṭa-hāra: 29.
Because it has the nature of destroying unwholesome states, or because of the abandoning of unwholesome states, [it leads] to wholesome states...

It is the "element of initiative" (*ārambhadhātu*) because its nature consists in establishing [the mind] in the performance [of wholesome deeds]. "Endowed with such states" means being possessed of virtue (*sīla*) and the other [wholesome qualities].

The three realms beginning with the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) are themselves the "three realms" (*tedhātu*). Because he overcomes them, the King of Death (*maccurāja*) is the "Lord of the Three Realms.
Even though it has long been established in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), [it is overcome] by wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) cultivated for even a short time.
Because they are to be utterly severed, the defilements are "weak"; thus it is said, "weak, feeble. Therefore he said, "The weak become strong for him.

This statement is the fourth line of this verse. Regarding the phrase "the footing of concentration": here, "cause of concentration" should be construed as "because of directing [the mind] toward the application of equanimity.
This same method applies to the remaining [terms]. "Proliferations" (papañca) refers to greed and the rest. And it has been described in that very way.
The meaning is that the commentary on the meaning has been made precisely by way of the foundation for the teaching (*desanā*).

"That" (*taṃ*) refers to that teaching. "Of that" (*tassa*) refers to the turning back (*āvaṭṭana*) by way of similarity and so forth. For the sake of the attainment of distinction by those whose knowledge is matured.
Regarding the phrase "gain, decision, grasping, and avarice," and so on: "gain" (*lābha*) is the acquisition of objects such as visible forms. That...
"Because there is searching (*pariyesanā*)," it is included by the mention of "searching. "Discrimination" (*vinicchaya*) refers to the discursive thought (*vitakka*) that proceeds thus:

"This much will be for the sake of the object of form; this much for the sake of the objects of sound and so forth; this much is mine, this much belongs to another; this much I shall consume, this much I shall store away.
Because it has acquisition as its cause, [it is called discrimination].

Because it is rooted in searching, it is already included by the mention of "searching" itself; likewise for possession and avarice. Therein, "possession" (pariggaha) is the grasping [of things] as "this is mine.
"Avarice" (macchariya) is the inability to endure sharing with others, thinking, "Let this be mine alone.
For this very reason, the ancients explain its etymological meaning thus: "May this be avarice for me alone; let it not belong to others."
It is called *macchariya* (avarice) because it proceeds with the thought, "Let there be astonishment [that others possess this].

However, the determination (*vinicchaya*) and so forth regarding the place of use should be understood as being included within the category of use (*paribhoga*). *Chandarāga* (desire-lust) is weak lust.

*Ajjhosāna* (clinging) is a strong resolve by way of craving, thinking "this is mine"; thus he said, "Desire-lust and clinging are just craving. For the purpose of guarding, there is the closing of doors, locking them, keeping things in chests, and so forth.

"For the sake of good protection. One who commits evil acts, being impassioned, greedy, infatuated, and intoxicated for the sake of enjoyment, falls into negligence for the sake of consumption, like a deer; thus, guarding by means of the enclosure is for the sake of enjoyment.
Showing that negligence is described as being threefold by way of craving (*taṇhā*), he said: "It is stated as 'threefold by way of craving.'"
It is said "stated without distinction" because, although one might ask by way of analysis, "By which clinging are they 'with clinging'?",

it is stated without separating them, saying, "by ignorance and by craving. And [the phrase] "craving and ignorance by way of the four kinds of clinging" means having analyzed them by way of the four clingings,
such as sensual-clinging (*kāmupādāna*) and so forth, [showing that] the aggregates are suffering by way of their nature as the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).

The construction is as follows: it shows that [the fuel of craving] is to be fully understood together with its state of being something to be fully understood, and that it is to be abandoned together with the state of being the origin of the clingings, which is the state of being the truth of the origin.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "Whoever" (*yo*), the connection is that the threefold negligence described therein seeks after, guards, and uses [objects].
For negligence, in a person who is negligent, leads to the seeking after, guarding of, and [use of] possessions.
And although it is actually the cause, it is figuratively designated as the agent; furthermore, it is the sign for enjoyment.

He explains the meaning of the phrase "by its opposite" with the words "through the practice of diligence," thereby showing its nature as serenity (*samatha*). "Destruction" means bringing about exhaustion.
"By way of factors discordant with the side of purification" means that which belongs to the side of purification and is a factor discordant with negligence.
...and purification... [etc. ...the Dhamma; by means of that, namely, serenity (*samatha*).

"When serenity exists" means when the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) has become a foundation; the meaning is: having made that the basis. "That which is wisdom" refers to the wisdom that functions by way of the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth. Therefore he said: "This is insight (*vipassanā*). "When they have been abandoned" means while they are being abandoned.

"Having set aside the side of purification" means having set aside the side of purification consisting of the element of exertion (*ārambhadhātu*), and so forth. "By way of discordant states" means...

“Merely by way of negligence. “By way of a corresponding state” means by way of a state corresponding to serenity and so forth—the state of purification consisting of the element of initiative and so on—which was previously established.
He says, “But that [purification] occurs through Arahantship,” because here it is intended as a purification that has reached its ultimate limit, rather than one that is not yet fully purified.

“Arising from delusion” is stated by taking the position that “delusion itself is the origin. Otherwise, malicious speech (pisuṇāvācā) would have to be described as arising from hatred (dosa), just as false speech (musāvāda) arises from delusion.

It is said, “by way of the classification of kamma into courses of action,” because unwholesome states—both those that have attained the status of courses of action and those that have not—are encompassed by the term “all evil.”

31. "Of the remaining words" refers to the remaining words of the verse beginning with "The undertaking of what is wholesome. "As it was attained" means the manner in which it was attained by oneself; subsequently, [the text mentions] the stages and directions.
"Causing them to go upward" means leading them from the human world to the higher divine worlds.

32. "Of the Dhamma as previously stated" refers to both virtue (*sīla*) and the Path (*magga*). Regarding the phrase "of craving, ignorance, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)— [Note: The provided source text for section 32 appears to be incomplete.]

The defilements associated with that [object] are included, as well as the phenomena that serve as their proximate causes (*padatthāna*). By the word "etc. in the phrase "calm, insight, etc.," the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are comprised.
To the extent that it is said here that "cessation protects," to that same extent the Path is stated to be the instrument for the act of protecting in the sense of "that by which one protects.
The preceding [terms] are [stated] by way of discordant factors (*visabhāgadhamma*).
It should be understood that the latter truths are determined by way of turning toward the common characteristics (*sabhāgadhamma*).
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Turning (*āvaṭṭahāra*) is finished.
8. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis (*vibhattihāra*).

33. "Regarding phenomena" (*dhammesu*) means regarding those phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*), which are divided into categories such as merit (*puñña*) and giving (*dāna*). "Obtainable therein" (*tattha labbhamāno*) means obtainable among those aforementioned phenomena. "Analysis of planes" (*bhūmi-vibhāgo*) refers to the classification of planes such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and the stages of vision (*dassana-bhūmi*).

"Analysis of proximate causes" (*padaṭṭhāna-vibhāgo*) refers either to those phenomena for which merit and the other qualities are the proximate cause, or to those phenomena which are the proximate cause of them.
The analysis of the sections. "Of which suttas" refers to the four types of suttas beginning with those dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), which serve as the fundamental basis.
For it is by way of this unmixed classification that the teachings (*dhammā*) are said to be analyzed with particular excellence within these suttas.
Therefore he said, "specifically. If this is so, why [are] the suttas dealing with spiritual cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) and penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) [not included]?

"Are they thus included here? No, this is not so; for by the inclusion of the others through their state of being the conclusion of emergence, both pairs are indeed included by the inclusion of the other two.
For those states belonging to the side of purification that have emerged from [the mundane], they belong to the side of defilement;

and those states belonging to the side of penetration that are the conclusion [of the path], they belong to the side of the Asekhas. Thus, by the inclusion of the two, the other two are also included. Therefore he said:

“Regarding the teaching of these four discourses”: by this, whether referring to the Pāḷi text itself or to the teaching that is about to be explained, the inclusion of the other two pairs should be understood, not their exclusion.
For that very reason—because no restriction has been made—it is established that one becomes a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī) through that [practice] and that which depends upon it.

...there is. Alternatively, the word *eva* (only/just) should be understood as having the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*). "There might be a rejection of that" means there might be a rejection of that holy life of the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti-brahmacariya*).
If this were so, the teaching would be incomplete (*sāvasesā*).

Since the two types of abandoning—namely, abandoning by way of its own constituent part (*tadaṅga*) and so forth—which serve as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), are not included here in the enumeration, [the text speaks of] "the abandonings of eradication (*samuccheda*) and subsidence (*paṭippassaddhi*)."

Thus it is said: "by means of. Here, some read "by that very [means]. The phrase "reading 'by that very holy life'" refers to the alternative textual reading mentioned in the passage "established in the virtue of restraint.
The statement "because... he will say" is a statement of reason for why the latter reading alone is appropriate.

How is it considered [as such]? Because the sublime merits (mahaggata-puñña) lack the nature of penetration (anibbedha-sabhāva), they are not included in the Discourse on Penetration (nibbedha-bhāgiya-sutta);
rather, because they belong to the category of the "partaking of habituation" (vāsanā-bhāgiya), they are included in the Discourse on Habituation itself.
Indeed, the latter reading is more appropriate as a supplementary inclusion. Otherwise, the teaching would be incomplete. Therefore he said: "For... [etc. ...he does not teach."
Because the portions dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and the portions dealing with the state beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*) will be explained later, it is said:
“by way of those that will be explained... etc. The term “from all sides” (*sabbato*) refers back to what precedes and forward to what follows.

Because it looks forward, it is applied in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as: “having included it in its entirety across eleven points. In that context, regarding the meaning of the analytical method (*vicayahāra*) beginning with the word [“all”]:
Having taken this into account, it is said: "In eleven places. However, with reference to what precedes, it should be connected as:

"By means of the teaching in all its aspects, by means of the fruit," and so forth. The method of teaching for those portions dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) should be understood through the defilement of craving (taṇhāsaṃkilesa), etc. The fruit [is understood] by way of the suffering of the states of deprivation (apāyadukkha).

Among humans, [this is] by way of the factors conducive to decline. The method of teaching for those factors conducive to the state of one beyond training (*asekkha*) is by means of the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those beyond training.
The fruit is to be understood by means of the supreme fruit and the Nibbāna-element without residue (*anupādisesa*).

For the others, it is exactly as stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*). By the inclusion of the fetters of sensual lust, ill will, and those pertaining to the higher realms, [the section on] the factors conducive to defilement is shown; by the inclusion of dispassion (*virāga*), [the section on] the factors conducive to penetration is shown.

And because those things pertaining to the state of one beyond training (asekkha) will be explained by the very mention of "the one beyond training," it is said: "by way of those that will be explained... etc.
To show that an analysis of the Dhamma and so forth should be carried out by means of investigating the words, their meanings, their logical connections, and their distinctions, the text says:
"by way of investigation... etc., they are to be analyzed"; thus the Commentary says: "by way of investigation... etc., he shows."
34. "Thus" (*evam*): this refers to the [word] *dhamma*. "Dhammas" refers to those dhammas that have been stated as being of similar kind (*sabhāga*).

"By way of common and uncommon states" means by way of those distinguished by generality (*sāmañña*) and particularity (*visesa*). "Two dhammas are common": these two dhammas are called "common" because they are shared by those dhammas of similar kind.

Which two? Name (*nāma*) and the physical basis (*vatthu*). Therein, "name" is the designation of name (*nāmapaññatti*); it is precisely through the medium of that [name] that [the object] is known from sound.
The comprehension of that meaning. And by means of the sound, there is the grasping of such a meaning solely through its general form, not through its specific form;
therefore, meanings expressible by words are said to be "common to names" because they are to be grasped in dependence on a name characterized by a common form.
"Basis" (*vatthu*) means the place of occurrence. For whatever phenomena occur in a particular place, all those phenomena—
“Common” means shared by the bases (vatthu) designated as the stations of occurrence.
Since this dyad constitutes the commonality and the very nature of those phenomena, it is said: “Two phenomena means two natures.
“By way of falling within a single continuity” means by way of occurring in a common continuity; thus he says, “having a common basis.”
For just as those beings fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*) are the locus for the manifestation of states to be abandoned by vision, so too are those who are unfixed;
thus, both share the same objective basis (*samānavatthu*). This same principle applies to the others as well.

For even though these phenomena—personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rites and rituals (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*)—are distinct in their intrinsic nature, they do not transcend the state of being abandoned by vision; therefore, they possess a commonality of name.
Since greed for form and so forth are to be abandoned by meditation, he said: "Those to be abandoned together with [the defilements] are not common to the bases.

However, just as the meaning "common to the bases" is obtained from the phrase "common to the bases of the objects," he shows that this meaning—"common to the bases by way of the base"—is also obtainable, saying:
"Those to be abandoned together with [the defilements] are common to the bases."

He said: "For although they are distinct from one another due to their intrinsic natures such as contact and so forth, they are called 'common' by virtue of the physical basis (*vatthu*) upon which they occur.

And here, it should be understood that although the commonality of names such as 'wholesome' (*kusala*) and so on is also obtainable, this has been explained first as the commonality of the physical basis.
By the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*) in the phrase 'by opposites, etc.', [the author] includes having the same fruit, association, and so on."

"In the remaining passages" refers to the statements beginning with "of the worldling" (*puthujjana*). How so? For there, one should apply the logic as follows: because [the qualities] are possible for the worldling and the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), but impossible for the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and the arahant, and so forth.
In what manner are they taken specifically? In what way are those qualities described as "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) taken by way of their respective parts?

“Of such-and-such a person, and of such-and-such a person”—this is the meaning here. Since states that have become universal (sāmañña) are called common (sādhāraṇa), this being so, how can it be said that they are the basis for occurrence through a distinction such as being fixed in falsehood (micchattaniyata) or not fixed?
The intention is: it should not be said. Or, if it must be said with such a distinction, then surely it cannot be said that they are common?
Thus, they are "common" (sādhāraṇa) because these states are common to both those fixed in wrongness and those not so fixed.
Therefore he said: "They are not 'common' by virtue of being common to all beings. By the words "Because...
and so forth, he states the reason for this; thereby he shows that "certain states are common only to certain other states."
“They are not shared by others. Therefore he said: “For their locus of occurrence is specifically determined.

Otherwise—that is, if they were common to all because their locus of occurrence were undetermined, or if they were not shared—such being the case, this conventional designation, namely “shared” and “not shared,” would not even be a general term.
"These very same phenomena" refers precisely to those phenomena described as "common. "In this way" means in the manner stated by the phrase "of those fixed in falsehood," and so forth.

"With a fixed object" means having a delimited sphere of activity. The passage beginning with "And whoever... serves to clarify the very same meaning already stated by way of reference to the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
By the passage beginning with "For not...," that same meaning is established through both positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (byatireka).
"He causes it to be analyzed. "In the rest as well" means in such passages as "to be abandoned by cultivation," and so forth.
"Individual certainty" means pertaining to a specific person (*pāṭipuggalika*). "Of the other" means of that which is not individually certain. "In that way" means by way of being non-common.
A certain phenomenon, while being common with respect to one thing, may yet be non-common with respect to something else.
He said, "Because of the commonality of non-deficiency," meaning "by depending on this or that" and so forth.
For thus is explained the state of the first path mentioned as "the nature of things" (dhammatā), which is common to many such noble ones (ariya).

"Of the first" refers to the eighth-rank practitioner (aṭṭhamaka). "Of the second" refers to the stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Again, "of the eighth-rank practitioner" refers to the eighth-rank practitioner.
Regarding the phrase “and of the non-returner,” this refers to the eighth-rank person (aṭṭhamaka) mentioned therein. Therefore, he said: “of one standing on the path of non-returning.
Counting in reverse order starting from the one established in the highest fruit (arahantship), the one standing on the first path is the eighth-rank person.

Because they stand upon a path and because the defilements to be abandoned are [still] present, all those standing on a path are like the eighth-rank person; thus they are called “eighth-rank persons. It is said that “he does not remain beyond a single moment of consciousness.”
"An eighth person," according to others, following the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*). "Learners" (*sekkhā*) is the common name; this is the connection [of the text].
"In the others" refers to those non-noble ones mentioned as "capable and incapable. Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: "taking the inferior, superior, and intermediate [persons into account].

"By the entry into the fixed course" means by the state of having entered the fixed course (*niyāma*). "Of one who has surpassed through knowledge" means of one who has excelled in knowledge. "In the conjunction of such conditions."

In the combination of specific knowledge as a condition. For just as sluggish direct knowledge does not occur through the power of knowledge, so too one who has entered upon the practice is easily dried up [of defilements].
That pleasant practice is called the proximate cause for insight because it possesses swift direct knowledge due to the supremacy of the knowledge of one endowed with it.

“Reflection on the Dhamma” (*dhammacintā*) is reflection that does not depart from the Dhamma; it is reflection upon phenomena because it proceeds by means of appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*). Alternatively, “Dhamma” here means knowledge; therefore, reflection that brings about knowledge is “reflection on the Dhamma. The meaning is: reflection that serves as the cause for knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*).
By the inclusion of “wisdom consisting of what has been heard” (*sutamayapaññā*) in the canonical text, the sense of the Sutta passage beginning, “Those teachings which are good in the beginning...
such teachings he has heard much of,” is encompassed. Likewise, by the inclusion of “appropriate attention,” [the sense of the passage] beginning, “He... is encompassed.
By the passage beginning, “He attends wisely, ‘It is impermanent,’” the attention consisting of the means (*upāyamanasikāra*) is encompassed.
Showing that by the inclusion of “right view,” right view as described in the passage beginning, “He develops right view based on seclusion,” is also encompassed, he says:
“Then, however... [etc. ...to show. The remainder refers to such things as “the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma.”

And showing that for one who has not previously cultivated the goal, the confidence directed toward the objective through the influence of a good friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) and the tranquility of the mind bear fruit, he said:
"The presence of a true person... the proximate cause. Showing that because of being rightly directed toward oneself, one becomes abundant in revulsion toward evil and loathsomeness, he said:
"The goal... the proximate cause. The Dhamma is well-expounded from the beginning until—
Showing that [the Dhamma] is the cause for the complete fulfillment of all attainments up to the ultimate goal, he said:
"The well-expounded nature of the Dhamma... [and so on] ...is the proximate cause. For the planting of the roots of the wholesome culminates in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

"The Saṅgha’s being well-pleased" means for the sake of the Saṅgha’s state of being well-established and for the sake of the Saṅgha’s confidence, which consists in the state of accepting [the teaching] by saying, "Well, venerable sir! The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis is finished.
9. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal: 35.
Regarding the passage "For one of right view... [it] becomes worn away," here the meaning is according to the right view of the Path.
Thus, the meaning can indeed be obtained by way of the ownership of action (*kammassakatā*), the courses of action (*kamma-patha*), and right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) as well;
for this is a discussion on the courses of action. "In the manner already stated" means in the way it was said: "being unliberated," and "in non-liberation.

"By way of wrong adherence" means [adhering] to one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One (*asammāsambuddha*) as being a Perfectly Enlightened One, and to that which does not lead out [from suffering] as leading out.
"But what is non-existent, [one takes] as existent," and "what is ignoble, [one takes] as noble"—this is by way of a perverted adherence (*viparītābhinivesa*).

"False resolve" (*micchādhimokkha*) means misplaced confidence or misplaced determination. "Arising delusion is false liberation-knowledge and vision" (*micchāvimuttiñāṇadassana*)—this is the connection [of the sentence].

(36) "Discourses and counter-discourses" (*vādānuvādā*): discourses and the subsequent discourses; the meaning is "by taking up those discourses. "The continuations of discourses" (*vādānupavattiyo*) means the continuations of the faults of those discourses.
“Reversal of the two extremes” means a reversal by way of the opposite of the two extremes, namely, devotion to sensual pleasure and devotion to self-mortification.
“In these sections as well” refers to these sections: “The Dhamma is non-leading for them; happiness is non-Dhamma for them.
“By the method stated” means: if self-torment, which is the causing of suffering to oneself, were Dhamma, then that which is opposed to Dhamma—

They should be told: "It would follow that it is non-Dhamma (*adhamma*), and since suffering is opposed to happiness, it would follow that the happiness of the jhānas, the paths, and the fruits, as well as the happiness of enjoying blameless requisites, are non-Dhamma. The phrase "whatever, indeed...

and so forth is intended to include the remaining portion of the text. Here, "whatever Dhamma" means any kind of Dhamma whatsoever—whether wholesome (*kusala*) or unwholesome (*akusala*), or desirable (*iṭṭha*).
"Or undesirable" is what is meant. "He relishes or he approaches" means he relishes with his mind and approaches with his view.
"That which is the opposite of each respective phenomenon" means that which is called the opposite of whichever phenomenon has been relished or approached.
That phenomenon becomes "entered upon" as something undesirable for him. As for the phenomenon...
When one has accepted a doctrine that is pleasing or has been approached, yet [the teacher] accepts it as undesirable or contrary, there is a turning back of the teaching by way of its opposite;
this is the meaning of "the method of reversal" (*parivattanahāra*). Therefore he said:
"It clarifies the characteristic of the opposite."
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal is finished.
10. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacanahāra) 37.
“By means of various [terms]” means by this or that [synonym]. “At the time” means at the time of reflection. “In whatever way” means by whichever [method].
The intention is that one who does not penetrate [the truth] by means of the first method stated might penetrate it by another method.
"He explains the methodical statement" is the connection; this applies in all instances.
"At that moment" refers to the moment stated for the methodical statement. "Of those with distracted minds" means those whose minds are scattered in various ways among different objects.
"Aññavihitānaṃ" means "of those thinking of something else. But why explain that meaning by another method?
Is it not rather a strengthening when it is stated by that [very same method]? Addressing this objection, he says "teneva" and so forth.
Therein, "tadaññesaṃ" means "of others than those"—that is, other than those whose minds were distracted and so on, by whom the first statement was correctly grasped. "Tattha" means...
By means of the very words already spoken, through repeated utterance;

for the purpose of avoiding redundancy due to the fact that the matter has already been understood, by way of qualification, through various designations, establishing that "this word is the designator of this meaning" and "this word is the designator of this meaning";
[and] regarding each respective meaning to be taught within one's own mind...

“Upanibandhanaṃ” means fixing or establishing. “Tattha” means in the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and its terminology (dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidā). “Bījāvāpanaṃ” means the sowing of seeds, that is, the provision of causes.
Having thus stated the many purposes for the Blessed One’s teaching by way of various methods (pariyāyadesanā), he now says “What need for much?

and so forth, in order to show that it is precisely because of his own state of Perfect Self-Enlightenment (sammāsambuddhatā) that the Tathāgatas teach the Dhamma through numerous methods with such Buddha-play (buddhalīlā).

In the Pāḷi, after showing that *pihā* has the present as its object with the words, “*Pihā* is the longing for an existing thing,” the passage beginning with “or for something better” is stated in order to show that it also has the future as its object. Thus he says: “*Taṇhā* (craving) that has the future and the present as its objects is *pihā*.

Alternatively, this is because in the phrase “the preservation of the accomplishment of the goal,” the state of having the future and present as its objects is indicated by the very meaning of *pihā*.

Being comprised solely by that which has mental phenomena (*dhamma*) as its object, it comes to be designated simply as "having mental phenomena as its object. Regarding the phrase "twenty-four terms": here, there are twenty-four sections based on the four sets of six, beginning with the discursive thoughts of sorrow associated with the household life.
38. "That same [craving] is called 'delight in mental phenomena' (*dhammanandi*) in the mode of aspiration," and so forth. Herein, this is the meaning:

that very craving, when occurring in the mode of aspiration and described through the sequence beginning with "longing" (*āsā*), is "delight in mental phenomena" in the sense of finding pleasure in phenomena such as form. Of these...

Thus, *dhammapema* (love for the Dhamma) is in the sense of cherishing it. *Dhammajjhosāna* (clinging to the Dhamma) is so called because one has swallowed it and digested it, remaining fixed in its position.

By this [phrase] as well—meaning that not only should synonyms be stated by way of the unique expressions such as "wisdom is understanding," but also synonyms should be stated by way of this common expression beginning with "predominance" (*ādhipateyya*). By this very [expression]...

"By way of" means by this figurative expression (*pariyāya-vacana*). It shows that the demonstration of the method of the Pāḷi text beginning with "Thus indeed is the Blessed One" is not itself the accomplishment of the purpose of the teaching.
In the ten [qualities] such as "having reached the perfection of the powers," he has attained the fulfillment and completion of the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
The four knowledges consisting of confidence (*visāradabhāva*) regarding the specific exhortations—the teaching on enlightenment, abandonment, obstacles, and instruction—[are also included].
"Attained" (*patto*) means having attained self-confidence (*vesārajjappatto*).

"Transcending dispositions" (*ajjhāsayavītivatto*) means he has especially transcended the underlying tendencies (*ajjhāsaya*) such as that of greed. He has "gone to the unreckoned" (*asaṅkhepagato*);

that is, he has gone to Nibbāna, which is called "unreckoned" because it is devoid of the reckonings of past causes and so forth, and because it is "unreckonable" (*asaṅkheyya*) due to its immovable nature or its qualities.
"Upagata" means having reached the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*). The rest is easily understood. "Uddheyyaṃ" means that which is to be extracted. The connection is:

"In the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*), the meaning should be seen in this way. It is called "pāraṃ" because it protects from the suffering of *saṃsāra* and delights with peaceful happiness;

or alternatively, it is "pāraṃ" because it has not existed before (*abhūtapubbattā*), and by that very fact it reveals its permanence, since it cannot be afflicted by any deity, calamity, or the like, and is thus unassailable (*anupasaṭṭhattā*).

“*Duppassan”* is also a reading in the text; the meaning is “difficult to attain. By means of the splendor of its qualities and its state of being fragrant—by the radiance of its virtues and its sweet scent.

Just as a person who is a master archer, by means of the light of a momentary flash in the thick darkness of night, pierces even a very subtle target situated at a great distance through the perfection of his craft, so too does the noble disciple, by means of the perfection of his virtue (*sīla*), [pierce] that which is extremely subtle.
One penetrates Nibbāna, the Dhamma of the Four Truths, by means of a single penetration alone; thus it is said: "Craft, virtue, and hitting the mark.
The term "worldly" should be regarded as merely illustrative, since even the contemplation of supramundane states serves as a basis [for this].
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms is finished.
11. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions (Paññatti-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) 39.

Regarding "the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma that is natural" (*sābhāvikadhammakathā*): one's own state is the "natural state" (*sabhāva*). That which is produced by the natural state, or that which has come from it, is "natural" (*sābhāvika*).
That very thing being a discourse on the Dhamma is a "discourse on the Dhamma that is natural. It is the "discourse on the Dhamma that is uniquely exalted" (*sāmukkaṃsika*) for the Buddhas.

Although there is no actual difference between the meaning and the teaching of the Dhamma which serves as its instrument, it is stated thus by means of a distinction established through conventional usage between the discourse and the teaching, or else by distinguishing the whole from its parts. Therefore he said: "And what is the teaching of the fundamental discourse?
It is the Four Truths. For this was stated by applying the designation of non-difference to the teaching of the meaning. Of that teaching...
"Making known. This is the brief statement of the nature of the "method of description" (*paññatti-hāra*). "That" refers to the teaching as previously described.
"In such and such a way" means in whatever manner the truths are to be taught, in that very manner. And how are these to be taught?

By way of the categories such as "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) and so forth. "As intended" means according to what is intended, conforming to the purpose of awakening those who are kinsmen among those to be awakened.
*Attha*: "Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning that is to be taught, or specifically the meaning of suffering and so forth. *Nikkhipati*: "He sets down" means he establishes;
for this reason, it is said in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) that "there are four ways of setting down the discourses" (*cattāro suttanikkhepā*), and so on.
*Tattha*: "Therein" means in the teaching of the ways of setting down. *Maggapakkhiyā*: The intention is that they are excluded from the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).

"In whatever place" means in whatever place reckoned as existence (*bhava*) and so forth. "The teaching as previously stated" refers to the aforementioned type of teaching that illuminates the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of passion and other defilements bound to the four nutriments (*āhāra*). 41.

Regarding the phrase "by way of three turns," here too it should be construed with the word "truths" (*saccesu*). The connection is: "he declares the designation of full understanding" (*pariññā-paññatti*).
By the two phrases "delighting in the internal" and "composed" (*samāhita*), he illustrates the cultivation of delighting in the internal, which is distinguished by concentration (*samādhi*).

Because it illustrates the state of having the internal as its objective domain (*gocarajjhattatā*). For the word *ajjhatta* alone applies not only to what is internal (*ajjhatta*), but also to what is extremely internal (*ajjhattajjhatta*) and to what has the internal as its objective domain (*gocarajjhatta*).

And since concentration distinguished by internal delight (*ajjhattaratatā*) demonstrates an especially superior stability of mind (*cittatthiti*), he shows this meaning with the words, "of that which is distinguished by concentration," and so forth.
"In the sense of clinging" means in the sense of attachment. "Seeing as such" means the manifestation of oneself as if one were of a suitable form, even though one is not actually so.

"Unlucky" means devoid of fortune. "Of sensual pleasures" refers to phenomena of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). "Of forms" refers to phenomena of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). "The escape": the fine-material sphere phenomena are the escape from sensual pleasures;
immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) phenomena are the escape from those [fine-material phenomena]. Thus, [it is the escape] from things of that same nature.
"Of those things that have a superior state. "In that way" means:

just as the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) exists because it is the state of escape from conditioned phenomena and because it is the object of the Noble Path which cuts off the defilements, so too does the unconditioned element exist by the reason being stated here;
this is what he shows. "In some cases, as an object" refers to the unconditioned element.

"Unmistaken meaning" means "actual meaning. This is because, in such passages as, "When, sir, this self enjoys itself, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, to that extent, sir, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this very life, being one destined for Nibbāna with its remainder," there is the presence of figurative usage (*upacāra-vutti*).
Just as in the case of the word "lion," as in "the young man is a lion," and so forth.

Just as the term "king of beasts" (migarañño), though used metaphorically when applied to young boys and the like, is seen to have its meaning realized in the actual object [the lion], so too the word *nibbāna*, while being used metaphorically when applied to the possession of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), the form-body (*rūpa*), or the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), has an unerring meaning in a certain specific object.
And that object wherein it has an unerring meaning is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). The knowable is [grasped] there as clearly as an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Showing that for one who sees through direct perception, the word of the Teacher alone is the authority in this matter, he says, “What is the use of this investigation of reasoning,” and so forth.
He speaks with reference to the conclusion: “The exposition and establishment [of the teaching] is for the sake of proving the meaning that has been promised.”
The commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions is finished.
12. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Ways of Entry (Otaraṇahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 42.

“By means of the faculties” (*indriyehi*): this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the instrument, as in “he goes by way of the path,” and as in “he cuts with an axe,” and so forth. “Ways of entry” (*otaraṇā*) means ways of penetration.
The construction is: "Like right intention, [it functions] by way of encompassing the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha).

Showing that wisdom accomplishes its function of seeing only when faith and the other factors assist them—by means of conviction, exertion, establishment, and concentration—in those devoted to higher consciousness (adhicitta), he said: "Faith... [etc.]...
are so stated. And "not as life-continuum (bhavaṅga)" refers to those formations (saṅkhārā).
This shows the absence of the cause for its continued occurrence.
43. "So-called 'support'": it is called a "support" (nissaya) because it has been so stated. By the term "volition," he refers specifically to craving, because of its association with volition.
"Of one who is lustful" means of one whose lust has not been eradicated by the Path; [it refers] to that lust by which a person is called "lustful."
Pleasant feeling is said to be associated with that [craving] because it lies latent therein. Therefore he said: "Pleasant... is said.
This same method applies to the others as well. Hence he said: "In the same way," and so forth.
"Those very faculties" refers to the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity. The statement "included within formations" (saṅkhārapariyāpannāni) [is made].
Having intended this, he said: "Here, volition is spoken of under the heading of feeling. For feeling is not included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Showing that [the words] "by craving" and "by view" are used in the instrumental case, he said "by craving," and so forth.
Now, in order to show the meaning of "by craving" and so on precisely by way of the instrumental case, he said "or just as," and so forth. Therein:

“Of the remaining phenomena” (*sesadhammānaṃ*) means of those phenomena excluding craving (*taṇhā*), which are not specifically distinguished [here]. “In the state of being the support for craving” (*taṇhāya nissayabhāve*) means when craving is their support.
“In the state of being the condition for the remaining phenomena through craving” (*taṇhāya sesadhammānaṃ paccayabhāve*) means when the remaining phenomena have craving as their condition.

By the phrase “dependent on the body born of karma” (*karajakāyasannissitā*), the dependence on the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) is also included, because of the state of tranquility of the body (*kāyappassaddhi*). “The state of being the cause” (*kāraṇabhāvaṃ*)...
The state of being a successive cause (*paramparahetubhāva*). "By means of craving and views" means by means of views and by means of craving accompanied by views.

To make clearer the very meaning stated by the two terms "coming" (*āgati*)—which here means coming to this world—and "going" (*gati*)—which means existence after death—the text says, "neither coming nor going exist. Here, "huram" indicates the phenomena that serve as doors and objects.
Because they are grasped by excluding door-objects that are either near or far. Herein, the phenomena occurring at the doors are stated as the meaning of the phrase "between both.
However, in the *Catubyūha-hāra*, non-faculty-bound material phenomena are stated in that way.

[They are so stated] by way of being a cause, by way of being an immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*), and by way of being a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). Those which...
The conventional designation “self” is based upon phenomena; the meaning is that by the absence of those phenomena such as consciousness, [the self] has been brought to a state of non-arising.

Demonstrating that the nature of being a condition has been shown in reverse order by the passage beginning, “For one who is independent, there is no wavering,” the text states, “‘This indeed is the end of suffering’ refers to dependent origination. Is it not then [the case that... ignorance is the condition?

With reference to the objection that [the formula] beginning with "formations" (*saṅkhārā*) is dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), the dependent origination is analyzed according to the mundane and supramundane categories by means of the passage beginning with "It is twofold," in order to demonstrate the status of dependent origination in the case of what has been stated above.
"For the sake of that" means for the sake of the liberation of one free from passion. "Its state" refers to the state of supramundane dependent origination.
The commentary on the analysis of the “String of Penetration” (Otaraṇahāra) is finished.
13. Commentary on the Analysis of the “String of Purification” (Sodhanahāra) 45.
Regarding the phrase “he purifies”: this refers to showing the matter in question directly, as if holding a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one’s hand.
Having made it free from tangles and free from roots, one clears it by removing the stains of ignorance, doubt, and so forth regarding its object.
While clearing it in this way, by applying a metaphorical identity between the word and its meaning, it is said that "one clears the word.
Therefore he said: "It is called 'clearing the word. Here, the answer to the question itself is what constitutes the clearing; thus he said: "of its meaning..."

"From the answering. "It is undertaken" (*ārabhiyati*) means it is commenced (*ārambho*), referring to the meaning being manifested through the teaching. Therefore he said: "Not yet... because of not having been awakened.
Here, "clarification" (*sodhana*) means making a hidden form of meaning manifest through the power of the teaching;
to illustrate that meaning by way of a simile, he said: "Of those who have plunged into ignorance," and so forth.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification is finished.
14. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) 46.

"Should be maintained" (*dhārayitabba*) means it should be scrutinized (*upadhāretabba*), that is, it should be characterized (*upalakkhetabba*). This has already been stated [in the previous section] by such phrases as, "Because of the lack of stability due to the conventional designation of generalities and particularities," and so forth.
They ripen into various results, such as the hells and so forth; that is their respective fruit. *Añcitā* means gone. *Yoni* means a single birth (*ekajāti*).
It is called *yoni* because one becomes mixed with others by way of equality; it is a rebirth. *Pecca* means having died. *Ussannatāya* means due to an abundance of applied thought (*vitakka*).

Some also say "because of being increased" (*ussannattā*). Or, it is because of being increased by eternalism and so forth. *Asurajātinibbattanako* means that which causes one to be reborn into the class of asuras.
“Discernment” (*saṅkhā*) means wisdom (*paññā*). Since meditation has wisdom as its primary factor, it is said:

“by discerning through the cultivation of the counteractive. 47. It is “earth” (*pathavī*) by virtue of its expansive nature. It is an “element” (*dhātu*) in the sense of maintaining its own intrinsic nature, and in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a living soul.

It is “water” (*āpo*) because it is drunk (*āpiyati*) or because it causes growth (*appāyati*). It is “fire” (*tejo*) by way of heating, by way of sharpness, or by way of burning. It is [wind] by way of blowing (*vāyanavasena*).
Wind (*vāyo*) is so called by way of its rapid movement or its oscillation. "Twenty aspects" refers to the twenty parts, beginning with hair, or alternatively, to the letter *pa*.
Hair and the rest are described as having the characteristic of hardness because they possess an excess of that characteristic.
"A distinct portion of the earth element" means merely a portion of earth; the meaning is that it is merely a phenomenon empty of self.
Regarding the term *santāpa*: here, *santāpa* refers to the state of heat that transcends the body’s natural temperature, a great burning that proceeds by way of consuming the body;

this is the distinction between these two. And regarding the phrase *yena ca jīrīyati*: it is also appropriate to understand the meaning as "it is decayed by means of diseases of decay such as those occurring every day (*ekāhika*) and so forth.
[As for the term *satadhota-sappi*: "Clarified butter (*sappi*) that has been heated a hundred times and then thrown into water is 'clarified butter washed a hundred times' (*satadhota-sappi*)."
They say: "The 'nutriments' (rasā) are chyle, blood, flesh, fat, sinews, bones, and bone-marrow.
Some, excluding the sinew, state that semen is the seventh constituent (dhātu). "Separation" (viveka) means a state of being distinct; the meaning is a dissimilar state.

For nutriment, consisting of the physical basis (vatthu), as it undergoes transformation, [becomes] by its own nature—just like the states of excrement, urine, phlegm, and spittle in those who consume living beings.

It is said that it "goes to that state" because it produces a distinct nature known as a specific taste, and likewise for the other [nutrients] such as flavor with respect to portions of blood and so forth.
Therefore he said: "it goes to a state of distinction by way of its flavor and so on.
"By way of its own-nature characteristic" means because it is to be characterized by its impure nature.
48. *Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ*: "Rasa" means that which is to be tasted; it is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) to be penetrated. One's own rasa is *sarasa*;
that which is according to its true state is *yāthāvasarasa*. Because it is characterized precisely as *yāthāvasarasa*, it is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*);

thus, it is the characteristic of being according to its true intrinsic nature (*yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇa*). Alternatively, *yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ* refers to one's own non-erroneous mode of occurrence (*pavatti*).
It is both its function (*kicca*)—consisting of oppression—and its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). Because of ignorance, one is unable to know, "This is the function;
this is the characteristic. It is said that it stands concealing and enveloping, obstructing the arising of knowledge regarding its own object.
Therefore it is said: "It does not allow one to know or to penetrate. And this is its function; thus, it is [defined] by way of its function.

It is called "declared. It is said to be "declared" because ignorance is said to have the nature of non-penetration (*asampaṭivedha-rasa*). Birth (*jāti*) is so called because beings are born therein;

it is the place of arising. Although ignorance does not take cessation or the path as its object, for one who desires to know them, it functions by way of concealing them, serving as the cause for the apprehension of non-cessation and non-path as being cessation and the path.
In this context, it is said that [something] "arises there"; for those [factors], ignorance is the place of their arising, and for others, it is by way of being their object.
"Benefit and non-benefit" means welfare and harm. However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated as "the meaning of benefit" (*atthattha*);

therein, the word "benefit" (*attha*) is qualified by a second word "benefit" (*attha*) in order to demonstrate the non-erroneous nature of the meaning—that is, "the very benefit which is the meaning."
For knowledge does not apprehend what is non-beneficial as being "beneficial. This should be understood in the same way regarding the terms "cause" and "non-cause.
Alternatively, *atthatthaṃ* is a reduplicated expression intended to clarify the state of making all meanings manifest;

the meaning is "fruit, fruit. This same method applies even when used as a synonym for "benefit" (*hita*). *Taṃ* refers to benefit, non-benefit, and so forth. *Ākāraṃ* refers precisely to the cause of benefit and so forth.

Re-examination (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is the further reviewing of what has already been penetrated. Folly (*bālya*) is the state of a fool, characterized by thinking what should not be thought and so forth.
"He is fully aware" (*sampajānāti*) means he knows correctly in various ways. Delusion (*moha*) is intense confusion. Complete delusion (*sammoha*) is deluding on all sides.
It is "not to be experienced" (*avindiya*) because it is a specific condition for karma leading to an unhappy destination. "He experiences" (*vindati*) means he obtains. Of blameless phenomena...
Because it is not a specific condition like true knowledge (*vijjā*), one does not find what is to be found. This is the differentiation of ignorance (*avijjā*);

this non-distinction of ignorance, stated by way of its function, genus, and characteristic as "ignorance regarding suffering" and so forth, should be understood in meaning by following the method explained for true knowledge and the other terms.
Ground free from stones, pebbles, and sand is called "smooth" in the sense of being smooth (*saṇhaṭṭhena*). "For just that long" means for five hundred kappas.

It is called "vibhūtarūpa" because by means of it, form—consisting of the perception of form—is transcended and overcome; such is the meaning of the term "attainment. For no attainment of the formless realm is accompanied by the perception of form.

Regarding "occurrence": there is nothing at all to be said concerning the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because it has been separately included under the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*);
therefore, it is stated as "the remaining formless attainments" (*sesāruppasamāpattiyo*).
"Not undergoing taming" refers to a wicked or unruly horse. "For the sake of further taming" means for the sake of the taming of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

Thus, there is the painful way with quick direct knowledge and the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge. "In both parts" means in the parts consisting of the body of form and the body of name. "In both ways" means by way of liberation through suppression and liberation through eradication.
"Though manifold" means though manifold by its own nature. "By being denotable by a single term" means by being denotable by a common term.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Foundation is finished.
15. Commentary on the Analysis of the Requisites for Sustenance (Parikkhārahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 49.
In order to show the meaning of the word “hinoti,” he says, “it goes toward the state of being a cause,” because verbal roots have multiple meanings. “Etī” means “comes”; the sense is that it arises.

Regarding the phrase “also as a cause for ignorance”: here, ignorance [acts] as a condition for subsequent ignorance by way of the conditions of proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), presence (*atthi*), absence (*vigata*), and repetition (*āsevana*).

It should be understood, however, that for an immediate [condition], it is a condition by way of the seven conditions—conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root—for what is conascent;

whereas for what is not conascent, it is a condition only by way of the extreme limit of decisive support (upanissaya). It is called a "cause" (kāraṇa) because it produces its own fruit; thus he said: "And the state of being a cause is in relation to the fruit."
The meaning of "arising" (*nibbatti*) is the meaning of "fruit" (*phala*), that is, the meaning designated as fruit.

"That which is the intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*) refers to the intrinsic nature of performing formative acts (*abhisaṅkharaṇa-sabhāva*) belonging to volitional formations such as merit; this is the cause (*hetu*).

"In the remaining terms" refers to the terms beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*). "Of the aforementioned classification" refers to the classification stated in such passages as "the cause has an uncommon characteristic."
"Any condition whatsoever" refers to any cause, such as the producer and so forth. "From the process of volitional formation" means from being produced either directly or through a succession.
The commentary on the analysis of the nutriment of equipment is finished.
16. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Samāropanahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 50.
"Included by the Thread" means stated in the Sutta. The application [of the terms] is as follows:

the mention of the "basis" (padaṭṭhāna) is for the purpose of showing the domain of the determination (adhiṭṭhāna), and the mention of the "synonym" (vevacana) is for the purpose of showing the differentiation of designations (adhivacana). This is because they possess the nature of being the domain and the determination, respectively.
Because it is the state of being a locus for the occurrence [of craving] designated as "objects. *Vanīyati* means "is attached to"; *vanati* means "attaches to" or "serves.

*Vanute* means "he begs," the sense being "he yearns for. The five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are the cause of sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) by way of being its object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

The grasping of signs (*nimittaggāha*) is the cause of the grasping of secondary characteristics (*anubyañjanaggāha*) by way of being its decisive support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*). In this manner, the causality should be stated accordingly for the remaining cases as well.

51. Regarding such passages as “Dwell contemplating the body in the body,” that which is to be said should be understood according to the method already explained in the commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra*) above.
This, however, is the distinction: “For the full understanding of material phenomena” means for the full understanding of the stations of consciousness associated with form.

It should be connected thus: “Seeing it as suffering” refers to the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*). “For the full understanding of the cause of feeling” means for the full understanding of contact (*phassa*).

“By way of feeling” means by way of the suffering produced by oneself. “For the full understanding of feeling” means for the full understanding of the stations of consciousness that are dependent on feeling.

The intention is: “by the contemplation of impermanence,” because it is the opposite of the adherence to permanence. “Of the sign of the perception of permanence” means of that which has the perception of permanence as its cause.
“For the full understanding of perception” means for the full understanding of the stations of consciousness that are dependent on perception. Because they are to be abandoned by the first path...
Regarding "going on a bad path," it is said: "...of adherence to views... and of going on a bad path.
"Through the full understanding of formations" means through the full understanding of the stationing of consciousness which is conditioned by formations.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Coordination is finished.
The commentary on the analysis of the strings (hāravibhaṅga) is completed.
1. Commentary on the Convergence of the Modes of Exposition (desanāhārasampātavaṇṇanā):

The passage beginning with "Thus" (evaṃ) shows the connection to the teaching on the convergence of the modes of exposition. Therein, by means of the first two similes, [the mind] is like a well-polished jeweled floor.
The Pāli text is like an ornament made of well-fashioned Jambunada gold.

In this context, it shows that the teaching on the various types of necklaces (hāravibhaṅga) is like an offering of flowers of many colors, and like a series of various gems bound together, radiant with a network of diverse rays.

By the latter [verse], he illuminates the fact that this [teaching] is even more difficult to perform than the exquisite and most precious matted locks (jaṭā). The construction is: "the verse which was spoken."

52. Since this section on the analysis of strings (*hāravibhaṅgavāra*) does not apply [the verse] for the reason already stated, the intention is that it is not repeated at the beginning of the section on the analysis of strings.
However, the section on the convergence of strings (*hārasampātavāra*) does apply it;
because the section on the convergence of strings applies that verse for the very same reason already stated, it says: “Sixteen... pe... he spoke.”
He said: "The vision of the method of application" means the seeing of the method by way of application.
"By that" refers to the statement, "That is the track of Death. "All perversions" refers to the twelvefold perversion. Regarding "of the commonality...":
that wherein the commonality is established is the specific distinction; however, in terms of meaning, they are perception and so forth.
Showing that the perverted perceptions (vipallāsa) grasp objects such as form in a distorted manner, he said, "perversion of perception" and so forth.

Regarding the five aggregates of clinging—which appear in the form of jewels and the like through the power of Indra’s net and other such illusions—the term "self" (atta) is used according to the method of etymological derivation because they are the cause for notions such as "I" and "mine.

Furthermore, the "personality" (attabhāva) is so called because it serves as the basis for the occurrence of that cognition and its conventional designation, and because it is the ground for [the experience of] pleasure and so forth.

Because it is the basis [for the notion] of "selfhood," it is called the "basis of personal existence" (*attabhāvavatthu*); thus he says, "by these," and so forth. "Of these" refers to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*).
The mode of occurrence of the perversions (*vipallāsā*) is "perceiving beauty in the ugly," and so forth. The objects are the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena (*dhammā*).

And ignorance... [etc. ...because all perversions are preceded by delusion. The word "and" (*ca*) should also be brought over and connected here with the phrase "of the perceptions of beauty and pleasure."
The application of the terms here is as follows: “Ignorance (*avijjā*) alone is the condition for the perceptions of beauty and pleasure, not craving (*taṇhā*) alone;
and ignorance is the condition for the perceptions of beauty and pleasure, but not for the perceptions of permanence and self alone.

Even though this is so, he said “nevertheless,” etc., to show that craving is the specific condition for the first two inverted perceptions, while ignorance is the specific condition for the latter two.
And here, it should be understood that view is included under the heading of ignorance.

Therefore he said, "the mind enveloped by views," and "whatever perversion of view there is," and so forth. And just as view is included under the heading of ignorance, so too might ignorance be included under the heading of view;
thus he said, "ignorance is spoken of under the heading of view. Regarding craving and ignorance, [there are] the perceptions of beauty and pleasure...
Just as craving is a specific condition [for clinging], ignorance is not so; however, just as ignorance is a specific condition for the perceptions of permanence and self, craving is not so.
Showing this, he said, "Delusion is the specific condition.
Regarding the latter two... [the phrase] "...occurs" is because, in the past, there was an absence of the state of craving being powerful through adherence. For that very reason...
For it is said, "He regards past form as self," and not "he delights in it.
"Perversion based on craving" means a perversion that occurs depending upon craving; for craving itself is not a perversion. Therefore he said, "Perversion has craving as its root.
"By way of delighting in views" means by way of delighting in views which themselves depend upon craving. Since...

Thus it is called "the perversion of craving. By this—namely, by the passage beginning "whatever is the perversion of craving"—there are sixteen theories of existence, eight theories of non-existence, eight theories of neither-existence-nor-non-existence, and five theories of Nibbāna in the present life;
these grasp at the aspects of beauty and pleasure through the mode of imagining how one might go to a [future] state or attain Nibbāna.
He said “for the most part” because not all beings are proponents of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). “Also by way of the opposite” means also by way of purification (*visuddhi*);
for as long as there are defilements (*upakkilesa*), the mind is certainly not purified, but when those are abandoned, it is then indeed purified.
Therefore he said “not indeed,” and so forth. Having set aside the canonical text “with an unguarded mind,” [he explains] solely by way of the perversion (*vipallāsa*).
Because it is being extracted from the teaching, it is said: “One should conclude the verse according to the sequence of the connection.

“Of Māra” means of the *kilesamāra* (the Māra of defilements). For one who stands under its power has already fallen into the hands of the remaining Māras. Therefore he said: “By the very mention of the *kilesamāra*,” and so forth.
“The bondage of Māra” (*mārabandhana*) means the bondage of Māra on the side of the seven Māras; for that [bondage] consists of the bondages of the defilements.
He conceives himself as being among his own assembly, including Māra. Therefore it is said: “In the midst of... you shall not be released.
On the other hand, for those on the side of the other Māras, Māra himself is the bond; thus it is “Māra’s bond. Nibbāna is the dissolution of the conditioned (*visaṅkhāra*).
Because of its association with delusion, the mind is called “deluded”; thus, even in the case of one who is lustful or hateful, because the state of delusion is present, he is called “deluded.”
Showing that the separate statement was made by way of specific delusion (*āveṇika-moha*), he said, "by way of the two types of utterly deluded (*momūha*) consciousness-arising.
He said, "Thus," meaning that because it cuts off the wholesome goods through the occurrence of unwholesome states such as lust, the mind becomes unprotected;
and since every form of wrong adherence is included and converges right here, he said, "wrong view" (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).
"...and so on... it should be understood. "All" refers to the phenomena described by the three phrases: "unprotected," "struck by wrong view," and "overcome by sloth and torpor.
"By the eye" means by way of the door. "Visible form" refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) associated with an unattractive object. "Grasping at signs" means:
One who grasps a conceptualized sign—whether as "woman" or "man," or as "beautiful" or "ugly"—or one whose habit is to grasp such [a sign].

One who grasps the secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*) means one who grasps the modes termed "secondary characteristics" because they are the successive manifestations (*anu-anu-vyañjana*) of defilements, such as the various distinctions of hands, feet, smiles, speech, and so forth; or one whose habit is to grasp them. *Yatvādhikaraṇaṃ* means...

The meaning of "the sign" (*nimitta*) is the sign consisting in the grasping of the primary marks (*nimitta*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*). Thus, regarding the phrase "dwelling with the faculty of the eye unrestrained":

this refers to that person who has been described as "one who grasps the signs and grasps the secondary characteristics," and who proceeds with the faculty of the eye—the door of the eye—left unrestrained, not closed by the bolt of mindfulness; and in the grasping of the desirable aspect of that visible form...
Covetousness, grief when grasping at what is undesirable, delusion when not looking with equanimity, and wrong view when forming a false resolve—

in this way, covetousness and ill-will, as well as other evil states in the sense of being blameworthy and unwholesome states in the sense of arising from lack of skill, would flow in and occur repeatedly.
“He does not practice for its restraint” means he does not practice for the sake of restraining that eye-door by closing it with the bolt of mindfulness.

Showing that this non-practice is the non-arising of the unrestrained non-protection of the eye-faculty, he said: “He does not guard... [and so on]... he falls into [transgression]. For even when arising in the course of a javana, non-restraint is [prevented] by that [mindfulness].

Because it proceeds through the door [of the eye], it is called specifically "non-restraint of the eye-faculty. The meaning in the case of the remaining doors should also be understood according to the same method already stated.

Having set aside the brief explanation given by the passage beginning with "And by way of the construction of the prior limit," and now showing that meaning in detail, he says "But the detailed exposition is another" and so forth, introducing the passage beginning with "And as for these... in order to summarize it.
"The unwholesome states as previously described" refers to the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising states, or their objects;
for these are the five aggregates of clinging, excluding the aggregate of origination. "In this way" means by the manner determined in the *Nettipāḷi* and in the commentary.
"Here" refers to this verse beginning with "With an unguarded mind."

Although the verse beginning with “Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded” was not taken in its literal form from the text of the *Desanāhārasampāta*, it was indeed taken by way of its meaning through the passage beginning with “The Blessed One, having fully understood those [cravings]...”.
To clarify that this verse had been included, he asked, “How does he teach? and then recited the verse beginning with “Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded.”

"Performing the work with wise attention" means performing the work of meditation—cultivating it—by means of wise attention known as insight (*vipassanā*), according to the method beginning with, "He attends wisely: 'This is suffering,'" and so forth.

"Knowledge of things as they really are" refers to the preliminary insight belonging to the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*): "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form..."
"Through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form," and so forth, by way of fifty modes.

By showing that in the destiny of hell there is the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), in certain superior happy destinies and in one part of the Brahma-world there is the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*), and elsewhere both [the suffering of formations and the suffering of change]—or even all three—he said:
"by way of the application of the threefold suffering according to what is possible."
The commentary on the section on the "Method of Exposition" (Desanāhāra) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section on the "Method of Investigation" (Vicayahāra): 53.
"Having wholesome states as their object" (kusaladhammārammaṇā) is said with reference merely to the occurrence [of consciousness] directed toward wholesome states; it is not...
Their status as object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) is intended here by the phrase "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*), because supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhammā*) are what is meant.
For never do states that are not subject to clinging (*anupādāniya*) become objects of clinging (*upādāna*).

It is said, "it should be understood as wholesome...," because it is grasped by craving (*taṇhā*) that proceeds with a view toward the resultant states (*phala-dhamma*). "In the nutriment of teaching" (*desanāhāre*) means in the occurrence of the nutriment of teaching.
But how is it that they have the nature of the wholesome? He raises this objection by taking up the mere expression "wholesome" (*kusala*).
This, however, should be seen as a mere illustration; for the fact that she is the cause of abandoning [defilements] would indeed be accepted by the objector.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning "Pride is also twofold," the fact that pride and that craving are to be cultivated is shown, because they serve as conditions for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the arising of wholesome ones.
The connection is as follows: "dejection based on renunciation" refers to the dejection that arises from grieving, thinking, "I was unable to reach the plane of the Noble Ones.

The construction is: "In this way"—meaning by the manner described in the Pāḷi—having established longing, one should apply insight (vipassanā) by way of impermanence and so forth when a desirable object enters the range of the six sense doors. And here, a "desirable object" is...
This is for the purpose of showing that the arising of the aforementioned sorrow and dejection occurs because the object as it has been adhered to is undesirable.
In order to explain the meaning of the phrase "by way of renunciation" (*nekkhammavasena*), the words "by way of insight" (*vipassanāvasena*) and so forth were stated.
Alternatively, wholesome states—whether occurring apart from insight and the like, or by way of the first jhāna and so on—are here termed "renunciation."
Since access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) alone is included by the mention of "recollection" (*anussati*), it is stated as "by way of the first jhāna, etc.
By the word "etc.," the higher distinctions from the second jhāna up to the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*) are comprised. "By that liberation through wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*);

"by way of the state of purity of mindfulness born of equanimity" (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi-bhāvena*) means by the presence of the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity. "Worthy of work" (*kamma-yogga*).
It is suitable, appropriate, and fitting for the practice of insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvanā) and other such tasks.

"By lack of faith" means on account of lack of faith; they also read it as "by lack of faith," which has the same meaning. "Attained to illumination" means attained to the illumination of knowledge (ñāṇa).
Granted that wisdom (paññā) was mentioned previously, yet the dispelling of other defilements (kilesa) by means of lack of faith and so forth also occurs through wisdom alone.
And in order to show that it is of such a nature, it is said: “Having reached illumination, it does not waver in the darkness of the defilements.

*Kopa* is anger; *appaccaya* is displeasure. Since the six supernormal powers, beginning with the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*), are already well known, he says “the two special qualities” to point out the specific states mentioned; namely, “the mind-made power (*manomayiddhi*) and the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*). *Aṅgaṇāni*.

Lust and the rest [are the defilements]. The secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*) are covetousness, improper greed, and so forth. "Conforming" (*anulomana*) means being associated with those [defilements].
"Quivering" (*phandana*) is a weak manifestation of distraction; "violent agitation" (*balavatī anavaṭṭhāna*) is instability.

All wrong adherence arises through unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and wrong thought (*micchā-vitakka*). In this context, unwise attention is an unwholesome arising of consciousness included within that [category].
It is said that wrong thought is accompanied by distraction; thus it is stated: "Because it is the cause of wrong adherence, it belongs to the side of views.
For this has been said: "Thought is a basis for views, and improper attention is also a basis for views.
Alternatively, *iñjanā* means wavering, which is the limited expectation regarding what has been seen. As it was said: "That too, for those venerable recluses and brahmins..."
“For those who do not know and do not see, feeling is merely the agitation and vacillation of those who have fallen into craving. “Instability” means non-abiding;

it refers to speculative thought (*diṭṭhivitakka*). For by that, the worldling—leaping from one grasp of views to another, sometimes eternalism and sometimes annihilationism—is like a blind man strayed from the path, or like a boatman who has cast away his vessel in the ocean.
It revolves in various ways, like a potter’s wheel or like a yoked ox. Therefore he said: “Views are a basis for views;

thought is also a basis for views. And in this interpretation, because it consists in wrong adherence and because it is the cause of wrong adherence, it should be understood that the term is formed by the *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (the retention of one part of a group of similar things) with respect to its two aspects.
With the words “Thus,” etc., he shows the connection with the Pāḷi passage beginning with “He [perceives] the upper,” etc.
By stating “in the perceptions of resistance,” he indicates that the word *saññā* is used in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) with the sense of the locative (*bhumm-attha*).

By “perceptions of the fine-material sphere,” he refers to the fine-material-sphere jhānas by way of their characteristic of perception (*saññā-sīsa*). “Perceptions of diversity” means perceptions that have diverse intrinsic natures, or perceptions directed toward objects of diverse intrinsic natures.

Excluding the perception of repulsion, these are the remaining perceptions of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). "He transcends them" means he correctly transcends those perceptions of form and perceptions of diversity together with their objects.
Even the radiance of the fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) jhāna has the kasiṇa as its object; for the arising of the immaterial-sphere (ārūppa) jhāna is the outflow of the kasiṇa. "Seeing" means...
