It is the seeing of the kasiṇa-forms. The arousal of energy together with the abandoning of covetousness and ill will is the supportive serenity;
mindfulness and tranquility are stated to be the requisites and factors. Since there is no contemplation devoid of mindfulness, it is said:
"That mindfulness which is established and unconfused—this is insight. Thus, by way of this heading of mindfulness, insight is included.
It shows [this]. The connection is: "He has stated the abandoning of delusions.

(54) The remaining specific qualities of this concentration—such as its peacefulness and loftiness—are described in the text by way of its being pleasant in the present, having a pleasant ripening in the future, being kamma-resultant, non-material, and not practiced by base men; these too are included here. Of those...

Showing the meaning of the terms, he said, “Because of the tranquility of the factors,” and so forth. Therein, “because of the tranquility of the factors” means because of the subsiding of the factors of the fruit-jhāna.
“Because of the tranquility of the distress of the defilements” means because of the allaying of the distress caused by the defilements. “Exalted” means sublime.
“By way of singleness” means by way of singleness consisting in path-concentration. “Singleness” means concentration. [This refers to] mundane concentration.
The adverse hindrances, attachment to the first jhāna, and so forth, must be suppressed, as must other defilements be prevented.
However, because the defilements have been stilled in this concentration of arahantship, there is nothing further to be suppressed or prevented;
for it is attained with little effort immediately after the path, and because it is stable.
Or, because it has been attained by way of non-decline, it is "restrained by the suppression of formations" (*na-saṅkhāra-niggayha-vārita-gata*).

By the phrase "one who has reached the fullness of mindfulness," he shows that even when mindfulness is not actually occurring, one is still called "mindful" due to the abundance of mindfulness. By the phrase "by way of the time delimited," he shows that one is mindful through a mindfulness that is delimited.
"By what will be stated" refers to what is immediately following, beginning with "the pervasion of rapture" (*pīti-pharaṇā*). Furthermore, "the state of pervasion by rapture" (*pīti-pharaṇatā*)...
This has come down in the Pāḷi. It is stated there because wisdom (paññā) is taught as a factor of concentration under the heading "five-factored right concentration.
For that very reason, the commentary provides an explanation of the meaning for such terms as "the pervasion by rapture" (pītipharaṇatā) and so forth.
In that context, according to the method beginning with "he drenches this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion," [it refers] to rapture and happiness.
And its pervasion is to be understood. The rest is indeed easy to understand.

When it is said that "serenity (samatha) is extracted by way of concentration," the intention is that serenity is extracted by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva), not by way of its contributory factors (upakāraka-dhamma).
Because concentration is the antidote to lust, it is stated: "training in the training of higher mind. [This is] according to the method already explained.

“By the uprooting of the aspiration for pleasure and so forth, it is ‘wishless’”—thus it is said. And herein, for one who correctly perceives the momentary perishability of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*), lust finds no foothold;
therefore, the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is said to be suitable for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).
Likewise, for one who correctly perceives the intrinsic suffering-nature of conditioned phenomena, [the contemplation of suffering is suitable] even toward those who are naturally suffering.
The contemplation of suffering is said to be suitable for one of a hateful temperament because, like pouring caustic water on a wound, no hatred finds a footing; likewise,
when the compactness of formations has been correctly resolved through their analysis,
and emptiness of self presents itself, no delusion finds a footing— thus, the contemplation of non-self is suitable for one of a deluded temperament.
It should be understood that [this] has been stated. Because concentration is the direct opposite of lust, it is said, "training in the training of higher mind.
This same method applies to the others. The rest here is easy to understand.
One who is abundant in patience, dwelling having overcome arisen discontent and lack of delight, attains concentration with ease.
Patience as the primary factor is also said to be the cause for inclining toward the side of serenity (*samatha*). "Exertion succeeds" means that bodily energy (*kāyika-vīriya*) is perfected.

Regarding the distinction between right action (*sammā-kammanta*) and effort (*vāyāma*) mentioned in the Canon, it should be understood in terms of their respective origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), namely, whether they originate from the body and so forth.

By the phrase “swift attainment,” he shows the state of practicing the path. By the phrase “attainment of liberation through insight,” he shows that, by the power of insight (*vipassanā*), there is liberation through eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*), just as there is liberation through suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*) by the power of serenity (*samatha*).
“From worldly things” (*lokīyehi*) is an ablative expression. “Of the great” means of the sublime; the sense is “of the excellent.”
56. This is the Mode of Conveying Investigation (*vicayahāra*).
"Purifying" means purifying in such a way that defilements such as ignorance do not arise regarding objects like the refuges; thus he purifies.
"Fulfilling" means fulfilling in such a way that virtue becomes complete—unbroken and so forth—and without deficiency; thus they fulfill it.

By the phrase "practicing in such a way," the Teacher’s state of being a great benefactor (*mahāpaṭikāra*) is shown to be complete; thus, in the first discourse it was said: "the plane of seeing and the plane of development.

"For the sake of which" means for the sake of abandoning whichever [defilements]. "Practicing in such a way" means practicing in the manner by which, having made the jhāna on the foul (*asubha*) and so forth the basis, there is the attainment of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) and so forth.
"Slaughtered" means killed.

“Being human” (*manussabhūta*)—this should be construed in relation to what precedes and follows as: “the father, being human, was one whose taints were destroyed,” and likewise, “the mother, being human.
*Anussāvana* is the proclamation in accordance with the division [of the assembly], or the making known by means of speech that conforms to that division.
57. "Humanity" means the state of being born as a human. "Perfection of gender" means the male sex.
"Causes" refers to the excellence of prior causes together with the accomplishment of mental and verbal aspirations. "Seeing the Teacher" means being in the presence of the Teacher.

"Perfection of qualities" means the attainment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). "Service" means performing service for the Teacher regardless of one's own body.
*Chandatā* is the firm desire for Buddhahood, the state of being irreversible.
As for the statement "they do not arise," it means they exist;

for while standing within this world-system, the Blessed One said, "I have no teacher, and no one equal to me is found," and so forth. [The interlocutor asks: "But, friend Sāriputta, is there now anyone else..."
“Whether it be a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, if asked whether there is anyone equal to the Blessed One in perfect enlightenment, I would say, ‘No,’ venerable sir.
Having said this, the Dhammasenāpati himself, in order to demonstrate the reason for this, presented the following sutta:
“It is impossible, it is out of the question, that in a single world-system there should be two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones.”
The intention is that, having set aside this world-system which has become a Buddha-field, non-arising is stated elsewhere.
It is as if a demarcation of the field has been made, such that it is designated: "This is the Buddha-field.
Thus, they have attained the state of being a proper location (*ṭhāna*) in the manner described; or rather, according to the method stated, others [locations] also [attain it] as appropriate.

They function by way of what is possible and what is impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*). He says this with reference to the aggregates bound to the faculties (*indriyabaddha-khandha*), as they serve as the basis for the designation of a "being" (*sattapaññatti*).

58. "The direct manifestation of the fruit" means the comprehension of the respective fruits of various karmas, such as "this is the fruit of this karma. "The absence of non-bestowal" refers to the absolute production of the fruit from karma when the conditions are assembled. Therefore, he says: "of those [deeds] performed and accumulated. 59.

"By means of the object of attachment" means by means of the object adhered to through the inclination of craving (*taṇhābhinivesa*). By mentioning "existence in the realm of form, existence in the formless realm, etc.," he himself demonstrates that it is like craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).

“By way of the three aggregates” means by way of the three aggregates beginning with virtue (*sīla*). “By way of the classification of the paths” means by way of the divisions of the path such as “leading everywhere,” and so forth.

“Leading to this or that place” means having the habit of going to those very respective places among the two classes of ghost-dwellings, namely from hell up to Nibbāna. “Leading everywhere” means having the habit of going to all the aforementioned places.
These eight are: Sañjīva, Kālasutta, Saṅghāta, Roruva, Mahāroruva, Tāpana, Mahātāpana, and Avīci.
The great hells. Each has four gates, and at each gate there are four secondary hells, such as the Gūtha-niraya (Feces Hell) and others;
thus they describe sixteen such subsidiary hells.
Sakka, Suyāma, and so forth, are the chief deva-kings. Pajāpati, Varuṇa, Īsāna, and others are like attendants who occupy the second and subsequent positions.

Regarding the phrase "in the category of defilement-desire" (*kilesakāmapakkhe*): this is stated by way of the "intention" (*saṅkappa*) mentioned in the passage, "Intention is desire, lust is desire, intention-and-lust is desire.

For that too is called "defilement-desire" (*kilesakāma*) because it arises as a state of defilement—since it afflicts and torments—and not because it is the objective basis (*vatthu*) for defilement.
"Connected with desire" (*kāmapaṭisaṃyutta*) means associated with desire known as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), or bound to desire.

Or rather, it should be understood that even though other phenomena associated with sensual desire exist, the terms "sensual desire" (*kāma*) and "element" (*dhātu*) are conventionally established specifically for these thoughts (*vitakka*), because thought functions preeminently as the conceptualization of sensual desire. This same principle applies to the element of ill will (*byāpādadhātu*) and the others.
Harm (*vihiṃsā*) is the causing of suffering to another and to oneself; however, that which is done through wrong means is [specifically termed] harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
The diversity of the aggregates and so forth should be understood by way of the diversity of the elements, beginning with the seed-element (*bījadhātu*).
"Aggregate" (*khandha*) means a mass of things that have become two-fold. 60. "Element of inclination" (*ajjhāsayadhātu*) means the essential nature of inclination.

Just as the essential nature of excrement and such is that it flows only together with excrement and the like, even so this is the essential nature of the inclinations of individuals: that those who are immoral and so forth flow together only with those who are immoral and the like.
Because wholesome action is rooted in faith, it is said: "That which by way of faith," and so forth. For it has been stated: "Faith is the seed. One should apply the same logic to:
"that which by way of greed and by way of faith," "by way of hatred and by way of faith," and "by way of delusion and by way of faith.
"By way of energy" means by way of the energy of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*). "By way of wisdom" means...
By way of right view of the path.
It is said, "obstructed by the obstruction of fruition" because the Pāḷi states that unwholesome kamma has been given scope;
however, that should be regarded as merely illustrative, since it is intended that [the mind] is also obstructed by the obstructions of kamma and so forth. Likewise...

For just as Devadatta, Kokālika, and Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son were mentioned—even though the Blessed One, seeing that penetration [to the ultimate] was impossible for them, did not teach a discourse pertaining to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)—he nevertheless taught such a person a discourse pertaining to the cultivation of latent tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya).
Demonstrating this, he said, "penetration of the truth," and so forth. Regarding Ajātasattu and the others...

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of Saccaka and others is to be understood. For him as well, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma for the sake of creating a latent impression (vāsanā) for the future.

Indeed, thinking, "In the future, the Dispensation will be established in the island of Tambapaṇṇi," the Teacher ordained this man—who was born into that family—and he became the Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, one who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and whose taints were utterly exhausted.
Having seen that "it will be," he taught the Dhamma, and it indeed came to pass accordingly.
"Incomplete" means not having reached fullness by way of its absolute capacity to yield a result. With reference to karma accompanied by views and associated with views, it is said:
"when the karma is incomplete. Therefore, he said: "having shown the obstacle of defilements and the mixed obstacle of karma."
61. Here, however, *diṭṭhi* (wrong view) is mentioned in the text by way of its predominance, because it is the adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) that is intended.
For it has been said: “As, for example, Puṇṇa the cow-tail ascetic and Acela the dog-duty practitioner.
Precisely because of the incompleteness of that undertaking of actions based on wrong view, the Blessed One addressed them with the words, “Puṇṇa, there are these four kinds of kamma,” and so forth.
He taught the Dhamma. Through that teaching, they relinquished that view and became established in rightness.

62. "Mastery-purification" (paguṇa-vodāna) means purification through mastery. That very [purification] is called "emergence" because it serves as the condition for attaining the second jhāna and so forth after emerging from the first jhāna and so forth;
thus he said, "Emergence is mastery-purification. This refers to emergence from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
The arising of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). For when the life-continuum consciousness has arisen, one is said to have emerged from the attainment possessed by it.
The departure from perception and feeling itself is the "liberation through departure.
This is "emergence": this aforementioned skill is "emergence" because it serves as the cause for emergence. For thus—
It is stated: “Emergence from this or that concentration is also purification. However, because it is not included in this scriptural passage on emergence, the *Sammohavinodanī* states:
“The emergence from the attainment of cessation is called ‘emergence outside the scriptures’ (*pāḷimuttaka-vuṭṭhāna*).
As for those who might say, “There is no such thing as ‘emergence from the attainment of cessation into the fruition attainment’ in the scriptures,” [the response is as follows:]...

They should be refuted by this textual passage: "For one emerging from cessation, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition by way of immediate proximity for the attainment of fruition.

63. Regarding the phrase "this is his disposition," here, by means of the knowledge of dispositions and so forth, [one discerns] those faculties and those various [states] by which beings [are characterized].
It should be understood that this makes manifest the understanding of those [states] such as the inclinations toward the wholesome and the unwholesome.

And by doing so, the distinctness of the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of their inclinations and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*) as separate and uncommon [knowledges], as well as the distinct power of the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties and the knowledge of their various dispositions (*nānādhimuttikatā-ñāṇa*), are established.

Regarding the term "firmly rooted" (*thāmagata*): here, "becoming firmly rooted" should be understood as the unique, individual nature of sensual lust and the other [defilements] which is not shared with others, since it is said: "One abandons an underlying tendency when it has become firmly rooted."
He remembers by mere advertence (āvajjana), because his state of being is dependent upon his wish. For it is said:
"The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is bound up with his wish; the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is bound up with his attention," and so forth.
Indeed, like the knowledge of omniscience, all the knowledge of the Blessed One is independent of preliminary effort (parikamma).

64. Regarding the phrase "due to freedom from defilements" (*upakkilesavimuttattā*): here, the mind and so forth are themselves the defilements, or rather, they are the obstructive defilements of the karma that produces [the jhāna].

Since the power of energy (*vīriyabala*) is of great assistance in all instances—whether it be the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*, the production of the jhāna, the state of the *kasiṇa*, the fourteenfold taming of the mind, or the launching of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*)—it is stated: "produced by the power of the development of energy."

"Divine-like" (*dibbasadisatta*): that which exists in the divine is "divine" (*dibba*), namely the eye of clarity as previously described; or it is "divine" because it is like the divine, being the pinnacle of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
The "divine abode" (*dibbavihāra*) refers to the four fine-material-sphere jhānas. It is called "divine" because it is to be acquired by being produced through them;
thus he shows that it is called "divine" because it has the divine as its cause. "Because of being dependent on the divine abode" (*dibbavihārasannissitattā*)...

Because it is produced by means of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere as its supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), this shows that they "shine" (*dibbanti*) while supported by the divine (*dibba*).

It is stated that "the etymologists (*akkharacintaka*) recite the word *divu* in the sense of play and so forth"; therefore, it is said: "all of that should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
For the first three meanings are shown by way of the sense of "play," while the others are shown solely by way of the senses of "shining" (*juti*) and "going" (*gati*).
“Within the range of humans” means within the domain of humans. Because the momentary present (*khaṇapaccuppanna*) lasts only for a brief instant, it is impossible to see [beings] by that definition.
By the phrase beginning with “on the verge of death,” he shows that the expressions “passing away” and “being reborn” are stated in terms of the continuity present (*santatipaccuppanna*).

By the phrase beginning with “because they are associated with the outflow of delusion,” he shows that the states of beings—whether inferior or superior—are caused by the roots of karma such as delusion.
And it shows the result of outflow (*nissandaphala*). They have the divine eye as their basis, thus they are "based on the divine eye" (*dibbacakkhupādakāni*).
Therefore it was said: "They succeed together with the divine eye. For these are his ancillary knowledges (*paribhaṇḍañāṇa*). They are undertaken, thus they are "undertakings" (*samādānāni*);
those for whom there are undertakings of action are "those who undertake actions" (*kammasamādānā*). [This refers to] various kinds of actions that are to be undertaken.
The first meaning is "meaning" (*attha*); however, in the second sense, they are called "undertakings of action" (*kamma-samādāna*) because they cause one to undertake actions.
"Undertakings of action through wrong view" means undertakings of action by means of wrong view; here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
"That speech" refers to that speech which reviles the Noble Ones. "That mind" refers to the originating mind. "That view" refers to...
By whatever wrong grasp he reviles the Noble Ones, that is a false adherence. This is the meaning here:

just as for a bhikkhu endowed with the cause who, having accomplished pure virtue and concentration, stands firm, the arising of mindfulness is slow [yet] there is either final knowledge in this very life through swift direct knowledge, or, if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning; even so...
One who reviles the Noble Ones— having not departed from the aforementioned states of mind and views, and being of an unsuitable nature— does not ask for forgiveness by confessing his transgression,
saying, "Venerable sir, I have spoken thus concerning you," then, with the breakup of the body, he goes to hell. In this context,
asking for forgiveness from those toward whom one has a confident mind is indeed the abandoning and relinquishing of those very words and other such actions.
There is nothing more blameworthy than this, because it ordains every kind of misfortune and consumes all benefit and happiness.

Regarding the phrase "with the breakup of the body" (*kāyassa bhedā*), the word "body" (*kāya*) here is a synonym for the personal existence (*attabhāva*); thus he said, "due to the relinquishing of the acquired aggregates" (*upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā*).
"Immediately after that" (*tadanantaram*) means immediately after that relinquishing of the aggregates, which is termed death. The meaning is the aggregates that have been reborn.
The word *para* may refer either to an object that is not proximate (*anorima-bhūta-vatthu*) or to a mere qualification of a limit (*avadhi-visesana-matta*).
With reference to the former, he says, “in the grasping of the reborn aggregates”; but with respect to the latter, “after death.

“By the reverse of what was stated” means by such expressions as “well-conducted” (*suṭṭhu-carita*) or “beautifully-conducted” (*sobhana-carita*), and so forth. “Killing” (*hanana*) means slaying (*ghātana*).

"Reasonable and unreasonable" refers to what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*). Having taken as "kamma" those mental factors associated with volition (*cetanā*) that constitute the path leading to states such as hell or to Nibbāna, he says, "only the delimitation of kamma. The interval between kamma and its result is the distinction or differentiation of the result of kamma.
It is unable to project [the result] like the eighth and ninth powers; the knowledge of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) is similar to that.
"Like [the power] to transform"—by this, he precludes its being like the hundredfold power of physical strength. Or, "like the knowledge of jhāna and so forth," it is applied and transformed.

For although the reviewing-knowledge of jhāna and so forth is called the sixth power here, and its state of having both initial and sustained application (savitakka-savicāra) has been stated, nevertheless, since there is no reviewing without jhāna and so forth, the knowledge associated with jhāna and so forth is included within that.

It was said thus for this reason. Alternatively, it was stated—"having become jhāna, it cannot enter [attainment], nor having become psychic power (iddhi), can it perform transformations"—in order to show that omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is not capable of performing all the functions of power (bala) in the same way as jhāna and so forth does;
however, it should not be understood that any particular power itself becomes jhāna or psychic power.
The commentary on the Mode of Conveying Investigation is finished.
3. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Reasoning: 65.
Wholesome states that are obstructed by their opposites are unable even to arise; and even when they have arisen, they do not [persist] correctly.
Because they are like those that have not yet arisen due to their inability to perform their own function, the phrase "the six bases beginning with the mind...

will be" was stated in order to show that wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) perform their functions by warding off their opposites. Regarding the word "viharaṇtassa," it means "for the sake of dwelling.
The same principle applies here for the word "viharanto"; thus, by that [phrase], the state of having a guarded mind is expressed according to the method already stated.

And it shows that this leads to right intention as one’s range of activity. "In the manner stated" means by way of having purified thoughts of renunciation and so forth, without giving any opportunity for wrong intentions.
"Only non-perverted" refers to the grasping [of the object] from the perspective of the impurity of the body and so on.
"Fear of falling into ruin" means fear of an unhappy rebirth. And all this meaning is expressed by the phrase: "right intention as one's range of activity."
In such passages as “right view will come to be,” the meaning is indeed consistent with logical reasoning (*yutti*), because it functions as a non-discrepant cause (*anarūpa-kāraṇa-bhāva*).
The commentary on the section on the Mode of Conveying Logical Reasoning (*Yuttihārasampātavaṇṇanā*) is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Section on the Mode of Conveying Footings (*Padaṭṭhānahārasampātādivaṇṇanā*).

66. Or, because the three types of good conduct reach their fulfillment for one whose mind is guarded against defilement, therefore, regarding the phrase "for one whose mind is guarded," this state of having a guarded mind should be understood here as the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for the three types of good conduct, beginning with bodily good conduct.
"Dependent upon oneself" means dependent on oneself and not on another.
"Tato eva" (from that very [cause]) means precisely because the fruit is included by the mention of the cause.
68. Therein, the word "iti" refers to the word "is protected. 73–4.
Regarding the statement in the Pāḷi that the five faculties are comprised within three aggregates: herein, [they are so comprised] by way of the faculties of faith, energy, and mindfulness.
The threefold virtue beginning with the Pātimokkha is included because it must be purified. "Of these" means that the aggregate of virtue is comprised by them.

It is evident that the aggregates of concentration and wisdom are included by the faculties of concentration and wisdom; since the rest are likewise [included], he said: "In what follows... the method is exactly as stated."
76. Regarding the phrase "of that which is reckoned as cause, cause-arisen, condition, and condition-arisen": here, the analysis of the cause-condition has already been stated above.
The commentary on the modes of conveyance such as the foundation and the sequence is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the mixed modes of conveyance and sequence.

Now, because in the Suttas the teaching on the application of the modes (*hāra-sampāta*)—unlike the teaching on the analysis of the modes (*hāra-vibhaṅga*)—is intended to show the method of applying the modes rather than merely showing the nature of the modes themselves, [the author] says "Moreover...
and so forth, demonstrating the procedure for applying the application of the modes through other permutations according to the method found in the *Peṭakopadesa*.
Therein, regarding "knowledge and ignorance" (*vijjā-vijjāya*), it refers to the occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states of consciousness.
Showing that even non-greed and non-hate proceed by way of succession because they serve as the cause, he said: “Six things... [are] roots.

And just as they have the status of being forerunners by way of being the cause, so too they obtain the status of being forerunners by virtue of turning [the mind] under their own control; thus it was said:
“They are the masters of those states accompanied by a master, and the faculties of all mental arisings. Regarding “of non-greed”:
Of a state of consciousness associated with non-greed. By "desire for renunciation" (*nekkhammacchanda*) means by wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*).
The term "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) is established in such contexts as going forth (*pabbajjā*). For it is said:
"Going forth, the first *jhāna*, Nibbāna, and insight (*vipassanā*)."
“All wholesome states are called ‘renunciation.
Among these, it is the wholesome states that are intended here. Therefore it was said: “by wholesome desire.
This means by renunciate desire acting as a decisive support (upanissaya), not as a dominant influence (adhipati). What is meant is this: when an arising of consciousness is dominated by non-greed...

When there is the desire for renunciation (*nekkhammacchanda*) acting as a decisive support (*upanissaya*), the mind becomes their precursor. The same principle applies to the other two phrases as well.
To the extent that the mind is the precursor of those states, to that same extent it is their eldest and their chief;
thus it is said: "Mind is the best of these states," and so forth. "Mind-made-ness" (*manomayatā*) is the state of being produced by the mind and so on. That...
And it is because of this very fact that mind serves as a condition for them through such relations as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth, that it is said: "Mind-made... [etc. ...condition.
Now, regarding the word *pana* in the phrase "But those," the particle *pana* indicates a specific distinction;

by this he shows that although desire and the other factors are indeed conditions for those mental states, it is specifically mind—which functions as a condition with particular prominence by way of the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*)—that is being referred to.

It is stated as "mind-made" (*manomaya*) precisely because of this [mental] basis. In that context, "produced by desire" (*chandasamudānītā*) means properly led higher and higher by the aforementioned desires for renunciation and so forth;

thus, the meaning is "arisen from that. For that very reason, because they have arisen from thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and the like, they are "originated by an undisturbed intention" (*anāvilasaṅkappasamuṭṭhānā*).
Because they are determined together with the contact of the corresponding mind-consciousness element (*tajjā-manoviññāṇadhātu-samphassa*), they are "conjoined with contact" (*phassasamodhānā*).
For it has been said: “Touched, monks, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one wills.
This is mental action (*manokamma*). That which occurs through a mind endowed with faith and clarity, without moving the limbs of body or speech, is wholesome mental action.
Furthermore, that is threefold: accompanied by non-covetousness, accompanied by non-ill-will, and accompanied by right view.

"Bhāsati" (he speaks) means that one accomplishes what is to be accomplished by means of vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), which functions through the medium of speech by way of non-deception and so forth; by this, wholesome verbal action proceeding from the door of the body is also included.
For he will say: "One speaks by the diffusion of vocal intimation and likewise by assenting. All verbal action is thus comprised.

It is fourfold by way of truth and so forth. "It performs" means that it accomplishes what is to be accomplished by bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), which functions through the movement of the limbs of the body by means of doing and not doing for the sake of one's own and others' welfare and harm; by this, wholesome bodily action proceeding from the door of speech is also included.
And thus he will say: "It performs by means of the expansion of bodily intimation and likewise by way of approval."

When understood by way of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*), it is threefold, namely through killing living beings and so forth. Therefore he said: "Thus, as shown by the ten wholesome courses of action.
The meaning of the verse is also applicable by way of the ten bases of meritorious activity (*puñña-kiriyā-vatthu*); for he will say later: "With a confident mind," and so on.
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of non-restriction, meaning that one either speaks, or acts, or engages solely with the mind. It has been commented upon in exactly this way.

"Of the tenfold wholesome kamma" means of the tenfold kamma of the paths of wholesome action, or of the wholesome kamma comprised of the ten bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu) according to the method that will be explained. [Objection:
But was not only the threefold basis of meritorious action consisting of giving and so forth mentioned there? [Response: True; however, that is because the others are included within it.
“‘Happiness follows’—having stated this in brief, he speaks the passage beginning with ‘Now suppose there were a man’ in order to show in detail that happiness follows along.
Therein, “being thus” (*evaṃ santaṃ*) means being thus become; the sense is:

having not abandoned the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), it has arisen from contact productive of pleasant feeling. Therein, by means of the meaning of the verse beginning with “Whatever mind,” he determines the Four Noble Truths. Among those [truths] established from the outset...
Since the Truths were explained under the heading of the aggregates (*khandha*) among the aggregates and so forth, and because beings have diverse inclinations, this was stated thus—"In this way...

[etc. ...they are to be determined"—for the sake of skill in the planes of insight (*vipassanā-bhūmi*) through various methods, and for the sake of showing the connection between what precedes and what follows.

Having determined the gratification (*assāda*) and so forth under the heading of the Truths, it is now said in order to apply them to the convergence of the "nutriment" of the teaching (*desanā-hāra*).

Regarding the phrase beginning with “therein, by way of origin,” it is exactly as previously explained. Whatever else here has not been analyzed in terms of its meaning should be understood as being because it follows the method already stated below and because its meaning is obvious. “In that which has the characteristic of cognizing” means:

having as its cause the characteristic of cognizing. Alternatively, the reading is “by way of the characteristic of cognizing. [It is said to be] due to the absence of striving, that is, the absence of activity.
Because it is endowed with that confidence (*pasāda*) by which the mind is called "confident," he assigns the function of that confidence to the mind and says:

"by being untroubled and by fixing upon the object. Likewise, instead of saying "by way of approval" (*sādiyanato*) in terms of speech, he says "by approving through contact" (*phassasādiyanato*), meaning by way of assent. In the second [case], "by way of approval" refers to the body.

"It should be done" means that it has been performed; this is because of the verbal arrangement [of the vow]. "Because of being well-practiced" means because of having accumulated [merit] in such a way that it follows after ease;
this is the meaning. "Therefore" means for that reason—namely, by reason of a mind that is confident, by speaking, and by acting;
this is what is meant. "In this other matter" refers to this specific sense. "Therefore" means for that very reason. For he who...
What is meant is that because of that speech and action performed with a serene mind, happiness follows one for that very reason.
"Because of its pleasant nature" means because of the presence of pleasant feeling (*sātavedanā*). "Because of its desirable nature" means because of its agreeable quality.

He said, "It is stated that... follows," because while the *kamma* is produced by virtue of its capacity to yield the fruit of the arising of a result, the actual result (*vipāka*) itself is not yet produced.
"Dependent on causes for its occurrence" means that action has as its cause the state of having been performed; this is the intended meaning.
"Without transmigration" means because it does not migrate from one continuum to another continuum different from that in which the action was produced.

"By way of predominance" means because it is endowed with predominance by way of co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*); for among co-nascent phenomena, it [predominates] over those associated with it.
Here, "precedence" is intended in the sense of being the forerunner by way of the mind (*manas*). "From that very [fact]" means precisely because of its connection with predominance (*ādhipacca*).

The genitive case in *manassa* is used in the sense of the accusative. It is connected with the phrase "of those phenomena. The state of being wholesome (*kusala*) is appropriate for confidence (*pasāda*), because it has wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) as its cause.
But is it not said in the analytical explanations (*vibhajja-vyākaraṇa*) that "faith arises in those disciples"?
It should be understood that this is not faith; rather, unwholesome states possessing those same characteristics are so designated.
For he will say later, "This is not clarity," and so forth. It is appropriate to say that it "follows after pleasure" because of its capacity to yield the fruit of karma.
For just as an action performed becomes capable of yielding a fruit, so too what has been performed and accumulated is said to be "accumulated."

Here, the mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) based on renunciation should be understood as wholesome (*kusala*), because they pertain to the wholesome side; these include both explorations accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) and explorations accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).
Since, however, they proceed only by depending upon the mind and not without such dependence, it is said: "The mind is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the mental explorations.
Regarding the phrase "the proximate cause for the wholesome side," first, wholesome contact is [the cause] for the wholesome.
It is a condition for the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations by way of co-nascence and other modes.
As it is said: "Monks, one who is touched feels; one who is touched perceives; one who is touched intends. In this same way, it should be understood for feeling and the others as well.
There is no need to state that faith and the rest are also conditions. "Of all" refers to those belonging to the four planes.
For wholesome states belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) serve as conditions for wholesome states of all four planes as appropriate;
likewise do those belonging to the other planes.
Because it is said, "He speaks with a confident mind," what is intended here specifically is speech that is a condition for right speech (sammāvācā).
It is said: “He speaks, thus it is right speech. Herein, this is the intended meaning:
“By this word ‘speaks,’ right speech is included. The same method applies here to the phrase “he acts, thus it is right action.

For one who stands in perfectly purified bodily and verbal action, there is purity of livelihood, not for another; thus it is said: “Those two are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of right livelihood.”

In that context, "those two" refers to right speech and right action. However, because for one established in the virtue consisting of the eight factors including right livelihood, there occurs the abandoning of unarisen unwholesome states and the non-arising of those already arisen, as well as the arising and fulfillment of unarisen wholesome states;
likewise, for one established in right effort alone, there arises right mindfulness which destroys the perception of beauty and other such perceptions regarding the body and so forth.
Since it is possible [for right livelihood to arise], therefore it is said: “Right livelihood... is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).
Because the foremost virtue is the restraint of the Pātimokkha, and because it has faith as its means of accomplishment, he says: “That is the proximate cause of virtue.
“Of those” refers to bodily and verbal actions. “By way of being a condition for action” means by way of having wholesome action as its cause.
And the word-meaning is according to the method already stated, namely: "because of conceiving, because of cognizing the object," and so forth.
This is the "turning back" (*āvatta*); it is called "turning back" by way of turning back toward both similar and dissimilar states.

For herein, the determination of wholesome roots, rightness, the path, and so forth, is the turning back toward similar states; the determination of ignorance, existence, and craving is the turning back toward dissimilar states.
The analysis of the divisions of the word-meanings and the levels of their foundations has been explained according to the method already stated and is easy to understand;

thus, showing only the analysis of the Dhamma, he says, "This is not... and so forth. Therein, having stated that the Sutta possesses a meaning to be inferred (*neyyattha*) by saying, "This is not to be taken according to the literal expression," he explains it with the words beginning with "For whoever... as to why it was said, "Suffering alone follows him."
Is it not the case that wherever there is a desire for the welfare of others, that is simply wholesome? This was not said with reference to such [wholesome intentions].

Rather, it was said with reference to the false resolve that arises among sectarian teachers—who are the seeds of all misfortune for the world and who reject all means for welfare and happiness—due to their attribution of non-existent virtues to themselves, whereby they represent what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma and Dhamma as non-Dhamma.
For even one who, wishing to perform even a small amount of merit in the world, obstructs another by relying on an evil view is censurable;
how much more so those who obstruct right practice in the Noble Discipline?
Thus, esteem, praise, and attendance toward them result only in the fruit of suffering. For it has been said: "I do not [approve], O foolish man..."
“I am envious of your arahantship; moreover, this evil course of views of yours...
will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time,” and, “He who praises one who deserves blame—the root of all misfortune is association with fools.
This is called a sutta because he speaks with reference to the first verse: “Mind is the forerunner... [the path]. “Of this” refers to the sutta being commented upon.

“Description of function” (*kiccapaññatti*) means the description of a function (*kicca*) consisting of the dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*). “Description of predominance” (*padhānapaññatti*) means the description of the state of being predominant. “Description of co-nascence” (*sahajātapaññatti*) means the description of the simultaneous existence of those phenomena (*dhamma*) with the mind (*manas*).

In the phrase “the great elements” (*mahābhūtāni*), the word “etc. (*iti*) has the sense of “beginning”; by this, all material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) that are inseparable from the great elements are included.

Regarding the compound word “preceded by the mind” (*manopubbaṅgamā*), he says, “it is not a purification of the word,” because the word “mind” (*mano*) is merely a constituent part of that [compound].
For this very reason it was said: “‘Mind precedes all,’ this is the purification of the words.

The phrase “like a shadow that never leaves” is merely an illustration of following after happiness; it does not complete the intended meaning. However, the statement “it follows after happiness” does complete the intended meaning;
thus it is said: “both the purification of the words and the purification of the undertaking.”
“Unity” is said with reference to the commonality [of all phenomena] beginning with “mind is the forerunner. The same applies to the remaining [terms].

“Diversity” is so called because, having directed the faith toward the qualities described in general terms such as “mind is the forerunner,” one establishes them in their specific excellence known as “clarity.
The same method applies to the rest as well. Faith has the nature of moisture; it dispels the fault of harshness, which is like lack of faith.
He said: "Because it suppresses ill will. "Externally" is said with reference to an object worthy of faith.
"By way of conviction" means by way of believing after having entered into and immersed oneself in the object.
"The objects of giving and so forth"—here, by the word "and so forth," agitation, moral shame, moral dread, the kasiṇa-maṇḍalas, and others are included.

Regarding "desirable objects and so forth" (*iṭṭhārammaṇādayo*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should understand the inclusion of such factors as neutral objects (*iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇa*), the doors and mental phenomena (*dvāradhamma*), and attention (*manasikāra*).

Similarly, regarding "contact" (*phassa*): the word "similarly" (*tathā*) brings forward the commonality of being a condition, in that just as desirable objects and so forth are conditions for feeling and the rest, so too is contact.
For "of feeling and the rest" (*vedanādīnaṃ*) refers to feeling and the other [mental factors].
Three aggregates are included. He speaks with reference to name-and-form (nāmarūpa) when he says, “of consciousness, [there are] feeling and so forth.

It is said that “non-hatred is the proximate cause for that which consists in virtue,” because virtue has patience as its primary characteristic. “He resolves” means he devotes himself to it and brings it forth.
“He who thus develops wholesome consciousness”—by the passage beginning with “of those not yet arisen,” etc.—[the author sets forth] the application of development and abandoning.
One who demonstrates [the meaning] by investigating the sense of the verse according to its penetration-facilitating aspect (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) may also apply it in this way;
thus it is cited as an example in the *padaṭṭhāna-niddesa* according to its habituation-facilitating aspect (*vāsanābhāgiya*).

Having thus shown the method of applying the "Modes of Conveying" (*hārasampāta*) by means of the verse beginning "Mind precedes all phenomena" (*manopubbaṅgamā dhammā*), he now says "Likewise, merit for the giver... and so forth, in order to show it by means of another verse. Therein, "consisting of development" (*bhāvanāmaya*) means consisting of the development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanāmaya*).

“Non-greed is a root of the wholesome,” and so forth, is stated because non-greed and the others are predominant in giving and the other perfections. In all instances, the word “stated” (*vutta*) should be supplied and connected [to the respective terms]. “Of these” refers to greed and the other defilements. By “escape” (*nissaraṇa*), he means specifically final *nibbāna*.
One whose nature is renunciation, whose inclination is toward non-greed, and who sees the danger in sense pleasures, fulfills virtue properly;
thus he says, “For one who gives... [is] the proximate cause. Here, “coarse” defilements refer to the state of transgression, and their abandonment is [the goal].
It should be understood by the abandoning of those factors. "Of the middling" refers to the state of active obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
"Of the subtle" refers to the state of latent tendencies (*anusaya*).

"The plane of the one who has done" refers to the plane of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "Giving" means giving the gift of fearlessness to the world with its devas through non-greed accompanied by the Path. "Merit" means...

Supramundane wholesome [action]. "By restraint" means: for one who restrains by means of the restraint of the Path—namely, through right speech, right action, and right livelihood included within the Path—from defilements such as those associated with views (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*).
"Enmity" (*vera*) refers to evil such as the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*).

"Wholesome" (*kusala*) means skilled and discerning through right view of the Path. "He abandons evil" means: by means of each respective Path, he abandons the various evil states that are to be abandoned.
He abandons and completely cuts off [the defilements] by way of specific conditions; therefore he said, “The path has been described.

Since the roots of the wholesome were previously mentioned without distinction in the passage beginning with “of one giving,” he now mentions them with distinction, saying, “the mundane root of the wholesome,” and so forth.

The stage of the worldling (*puthujjana-bhūmi*) and the stage of the trainee (*sekha-bhūmi*) are shown because they illustrate the state of abandonment being incomplete. The stage of the adept (*asekha-bhūmi*) is shown because it illustrates final *nirvāṇa* through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*).
The practice leading to heaven is the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipatti*).

Since merit has been discussed, its fruit has also necessarily been discussed; thus it was said: "For one giving... [and so on]... he proclaims the teaching. Showing that there is no abandoning of defilements without the meditation subject of truth (*sacca-kammaṭṭhāna*), he said: "The skillful one... [and so on]... he proclaims the teaching.
The word *vera* (enmity) is also conventionally used for evil states such as taking what is not given; thus it was said: "In this way, all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*)..."

“They should be explained in detail. There are two kinds of liberation: the liberation of those in training (*sekha*) and the liberation of those beyond training (*asekha*), as well as liberation with a residue remaining (*saupādisesa*) and liberation without a residue remaining (*anupādisesa*).
For it will be said: “‘Extinguished’ refers to the two elements of Nibbāna,” and so forth.

By the metaphorical application of the cause, or by the inclusion of the cause within the fruit, he says: “the two happy destinies,” and so forth. These are the excellences of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*).
The fruit of this teaching is that giving, virtue, and meditation are the means;
"one who desires the two kinds of success must be heedful in giving and the rest"— it is with reference to this instruction of the Blessed One that he said,
"the fruit and so forth should be understood according to their respective order."
"Vicaya" means "investigation"; thus, the sense is that it is a convergence of the modes of investigation (*vicayahāra*).
This same method applies to the subsequent [terms] as well. By the phrase "the threefold gift-based [merit]," etc., he demonstrates the investigation of the meaning of the words (*padatthavicaya*);

by this, the factors such as gratification (*assāda*) and the other meanings of the words for the modes of investigation are indeed investigated in their actual sense. The connection is that the relinquishing of objects such as visible forms has been stated. "All" means...
Because all duties have been stated without exception.
It is said that for one who delights in giving, the foundation of generosity reaches fulfillment; thus it is stated: "For one who gives... [the basis]...
For one who stands firm in the truth of abstinence and the truth of speech, the foundation of truth reaches fulfillment; thus it is stated: "Restraint... [the basis]..."
“...the proximate cause. Because of its association with skill and because of the abandoning of evil, it reaches the full perfection of wisdom; thus it is said: “Skillful... [etc.
...the proximate cause. When greed and the other defilements have been abandoned without remainder, tranquility is said to be established;
thus it is said: “Greed... [etc. ...the proximate cause.”

Regarding the term "skilled" (*kusala*), he says, "The skilled one... because of having a single characteristic through the state of being path-factors, etc.," by way of referring to a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānena*) as one possessing skillful right view (*kosallasammādiṭṭhi*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), he includes the state of being factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyabhāva*), and so forth. "By way of being something to be exhausted" means by way of being something to be abandoned (*pahātabbabhāvena*).
"Free from enmity" means the absence of adversaries. "By wholesome states" (*kusaladhammehi*) means by blameless states; the intended meaning is by way of the fruits and Nibbāna.

The reflection upon these three—the great fruitfulness of giving, the Teacher’s state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings due to qualities such as virtue, and final nibbāna through non-clinging—is the source of this gift;
this meaning is indeed established in the Pāḷi. Since the etymologies, sources, and connections are easy to understand, he said:
"The etymologies, sources, and connections should be told."

By way of describing its opposite, this origin—which belongs to the side of defilements such as stinginess—is determined for the purpose of teaching through the description of its opposite. [The text says: "By non-greed... by giving and so forth.
By the mention of "giving and so forth," those factors such as non-greed by which giving and the other wholesome states arise are included; thus, he determines these as the roots of the wholesome.
"Three wholesome [roots]. "Of these" refers to the wholesome roots.
One gives out of fear by way of a gift of honorarium and so forth. One gives out of lust for a similar object. One gives for the sake of some small material thing by way of bribery and so forth.
Or one gives out of compassion toward a field of compassion, or out of respect toward a field of virtue, or toward a field of benefactors.
“Ceased through fear” means ceased out of fear. By such restraint, enmity is certainly not accumulated. Thus, the construction is:
for all unwholesome [action], the ripening is evil.

Just as the reversal was shown by way of the negation of giving in the passage beginning with “of one who gives,” so too the reversal should be shown by way of the negation of abandoning; hence it is said: “But the unwholesome one does not abandon.”

"One who has faith in the fruit of kamma, who exerts himself in the act of giving, who establishes mindfulness regarding the manner in which a gift should be given, who concentrates the mind, and who places right view foremost, is one who practices rightly in giving.
Thus it was said: "Giving, indeed... [is]... and so forth.

Since the applications regarding development (*bhāvanā*) and abandoning (*pahāna*) are clearly understood from their literal form in the text, the passage beginning with “That is the footing (*padaṭṭhāna*) for virtue” was stated in order to show the applications of synonyms and footings; this is easy to understand.
Furthermore, whatever else here has not been analyzed in terms of its meaning should be understood as being because it follows the stated method and because its meaning is obvious.
The commentary on the section on the sequence of strings is finished.
Commentary on the section on the arising of the methods: 79.
To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly as "by way of the difference in objects," he says "for just as... and so forth.
In this context, "by way of method" means by way of grasping the method. For insight-knowledge does not proceed as a direct perception in the same manner as penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*).
"Being awakened to accordingly" means being awakened to in a manner conforming to the knowledge of clear comprehension (*abhisamaya-ñāṇa*).
The meaning is that just as path-knowledge proceeds through a single penetration, so too it is grasped by insight-knowledge in a manner suitable thereto. And thus...

Having done so, the status of the three methods beginning with the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* as modes of meaning (*atthanaya*) is established. For indeed, because they possess the specific nature of the meaning of the suttas, the three methods are called "the meaning of the sutta" (*suttattha*);
yet, even though they consist in the investigation of the meaning of words, the *hāras* are called "the investigation of the phrasing" (*byañjanavicaya*).
If this is so, how [can there be] "three"? Addressing this objection, he says: "But for those who penetrate... and so forth. Therein, each one...
The construction is: "There is a twofold inclusion by way of the distinction between defilement and purification.

"Like four and eight" means that those [diagrams], such as the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* and others, do not individually consist of four or eight directions; rather, they follow their respective order. The words "Thus," and so forth, are the conclusion of the meaning as previously stated.
"And likewise" is the corroboration through the accumulation of the meaning as previously stated. "A prior limit is not discerned" means...
What should be said here will be made clear later in the discussion on the *Paṭṭhāna*.
Because of such statements as, "Then there is blinding darkness for the man whom greed overcomes," craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) also has the nature of concealing;
hence, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is called an "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*). However, the concealment of the danger in states of existence (*bhava*) by ignorance (*avijjā*) is particularly prominent.
In the same way, ignorance (*avijjā*) also has the nature of a fetter (*saṃyojana*), since it is described as a fetter directed toward the external. Even so, he said, “Nevertheless... [etc.

...is stated,” in order to show this point: that although this is the case, the sense of being a bond (*bandhana*) is especially predominant in the case of craving (*taṇhā*) because of its status as that which is depended upon.
Regarding the word “bound together” (*saṃyuttā*), he said “mixed” (*missitā*) as its meaning. “Overcome by ignorance... [etc. ...clinging firmly.”
By this, he shows that ignorance (*avijjā*) is the cause of grasping at things as they are not; therefore, because one finds what should not be found, it is called "ignorance.

Regarding "defilement" (*kilissana*) and "torment" (*upatāpana*), he says: "the practice of self-torment, which is the application of defilement. "Clinging" (*allīyana*) means "association. Regarding "suffering" (*dukkha*)...
[they] "know" it as the bodily and mental suffering that is being experienced by oneself and appears in various ways.
Or they know another part as well. The same method applies to craving (*taṇhā*).
By saying "This is suffering" and so forth, [the author] shows that they possess no knowledge at all regarding the modes of proceeding there—whether in a similar or dissimilar manner.

"Even the mere occurrence and the cause of occurrence" means even this much: "occurrence and the cause of occurrence. But what kind of talk is this? Even regarding the mundane, which is common to ordinary people...

When there is an obstruction to knowledge regarding the meaning, what more need be said about that meaning which is supremely profound, the exclusive domain of the Noble Ones, and designated as the cessation and the cause of cessation in the supramundane? The meaning is that "the discussion is cut off.
At such a time, when both the entire serenity (samatha) consisting of the eight attainments and the success of outsiders are present, [it is called] "the foundation of insight" (vipassanādhiṭṭhāna).
It is specified [as follows]: cessation is both complete eradication and subsidence.

The phrase "because of the non-interruption of the round of existence" (*saṃsārassa anupacchedanato*) is a demonstration of the views held by those who follow wrong views. For he fears that if he does not see the face of his son, the round of existence would be cut off. Hence it is said:
"Gaṇḍuppāda, Kikī, and Kuntī, the Brāhmaṇa Dhammika;..."
"These four deluded persons fear what is fearless. Regarding the term *tadabhiññā*:

they "know thoroughly" (*abhijānanti*) those two aforementioned extremes by ascribing excellence [to them]; thus, they are "those who know thoroughly" (*tadabhiññā*). Because they destroy one's welfare and because they resemble diseases, tumors, and arrows, the defilements of the personal existence (*attabhāva-saṃkilesa*) are like diseases, tumors, and arrows.

In the phrase *sakkāyadassane*, there is the seeing of views; the meaning is that the view of a self-identity (*sakkāya*) itself is the seeing—thus, it is "the seeing of self-identity" (*sakkāyadassana*).
This is to be understood. "Of them" refers to those of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*). Their adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*) is powerful;

therefore, the intention is that they grasp whatever form appears as "self. The same applies to feeling and the other aggregates. However, one of craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*), taking whatever form appears as an object for craving and adhering to it through the adherence to "mine" (*attaniyābhinivesa*), regards something other than that [form] as the self.
The same applies to feeling and the other aggregates. Therefore, he said, "those of craving-temperament," and so forth. "Existing" means being apprehended in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
"Body" refers to a collection. Since a self or the like imagined by view is not apprehended in the ultimate sense, whereas the view itself is indeed apprehended, he said, "or existing as it is."
“By way of the view of a self-identity” means by way of the personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).

“Annihilationism and eternalism” refers to the views of annihilationism and eternalism because they accompany that [personality-belief]. There is also a reading: “proponents of annihilationism and eternalism.
“The spheres of the kasiṇas” means the jhānas of the kasiṇas.
"Having polished" means having sharpened.
At this point, since the side of defilement has been shown by way of the layout of the *nandiyāvaṭṭa* diagram, he says:
"Therein, by the words 'one of speculative temperament,' etc., he shows the side of purification. By the phrase "because of his intense reverence for effacement," [he indicates...]
In this context, he shows that [the person] exists because their conduct is continuous with austerity due to intense reverence.
The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. "Wrong resolve" is a counterfeit of faith, a confidence without a basis.
He says, "He shows that even beings...," because he analyzes the Dhamma itself by way of a reference to persons.
In the phrase "ye hi keci," the word *hi* is a mere particle. There is also a reading: "by these very four ways.
Since it is the Path itself that is spoken of here through the classification of the painful way (*dukkhāpaṭipadā*) and so forth, he says: "The way is indeed the path" (*paṭipadā hi maggo*).

"The path reckoned as the four directions" means the means for proceeding reckoned as the four directions. That which has two directions is "two-directioned" (*dvidisā*). Regarding "of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa": [it is so called because] it turns toward joy.
Of the method of the Turning of the Wheel of Joy (Nandiyāvaṭṭanaya). 82.

It is called *vivatta* because the round (*vaṭṭa*) turns away (*vivattati*) from it; *vivaṭṭa* is simply *vivatta*, namely the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*), or indeed Nibbāna itself. Therefore it is said: “Nibbāna. Alternatively, the Pāḷi reads: “Where is it to be seen?

Regarding “in the state of accumulation” (*upacaye*), the meaning is “in the stage of accumulation” (*upacayāvatthāya*). “Of the ten” refers to the ten bases of defilement (*kilesavatthu*), beginning with greed.
"By way of being the cause of perversion" means by way of being the cause for perversions such as the perception of the beautiful (*subhasaññā*).

For, through the mode of grasping things in reverse, one observes gratification (*assāda*) even in those phenomena that are associated with fetters (*saṃyojanīya*) and are actually fraught with danger (*ādīnava*). Indeed, such a possibility does not exist when there is knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*).
Therefore it was said: "By way of the state of the ten... [etc. ...of being. In "tenfold cause," [it refers to] the tenfold [cause].
Regarding the cause, or regarding the tenfold cause: "states conditioned by improper attention" refers to states such as the beautiful object;

"defilements with that as their object" refers to the defilements that constitute obstacles to the full understanding of nutriment. This same method applies to the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) as well.
The first perversion, occurring in relation to the body, operates both upon the aggregate of the body and upon a portion of the body, namely, edible nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*).
Thus it is said: "When the first nutriment has become the object, the first perversion occurs. Likewise, when occurring in relation to feeling, the second perversion occurs;
in relation to its condition, the nutriment of contact (phassa-āhāra); when occurring in relation to consciousness, the third perversion occurs;

in relation to its condition, the nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanā-āhāra); and when occurring in relation to mental phenomena, the fourth perversion occurs; in relation to its condition, the nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇa-āhāra).
It is said that "only when it has arisen" refers to "the fourth perversion in regard to the fourth nutriment.
Therefore he said: "The same method applies to the remaining nutriments as well. Alternatively, by means of the heading "nutriment," the desire-and-lust bound to nutriment is included.

This same method applies to the stations of consciousness as well. For this very reason he said: "By means of the heading 'nutriment,' the defilements having that as their object are intended. Regarding the first nutriment, which has become the object...
And when desire and lust for the first nutriment have reached the state of being its object—that is, have not transcended that state—the meaning is as follows:
for distortions (vipallāsā) arise therein for one whose desire and lust are not abandoned, but not for another.

Likewise, when the second distortion and so forth are unabandoned, the other types of clinging (upādāna) continue to occur simply because they have not been abandoned; thus he said, "The same method applies to the remaining sections."

And because even when clinging and the rest have not been abandoned, the fetters and so forth still continue as appropriate—due to their being of that same nature and due to their being of a nature associated with them—it is therefore said in the Pāḷi: "In the first clinging, there is the first fetter," and so on.
Hence he said: "The same method applies to the remaining terms as well."

83. "Of one who does not fully understand" means: of one who does not know by delimiting [them] through the three kinds of full understanding—namely, full understanding as the known (*ñātapariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), and full understanding as abandonment (*pahānapariññā*);

that is to say, of one who does not comprehend, as they truly are, their origin, their passing away, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them. There arises a fierce and thick desire and lust.

The intended meaning is: "because of the state of being characterized by craving. Thus, with reference to this point—that it is the cause for the defilement of adherence to views—he said, "in the manner already stated.

Perception of beauty, perception of pleasure, sensual clinging, clinging to existence, the yoke of sensual existence, covetousness, the bodily tie, the taint of sensual existence, the flood of sensual existence, the dart of lust, and inclinations toward various destinies—these are dominated by craving because they belong to the side of craving and because their essential nature is craving.

Furthermore, the predominance of craving is indeed found in the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), the ill-will bond (*byāpādakāyagantha*), and the faults of the dart of hatred (*dosasalla*), because these exist when craving exists;
in the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*), because they are the objects of craving; or in all [the other fetters], because they are the objects of craving.
The predominance of views (*diṭṭhipadhānatā*) in the latter ones should be understood according to the method already stated.
84. Regarding "in edible food": this refers to desire and lust (*chandarāga*) with respect to the object of edible food.

Having set aside the figurative explanation beginning with "when it is not abandoned," he shows it in its literal sense by stating that edible food "is by nature unattractive and is produced from what is unattractive.
For when a direct meaning is available, what is the use of figurative speech? Or, [it may mean] desire and lust for that [food].
"Success in purpose": this is how the meaning is stated here. For without desire and lust for that [object], perversion does not arise.
"Because its intrinsic nature is suffering" means because it has the intrinsic nature of suffering due to the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*).

"Because it is a condition for suffering" means because it is the cause of suffering characterized by the three types of suffering. [Those] who perceive permanence in consciousness: for instance, the monk named Sāti, the son of a fisherman.
“‘That very consciousness runs on and wanders about’—in this, he experienced the adherence to [the idea of] permanence.
The notion of a self among formations (*saṅkhāra*) for those following wrong views should be understood from the explanations of views such as “volition is the self,” and so forth.
The explanatory gloss for the term “purity of existence” (*bhavavisuddhi*) is “the bliss of extinction” (*nibbutisukha*). “Through rules and observances... [is it] happiness? etc.
By the phrase "he grasps firmly," it is shown that here the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) is the clinging to existence (*bhavupādāna*). For he will likewise say:
"by means of the clinging to existence, which is designated as the clinging to rules and observances.
They are conditions by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*) and so forth. "Established in the first yoga" means firmly grounded in the first yoga.
For the defilements that have not been abandoned, being the causes of the cycle of kamma and so forth, are said to be the "basis" for the being who possesses them.
"Coveting another" (*parābhijjhāyana*) means the act of coveting what belongs to another.

The statement, "They corrupt [the mind] through lust for existence...," was said with reference to the arising of mental distress when a cherished object undergoes change or alteration due to craving for existence, views concerning existence, or attachment to existence.
"Having knotted" means having made a knot. For "knotting" (ganthana) is the act of making a knot, as in the case of a rope or similar object that has become divided into two.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "The taints (āsava), remaining by completely seizing the mind, become the cause for the arising of the taints.

In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), the words are placed out of their regular order in order to show that certain defilements (kilesa), when they have reached the state of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), specifically become the cause for the arising of the taints.
The construction is: "it aspires toward an object that is the opposite of that.

"It aspires toward an existence abounding in such objects" means, for example, the arising among the gods for those who are weary of human sensual pleasures. "Because of its nature" means because of its nature as a view (*diṭṭhi*). "Successively" means mutually;
for one particular view becomes the cause for another's adherence to a view, just as the personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is for the others.

“Of one who adheres” means by way of adherence. The statement, “From improper attention... the taint of ignorance arises,” shows the taint of ignorance as the fruit of adherence to [the notion of] truth, just as the occurrence of a great flood is shown by the falling of rain from a cloud during the rainy season.
The taint of ignorance is established just as the falling of rain from a higher cloud is established by the occurrence of the great flood caused by that rain.

In passages such as "accompanied by delight and lust" (*nandīrāgasahagatā*), the word *sahagata* has the sense of "being that" (*tabbhāva*); thus he says, "the underlying tendencies... have become [associated].
He speaks of the "heart," which is reckoned as internal to the mind, with reference to the occurrence of resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*).
Even within the cycle of resultants, there exists some slight distinction consisting of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the defilements.

Of consciousness accompanied by greed; of the other [types], such as that accompanied by hatred and so forth. "Sauce" (*upasecana*) refers to the preparation or the enhancement of the object of perception, just as with food.
That which has "delight" (*nandi*)—meaning craving accompanied by joy—as its sauce is "delight-sauced" (*nandūpasecana*).
This is because even delight, acting as the sauce, serves as a proximate cause for the dart of lust (*rāgasalla*). But when it is sauced...
To show that there is indeed nothing further to be said, it was stated in the Pāḷi: “by consciousness which has craving as its ointment and the sting of lust.
In order to make this meaning clear, he asks: “But by what does it have craving as its ointment?

He says, “by the sting of lust,” showing that the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause: “by the sting of lust acting as the cause. This refers to the sense of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

And here, the sense is that of a cause (*hetvattha*). Having transformed the case-ending [from the instrumental], it should be construed as "by consciousness" because it is something to be approached (*upagantabbato*).

By the phrase "because of being a foundation" (*patiṭṭhābhāvato*), he states that consciousness possesses the conditionality of a support (*nissaya*) and so forth. Therefore, he says: "It stands supported by the aggregate of form.
In this way, the conditionality of support and so forth should also be stated for the second and subsequent stations of consciousness, because of the mention of "foundation" (*patiṭṭhā*).

85. Although he will explain the unwholesome roots and so forth as the "Triple Pivot" (tipukkhalo), and craving and so forth as the "Joyful Turn" (nandiyāvaṭṭo) by way of their directional aspects, nevertheless, because they do not enter into one another, when one method is established, the others are also necessarily established.

It is for the purpose of showing this distinction that it is said: "The nutriments and so forth... should be defined. Alternatively, [it is said] regarding the unwholesome roots, craving, and so forth which are to be explained later.
By including [the factors] through the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), when one says "nutriments and so forth," he uses the plural form "of the methods" (*nayānaṃ*).

"Of a single meaning" refers to a single purpose, namely the state of being an imperfection (*upakkilesatā*) in one characterized by passion (*rāgacarita*). The meaning of the phrasing (*byañjanattha*) is also included;
it is not merely the literal expression (*byañjana*) that is taken. Thus, the Sutta passages are mutually synonymous expressions, as appropriate, for the bases of craving (*taṇhāvatthu*).
Because craving was discussed there, it was stated: "Craving with its basis was spoken of.
Because the bases for hatred and the bases for views were also discussed there, he said, "in accordance with the method already stated," referring to this point:
"Hatred with its basis and views with their basis were spoken of."
The meaning is: "having grasped the aspect of suffering together with the aspect of suffering. As for the phrase "if this is so":

if the specific determination of the doors of liberation regarding the first two kinds of nutriment and so forth was made by way of one who is habituated to the respective contemplations (*anupassanā*), then this should be understood exactly thus and not otherwise.
Stating the reason for this, he says "for it is not," etc. Its meaning is: just as [it is not possible] for the noble paths...

There is a fixed rule regarding the phenomena to be abandoned because they are abandoned by means of specific defilements; however, such is not the case for insight, as its full understanding and abandoning are not final.
But others say: in the first two nutriments, the characteristic of suffering is very evident due to their state of being thoroughly afflicted and because they are conditions for suffering.
Therein, in the first two stations of consciousness—the nutriment of consciousness—the characteristic of impermanence is present in the third station of consciousness.
In the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*) and in the fourth station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) is very clearly manifest;

thus, because they serve as the gateway for the occurrence of the three contemplations (*anupassanā*), they proceed toward full understanding (*pariññā*) by way of those doors of liberation such as the wishless (*appaṇihita*).

Likewise, among the perversions (*vipallāsa*) and so forth, the first two are the direct opposites of the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), while the other two are the direct opposites of the contemplations of impermanence (*anicca*) and non-self (*anattā*).
Thus, by way of being the entrance to the process [of existence] and by way of being the direct opposite,

these states are said to be respectively to be fully understood and abandoned through the doors of liberation such as the wishless (appaṇihita), etc. Among them, the perception of beauty, the perception of pleasure, sensual clinging, clinging to rules and observances,

the yoke of sensuality, the yoke of existence, covetousness, the bodily tie, the taint of sensuality, the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the dart of lust, the thicket of views, and the state of going to the far shore— all these proceed by way of relishing pleasure.

Because they are the opposites of the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), ill-will (*byāpāda*), the bodily tie (*kāyagantha*), the fault of the dart (*salla-dosa*), and going on the wrong path (*agatigamana*) are to be abandoned through the door of the desireless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*), since these constitute the mode of occurrence [of those defilements].
