The third perception and so forth are to be abandoned through the door of the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*), because they are the opposites of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) due to their being the causes for the adherence to permanence and its signs. The fourth perception and so forth...

Because they are the opposites of the contemplation of non-self through the adherence to a self and the craving for it, they are to be abandoned by means of the void liberation door (*suññatā-vimokkha*).
In this context, it should be understood that pride, fear, and resorting to wrong courses have their cause in the adherence to permanence;
for one who sees things as impermanent, neither the conceit "I am" nor fear can arise. That ignorance, the fetters, and so forth have their cause in the adherence to a self is indeed evident.

86. The fine-material-sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti) that are free from the immeasurables (appamaññā), being considered "divine abidings" (dibba-vihāra) and "wholesome attainments leading to rebirth among the devas," are nevertheless the most excellent abidings because they consist in practice for the benefit of others and are faultless;

thus, the four immeasurables are the divine abidings (brahma-vihāra). The four attainments of fruition (phala-samāpatti) are the noble abidings (ariya-vihāra), being far removed from the defilements (kilesa).

“The abodes of the noble ones. The four formless attainments are “imperturbable abodes” because, although they are wholesome attainments that lead to rebirth among the gods, they reach the pinnacle among mundane states due to their imperturbable continuity.
“By way of distinction of basis” means by way of distinction of object.
To show that what does not occur frequently is marvelous, it is said: “...arising for a blind man... and so forth.

In the case of the coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*), the instrumental, locative, or abstract sense of the suffix should be understood according to the following: by means of this truth one resolves upon virtue and so forth;

or, in the truth which serves as the sign (*nimitta*); or, that truth is merely the act of resolution itself. Thus, the suffixes are to be understood through their respective functions as the instrumental, locative, or abstract case endings.
Likewise in the case of the *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound where the meaning is other than the constituent words).

In the other type of compound, however, the meanings are only those of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and these should be understood by way of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. "Happiness" (*sukha*) refers to the happiness of jhāna, insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), fruition (*phala*), and nibbāna.
Even mundane resultant happiness (*lokiya-vipāka-sukha*) is indeed included. For it is said in this verse: "Not otherwise than through the factors of enlightenment... [for] living beings."
The four qualities included here by way of the relinquishing of what is not-self—which bring fearlessness to beings and lead to the bliss of attaining Nibbāna—are called "conducive to happiness.
"By way of exhaustive inclusion" means by way of grasping everything without remainder through the method of pervasion.
The intention is that this refers to the first foundation of mindfulness as it occurs by way of the first mode of practice; the same applies to the others as well.
With the words “Just as,” etc., he clarifies by means of a simile that there is no necessary sequence between the aforementioned modes of practice and the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

Furthermore, although there is no fixed rule that all foundations of mindfulness must follow all modes of practice, it should be understood that this particular sequence has been established here solely according to the order of the teaching (*desanākkama*) due to their lack of necessary succession.
Alternatively, [it is because] of the perceptions of beauty and pleasure regarding the body and feelings...

Because the tasks of the contemplations on the foul and suffering are accomplished through their being difficult to resolve, the first two foundations of mindfulness are linked with the first two modes of practice;
the latter [foundations] are linked with the latter [modes] because of the absence of those [tasks].

For these [contemplations] are required for one who has performed the work in the first foundations of mindfulness. Alternatively, they are like [the remedies] for those of craving-temperament and view-temperament.

The sequence of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) has been established here in order to show that the four modes of practice (paṭipadā) are applied by way of the four types of wisdom— mild, sharp, keen, and extremely keen— and thus the four foundations of mindfulness come into being.
By the word "likewise" (tathā), it is indicated that just as the cultivation of the first foundation of mindfulness corresponds to its specific opposite, so too...

He summarizes this point as follows: "Just as the development of the second foundation of mindfulness and so forth, by virtue of being accompanied by rapture (*pīti*) and so on, brings about the distinction of the second jhāna and the others, so too [the other factors] bring about the distinction of the jhāna.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "experiencing rapture and so forth," he includes the experiencing of pleasure (*sukha*), the experiencing of mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*), and the tranquilizing (*passambhana*). And here, the mention of "gladdening the mind" (*abhippamodana*)...
This should be regarded as merely an illustration, since it is intended to apply by way of experiencing, sustaining, and liberating as well.
In the phrase "impermanence, dispassion, etc.," the word "etc. includes cessation and relinquishment.
Regarding the phrase "of the fine-material-sphere attainments," here the first jhāna that has merely been acquired is [the basis] for the attainment of the first jhāna.
It is a condition for bringing about mastery over proficiency, but not for the others.

However, it should be understood that for the others, it serves as a condition through the mode of being a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) in a successive manner. "Ill-will, cruelty, applied thought, discontent, and lust" refers to ill-will-applied thought and so forth.
"With ease" means without hardship; the meaning is "without difficulty."

Taking the four abidings, beginning with the divine abiding, as their proximate cause, the insight leading to emergence—which has arisen within various mental continuities—functions, in due order, by way of the non-arising of unarisen wholesome states and so forth;

it is with reference to this objective domain that the text says, “The first abiding, when developed and cultivated,” and so on. Herein, the right exertion is similar to [the standard] right exertion.
It has been said. This method applies to one who, relying on the lower noble abodes (*ariyavihāra*), strives for the attainment of the higher paths.

Or rather, it is said with reference to the various functions and so forth of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*) included within the path, which belong to distinct mental continua, by way of the approach of insight (*vipassanā*) as previously described.
For indeed, through the approach of insight, a specific excellence in the sharpness of the faculties such as faith and the rest is possible.
Thus, the specific domain of the function of energy (vīriya) can be understood as the Path.

Likewise, the first right effort, arising in dependence on the divine abiding characterized by purity of mindfulness and equanimity that has reached its culmination, promotes the abandonment of conceit;
the second right effort, arising in dependence on the sublime abidings (brahmavihāra), promotes the eradication of attachment to sensual pleasures (kāmālaya).
To show that the third right effort, which arises by relying on the noble abidings (ariyavihāra), abandons ignorance;
and that the fourth right effort, which arises by relying on peaceful liberation (santavimokkha), extols the subsiding of existence (bhavūpasama), it was said: "The first right effort," and so forth.
One who has abandoned conceit (māna) should not deceive; thus, the abandonment of conceit increases the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), as it is precisely the cause of deception.
Because of their non-existence. For one who has not abandoned conceit might deceive others by means of that conceit.

When the attachment to sensual pleasures (*kāmālaya*) and the attachment to views (*diṭṭhālaya*) have been eradicated, there is no opportunity at all for the opposite of generosity; thus, the eradication of attachment increases the foundation of generosity.
When ignorance (*avijjā*) is cut off, there is no obstruction to the growth of wisdom (*paññā*), regarding the formative forces of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*).

Since there is no opportunity for the subsiding of existence when [the defilements] are neglected, the passage beginning with "abandonment of conceit" (mānappahāna) was stated to show that the abandonment of conceit and so forth cause the factors based on the Truths (saccādhiṭṭhāna) and so on to flourish.

One whose nature is non-deceptive and who abounds in the desire for the Dhamma (dhammacchanda) produces concentration dominated by desire (chandādhipateyya). One who is intent on generosity (cāgādhimutta)...

One whose inclination is toward renunciation (nekkhammajjhāsaya) develops concentration dominated by energy due to an abundance of non-laziness; one who has knowledge as supreme develops concentration dominated by mind while bringing the mind under his own control;
and one whose nature is tranquil develops concentration dominated by investigation through the investigation that serves as the cause for tranquility.
Thus, [these are the bases] for the purity of resolve regarding the foundations of truth and so forth, and for concentration and the rest.
To show that it leads to fulfillment, it is said: "The foundation of truth is cultivated," and so forth.

One who abounds in the desire for the Dhamma, established in concentration through desire (chanda-samādhi), becomes one who practices blamelessly when encountering the six desirable or undesirable sense objects.
One who has aroused energy, established in concentration through energy (vīriya-samādhi), [accumulates] merit by means of the very burning away of the side of defilement.

He fulfills it. Controlling his own mind, established in concentration of mind (*cittasamādhi*), and discerning with wisdom those phenomena that are conducive or non-conducive to progress, he will bring about the expansion of his intelligence.

Established in concentration through investigation (*vīmaṃsāsamādhi*), being abundant in the discrimination of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*), he cultivates a practice that leads precisely to the relinquishing of acquisitions (*upadhipaṭinissagga*).
To show this meaning, [the text says] "concentration through desire" (*chandasamādhi*).
The passage beginning with “cultivated” and so forth has been stated.
Restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) is of great assistance in warding off near and distant adversaries;

because it is a cause for the arising of specific excellence in loving-kindness (mettā), one increases loving-kindness. By suppressing defiled states through asceticism (tapas), one who is preeminent in energy (vīriya) possesses the desire to remove the suffering of others.
"He practices with his own hand" means he increases compassion. Wisdom, being purified, grasps phenomena as faulty and faultless;
protecting joy from falling away through laughter, it causes it to flourish.

Having leaped forth into the relinquishing of acquisitions (*upadhi*), leaning, inclining, and tending toward it, one becomes truly equanimous toward the seven formations; thus, he increases the dwelling in equanimity (*upekkhā-vihāra*).

To demonstrate this meaning, it was said: “The restraint of the faculties has been developed,” and so forth. Therefore he said: “That which is the specific condition for something is said to fulfill it. 87.

Regarding the phrase “by way of being directions,” it should be construed as “by way of the directions of the methods. Its meaning is also [to be understood] according to the method explained previously.
It should be understood by which tetrad there is purification and cleansing for a person of a particular temperament, such as one dominated by passion (rāgacarita).

Just as the first distortions regarding nutriment and so forth—when not fully understood and not abandoned—are defilements for persons of passionate temperament and the like, so too, when the first way of practice and the others are developed and cultivated, they become their purifications; this is according to the method already stated.
"It can be known" was said; thus he says, "in the very manner explained below.
Alternatively, insight being accomplished by means of the first two modes of practice includes even the suffering of occurrence, which consists in the performance of its own function;
and by way of the specific excellence of the predominance of contemplation of suffering, it penetrates the characteristic of suffering.

It is called “the desireless door to liberation. When it is being accomplished through the third way of practice, because it proceeds with ease, it breaks the compactness of the continuity [of existence] in a perfectly correct manner and clarifies the characteristic of impermanence; thus it is called “the signless door to liberation.
Furthermore, when it is being accomplished through the fourth way of practice, because it proceeds with ease and because of the clarity of knowledge—
And by breaking through the density of the object consisting of the collective function [of the aggregates], it correctly clarifies the characteristic of non-self;
thus, it is called "emptiness as a gateway to liberation.
Likewise, the contemplation of the body and feelings specifically clarifies the characteristic of suffering, while the contemplation of the mind clarifies the characteristic of impermanence.
The contemplation of phenomena has the characteristic of non-self; thus, they are respectively called "the doors to liberation, namely the wishless and so forth.

Because the first and second jhānas possess rapture and gratification, they are called "the door to liberation, namely the wishless," by way of insight that specifically views them as suffering through the process of dispassion.
The third [jhāna] is [called the door to liberation, namely the signless], because of its peaceful happiness.

It is called "the signless door to liberation" by way of insight (*vipassanā*) which sees, according to its true nature, that which serves as the basis for outsiders' adherence to permanence as being "impermanent.

The fourth [door] is called "the void door to liberation" because it is completely purified through the removal of defilements and so forth, is well-concentrated, and—just as it is for others—serves as the cause for awakening to the true nature of things both for oneself and for others. Thus, it is rightly [described].
It is called the "emptiness door to liberation" by way of insight (vipassanā) that sees [things] as "empty.

Thus, the state of being doors to liberation for the abidings (vihāra) occurs precisely through insight. In this context, the state of being the "wishless door to liberation" should be applied by way of the fact that the divine and brahma abidings are desirable due to their peaceful happiness, and so forth.
This is because the noble abiding (ariyavihāra) has wisdom (paññā) as its predominant factor.
Specifically, the emptiness liberation (*suññatavimokkha*) is due to its being based on the contemplation of non-self (*anattā*).

The signless liberation gateway (*animittavimokkhamukha*) should be applied because the penetration of the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) possesses the specific causal nature for the abiding in the imperturbable (*āneñjavihāra*), which is the liberation of peace (*santavimokkha*).
Likewise, because the first two right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) have defilement as their object, [they lead] to the transcendence of the suffering of defilements.
The state of being the door to the wishless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkhamukhatā*) arises from the predominance of the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*).

For the third [jhāna], the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) becomes manifest through the discernment of the rise and fall of phenomena by means of producing wholesome states that have not yet arisen; thus, it is the door to the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkhamukhatā*).
For the fourth [jhāna], the state of phenomena not being subject to one's will is demonstrated by the non-engagement in activity toward the persistence of those states already arisen.
The characteristic of non-self is well-manifested as the gateway to the liberation of emptiness (*suññatavimokkhamukha*).

Because it assists in the abandoning of conceit and the uprooting of the underlying tendency by means of the abandoning of craving, and because it purifies the longing for craving, it is the gateway to the liberation of the wishless (*appaṇihitavimokkhamukha*).

Because the function of wisdom predominates in the abandoning of ignorance, it is the gateway to the liberation of emptiness. Because it is the antidote to the sign of formations in the pacification of existence, [it is the gateway to the signless].
The state of being the door to the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkhamukhatā*).

Not deceiving with regard to the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*)—which by their very nature have the characteristic of suffering—by means of the truth of knowledge, one sees them as suffering alone;

and by means of the liberation through relinquishment, one distances oneself from craving and dries up the longing for passion. Thus, the first two foundations (*adhiṭṭhāna*) are called "the wishless" (*appaṇihita*).

It is said, "the door to liberation. As for the other two foundations, their status as the doors to the liberations of emptiness (*suññatā*) and the signless (*animitta*) is exactly according to the method already stated.
One-pointedness of mind dominated by desire (*chanda*) occurs specifically in one who possesses a strong aspiration for the Dhamma and is abundant in thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*);
however, that dominated by energy (*vīriya*) occurs in one who is dispelling sensual thoughts (*kāma-vitakka*) and so forth. Thus, [one-pointedness] proceeds based on both of these.
Insight (vipassanā) is specifically called the "signless door to liberation" because it dries up the inclinations toward lust and so forth.

Those [insights] that proceed by relying on mental dominance and investigative dominance are respectively called the "signless door to liberation" and the "desireless door to liberation" due to their predominance in the contemplations of impermanence and non-self.
The restraint of the sense faculties, which removes covetousness, and austerity, which dispels sensual intentions and the like,

constitute the "wishless" (appaṇihita) gateway to liberation because they are the opposites of aspiration, according to the method already stated. Insight based on these two— namely, wisdom characterized by the contemplation of non-self as its sign,
and the relinquishment of acquisitions (upadhi) as the opposite of grasping at signs— is described as the "emptiness" (suññatā) and "signless" (animitta) gateways to liberation, respectively.
Loving-kindness (*mettā*), which repels lust for those who are near and is the antidote to the longing of lust, and compassion (*karuṇā*),

whose mode of activity consists in the removal of others' suffering and serves as a specific condition for the contemplation of suffering associated with suffering— insight (*vipassanā*) based upon both of these is called "the door to liberation that is the wishless" (*appaṇihita-vimokkhamukha*).
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which is characterized by a frequent apprehension of the joy of beings, [is so called] because of the vision of their impermanence (*aniccatā*).
The specific condition for the contemplation of impermanence is insight based upon it, which is the signless door to liberation.
Equanimity, due to its predominance in the function of knowledge, is the specific condition for the contemplation of non-self;
thus, the insight based upon it is called the "emptiness door to liberation. This is how it occurs here from the perspective of the mode of occurrence, the insight, and the basis.
Having analyzed them according to their functions, they are applied as the gateways to liberation.
"Surpassing" refers to both full understanding and abandoning. "In one's own and others' continuums" means in the continuum of oneself and that of others;
by this, he shows that the bodily and verbal dwelling is called "sporting" (*vikkīḷita*), taking it as "various modes of conveying" (*vividho hāro*).
However, its analysis (vibhāvanā) is intended here because it constitutes the ground for this method. By way of being their opposite:

"their state of being an opposite" refers to the state of being an opposite—and thus the state of being abandonable—of those [factors] such as nutriment; "the state of being an opposite of the practices (paṭipadā), etc.

should be construed as the state of being an opposite—and thus the state of being the abandoner—of the practices and so forth. In that context, by the mention of "practice," insight (vipassanā) is spoken of.
And since insight, by fully understanding the four nutriments, abandons the desire and lust bound up with them, their status as opposites is direct and immediate.
In the same way, the status of jhāna and the rest as opposites to clinging and so forth should be understood, because they are taught by way of insight.
The fact that the foundations of mindfulness are the opposites of the perversions is indeed evident. Thus it is said.
The *sīhavikkīḷita* (the lion’s sport) is analyzed in detail according to twenty tetrads from the perspective of their distinct characteristics;
therefore, it is said, "showing them in brief," because they are explained by grouping them under three headings.
"Of the faculties" (*indriyānaṃ*) refers to the faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*). The construction is: "the selection of ten tetrads."
88. "Niggacchati" means he goes out. For when something is stated by being extracted from that [context], it is as if it were going out.
"Four persons" refers to the four persons mentioned in the passage beginning with "the dull person of craving-temperament.
And since the Dhamma is here stated by way of a reference to persons, he says, "having pointed out the ground. "From that very [source]" means from the aforementioned tetrad of persons.

"Likewise" means: "also in the other case," namely, in the passage beginning with "for the sake of pleasure... [and so on]... persons. "Common" means mixed even with the first and fourth [types of nutriment].
"As previously stated" refers to the second and third [nutriments].
"Below" refers to the commentaries on the *Desanāhāravibhaṅga-vicayahārasampāta*.

“That same method” refers to the collection of twelve factors beginning with the roots of the wholesome, which constitutes the blameless side. He spoke thus with reference to the etymological derivation: “It is called *vodāna* because by means of it one is purified (*vodāyati*) and cleansed (*sujjhati*).
Desiring to clarify the reason and purpose for not applying the methods (*naya*) in the same way as the summary of the strings (*hāra-uddesa*) was done, he said, “But why?
and so forth. “By means of methods” means by means of other methods. “For the purpose of showing possibility” means for the purpose of demonstrating logical justification (*upapatti*).
In this context, "origin" (sambhava) refers to the cause, the demonstration, and the purpose in the exposition according to the order of the summary.
For if these methods were unmixed by way of their points of origin, they would have to be demonstrated according to the sequence of the summary, just like the strings (hārā).
Thus it was said at the conclusion of the summary of the strings: "These sixteen strings have been enumerated as unmixed in meaning."
However, because these [terms] emerge from one another through the selection of one root-term from among the root-terms,

when one is demonstrated, the other is also considered demonstrated by implication; therefore, it is said that "the demonstration was not made according to the order of the enumeration" in order to show this meaning.
Now, in order to demonstrate that same matter which was stated in brief in detail, it is said: "From the first method," and so forth.

Therein, having divided persons into two types according to their temperament of craving (*taṇhācarita*) and views (*diṭṭhicarita*), and having extracted the "turning of the plowshare" (*nandiyāvaṭṭanaya*) by way of those [two], one then divides those very same temperaments of craving and views according to the fourfold division of the paths (*catuppaṭipadā*), [which constitutes] the "lion's play" (*sīhavikkīḷita*).

The occurrence of the first method (*naya*) has been shown; those same individuals, who were previously distinguished by the division of the four modes of practice (*catuppaṭipadā*), are again divided into three types according to the classification of those who understand through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth, and thus the occurrence of the third method is shown. With reference to this, it was said: "From the first method... [and so on]... it is demonstrated.

Because greed arises from perceptions of beauty and pleasure, and hatred arises from the perception of permanence—due to the emergence of resentment thinking, "This person has done me harm"—[the second method follows].
Delusion is included within the perception of self. Likewise, non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] are included within the perception of the foul and so forth;

therefore, the second method arises from the third method by way of a reference to phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna). Furthermore, since hatred can arise when greed exists, hatred is included by the mention of greed alone.
Greed is craving, and delusion is ignorance; because they are the opposites of those, serenity is included by means of non-greed and non-hatred.

Insight arises through non-delusion; therefore, in order to show this distinction—that from the second method, the first method arises solely by way of the reference to phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna)—he said, "But by way of the reference to phenomena," and so forth, demonstrating that the exposition was not made according to the sequence of the summary (uddesa).
"For that very reason" means because the first method can arise from the second method, just as the second method arises from the third method.

Thus, relying on what has come down in the Pāḷi by way of a reference to persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), the extraction of the method (*nayaniggama*) was determined in the Aṭṭhakathā solely by way of a reference to phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*); this alone is the distinction.

If it is asked, "If that is so," and methods are to be extracted even by a manner other than the one appearing in the Pāḷi, then, while this is the case, [one might ask] how from the first method by way of a reference to persons...
The arising of the second method from the third method has been shown for the third method;

likewise, the arising of the third and second methods from the first method by way of the reference to phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), and the arising of the third method from the second method by way of the reference to phenomena, should be illustrated.
To this effect he said: "Having become two... may be."
In this context, "method" (*naya*) refers to the second method mentioned later. "By way of meaning" (*atthato*) means by way of implication;

the sense is that it was not stated in its own form precisely because it is obtainable through the meaning itself. Now, in order to demonstrate that implication as being definitive, the passage beginning with "because" (*yasmā*) was stated.
"Desired inclusion" (*anuppaveso icchito*) is due to the convergence of the root-terms of each respective method within the root-terms of other methods.

For it has been said: "That wherein the entire side of unwholesomeness finds its inclusion and convergence, and wherein the entire side of wholesomeness finds its inclusion and convergence. And this is the meaning:
"The mutual entry and emergence of the methods (nayas)"—this is the twofold meaning. The exposition of the meaning of the Piṭakas is the *Peṭaka*.
"Such is the instruction" means the *Peṭakopadesa*; the meaning is that it is a commentary on the scriptures (*pariyatti*) consisting of instructions.

"From the beginning" means starting from the first section of the investigation of the methods (*naya*), rather than merely revealing their mutual inclusion and emergence; it is the exposition, the illumination, and the clarification.
"The view of faults" means a view that grasps at defects such as the lack of relish; the meaning is "those who see faults. For they have not eradicated their underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
"And seeing the danger in sensual pleasures. For this pair of factors has been stated as the cause for the pursuit of self-mortification.
There is no benefit—meaning that benefit pertaining to the present life which is imagined by blind fools overcome by lust;
it is like licking the edge of a razor blade smeared with honey, providing little gratification and much suffering.

"Full of trouble, full of misfortune, with obstacles, with fever, and leading to future states"—thus, at all times, there is no purpose for one of wise nature in sensual pleasures. "Unclung to" means they dwell unovercome by them.
Therefore it is called a "pleasant practice," because insight is accomplished without difficulty for those persons due to that state of having dull defilements.
The practice is called "the pleasant practice. "Clinging" means being firmly attached.
"All these beings"—these refer to all beings who are practicing, divided into two types by way of their temperament of craving and views, and further distinguished into immeasurable varieties.
"They relinquish with ease" means they abandon the defilements without difficulty. "These four practices," and so forth.
This much is the demonstration that, among the paths, there is no deviation regarding their objective, state, and function.

"This is the path" is the conclusion; the intention is that these four types of persons have been determined for the purpose of showing the stages of the "Lion’s Play" method (*sīhavikkīḷita-naya*). "He points out the defilements by way of the fourfold path" refers to what will be explained immediately hereafter.
By means of the fourfold path beginning with nutriment, it explains the mass of defilements consisting of ten bases.
It should be explained by means of the fourfold path beginning with the way (paṭipadā) as the opposite of that, having distinguished [them] among the noble states (ariyadhamma),
which are the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya) serving as the objective domain.
And this measure—namely, the four nutriments—is the measure for the occurrence of these perversions.
This is what is meant: as long as the four nutriments have not been fully understood, so long do they give rise to the four perversions.
As long as the four perversions are not abandoned, so long... [do they persist].
“They nourish the clingings. In this way, it should be stated for all [terms] as appropriate.
Therefore he said: “Thus, all these ten terms... The words “are to be joined” are the ellipsis.

By the phrase “one is bound by covetousness,” he shows that covetousness itself is the bond. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. “Papañcento” means extending the adherence to views.

The defilements are called "outflows" (*āsava*) because they are the cause for the arising of remorse; thus he says, "they flow out. By asking "What is remorse? he refers to the basis for the transgression of those defilements.

Since remorse occurs only for one whose underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have not been abandoned, and not for another, it is said: "Those which are regrets are underlying tendencies. By both of these two phrases, the cause is stated by way of a metaphorical designation of the effect.

"By the first term" means by the first term among the ten sutta-terms as previously stated. "In the first direction" means in the first direction on the side of defilement within the *sīhavikkīḷita* (the lion’s sport), which is designated by that [first] meaning.

"Thus" (*iti*) means in this way; the sense is "by the method already described. "Of the wholesome and unwholesome" refers to the blameless and blameworthy phenomena as previously stated. "By way of side and its opposite" means by way of the side of purification and its opposite. "The application" is by way of being the first direction and so forth.
Having applied [the mind], there is mental equanimous observation. For it is said: “He surveys with the mind.
“Of that” refers to the surveying of the directions. That the state of being the culmination of the fruit of stream-entry and so forth is to be understood by way of the faculties (*indriya*).

For it is by way of those faculties, such as faith and the rest, that the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth are accomplished; and by way of those [foundations], the fruits of stream-entry and so forth [are attained].
This is the state of culmination. In that regard, the faculty of faith reaches fulfillment in the fruit of stream-entry;
for one who has entered the stream is a fulfiller of faith. The faculty of energy reaches fulfillment in the fruit of once-returning;
for a once-returner has initiated energy for the attainment of the higher paths. The faculty of concentration reaches fulfillment in the fruit of non-returning.
The non-returner brings concentration to fulfillment. In the case of the supreme fruit, arahantship, the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of wisdom reach fulfillment.
For the arahant has attained the fullness of mindfulness and the fullness of wisdom.
However, others say: by the power of faith comes the abandoning of the perception of beauty; for one who has faith applies attention to the repulsive.

One performs the task. Through the power of energy (*vīriya*), there is the abandoning of the perception of pleasure. For one possessed of energy overcomes the gratification of pleasure and applies himself to wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).

Through the power of concentration (*samādhi*), there is the abandoning of the perception of permanence. For one who is concentrated, while discerning the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), acquires the perception of impermanence. Through the power of wisdom (*paññā*), there is the abandoning of the perception of self.
For one who possesses wisdom, perceiving that mental formations (saṅkhāra) are not subject to one's control, penetrates the emptiness of self (attasuññatā).
Mindfulness (sati), however, is required in all instances. Therefore, he said: "And mindfulness, monks, I call 'all-beneficial' (sabbatthika).
Thus, for those who have abandoned the four perversions (vipallāsa), there are the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), which are the states of fulfillment for the four faculties (indriya).
The conclusions of the four directions have been stated by way of the four perversions (*vipallāsa*).
The passage beginning with “Greed is a root of unwholesomeness” shows the association of greed and the other [defilements] through their relationship as cause and fruit.
In that context, the term “by means of the agreeable” is stated by way of general prevalence; for even by means of an disagreeable object, [the perversions arise] by way of inversion.

Greed arises. "By way of what is agreeable" means by way of an agreeable aspect. Contact, feeling, mental exploration, lust, thought, and fever may be found both as co-nascent and as non-co-nascent. By the term "arising," there is the inclusion of the formations that are in the process of arising;
thus it is said, "it arises. However, if one were to include only the characteristic of arising itself, it would not be correct to say "it arises."
It may be so. For arising does not arise [itself]; and their state of being caused by the fever born of lust is due to lust having craving as its essential nature.
For craving is the origin of suffering, according to the teaching: "Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation. And thus it has been said:
"But greed is a condition for the feeling co-nascent with craving by way of such conditions as co-nascence and so forth. Thus...

Here, the arising of the pleasant feeling accompanied by greed that has arisen toward a desirable object is called "arising," which is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*). Its transformation is "the suffering of change" (*vipariṇāma-dukkhatā*).

Since the state of transformation does not exist without the state of arising, it is said—referring to the former—that it arises "depending on" the latter, as in: "Arising... [is] the suffering of change."
The meaning in the cases of "hatred is an unwholesome root," and so forth, should be understood according to the method already stated. However, this is the distinction:
"change of what is present" is called aging (*jarā*); because sorrow arises in dependence upon that, it is said:

"of what is present... [down to] the suffering of suffering. The fact that aging has as its cause the fever born of hatred should be understood from the rapid aging of a person in whom hatred is predominant.
“Passing away” (*vaya*) is the cessation of formations. And because conditioned phenomena are subject to impermanence, there is the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*);
thus it is said: “passing away... [and] the suffering inherent in formations. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering.
The characteristic of passing away has delusion-born fever as its cause because it is generally a sign of confusion, and because death has ignorance as its condition.
And these should be understood according to the progression of saṃsāra.

The fact that non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] have wisdom and the other [factors] as their causes for fulfillment should be understood through their status as conditions by way of decisive support (upanissaya), the limit of simultaneous arising (koṭisahajāta), and so forth, as appropriate.
For all wholesome states are, as far as possible, specific conditions for all wholesome states.

"They are thus. An investigation based on a thought of non-ill-will (*abyāpādavitakka*) is an "investigation of non-ill-will" (*abyāpādūpavicāra*). The same method applies to the investigation of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsūpavicāra*) as well.
This is the second method called "the three-pronged" (*tipukkhalo*), which has been demonstrated together with the method of "surveying the directions"—this is the remainder of the statement.
The passage beginning with "These four" and so forth is for the purpose of showing the ground of the "turning of joy" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*) method by way of a reference to persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

It has been undertaken. These are fourfold by way of the aforementioned fourfold scheme of the path (*paṭipadā-catuṣka*). "By way of distinction" means by way of the distinction of being dependent on either views (*diṭṭhi*) or craving (*taṇhā*).

For one of a view-temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*), who possesses either sharp or dull wisdom, is said to be twofold because he goes forth by a pleasant path with either swift or sluggish direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Likewise, one of a craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*) [goes forth] by a painful path with swift direct knowledge...
And this meaning is shown as being stated in two ways: that it leads out by means of both sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*) and swift direct knowledge. Therefore he said: "There are two:
the one of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) and the one of craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*).
"Having become four" means they stand having become four in the demonstration of the stages of the method of the lion’s play (*sīhavikkīḷita*), by way of the four paths of practice (*catuppaṭipadā*).

The meaning is: "having made four, they were spoken. "There are three" means that in the demonstration of the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Tipukkhalā method, there are three [types of persons] by way of those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññu*), and so forth.
"Having been three" means having remained as three in that way; having made them three, they were explained.
"There are two" means that now, in the demonstration of the stages of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, there are two. "Clinging" (*ajjhosāna*) refers to clinging to views (*diṭṭhiajjhosāna*).
“Adherence” (*abhiniveso*) means adherence through craving. “I-making” (*ahaṃkāro*) means the conceit of “I,” or the act of making “I”; thus it is I-making.
Through the influence of views, conceit, and estimation, the contemplation that “I am” is “mine-making” (*mamaṃkāro*), which is the grasping of craving through the act of making things one’s own.
The ten terms should be treated as “the first direction” according to the method of the Conversion of Relishing (*Nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*). Thus [ends] “the first direction.”
The things to be done are those that must be defined as "the first direction.

In brief... [etc. ...of the "side" (pakkhassa): even though the dark side—the side of defilement—has many divisions, they make it known and proclaim its meaning in brief, by way of summary, with reference to the qualities of purification occurring as the opposite side; thus the construction is: "they are to be made the first."
"The ten terms are the second" means that the ten sections beginning with craving (*taṇhā*) should be treated as "the second directions.
One should apply this by bringing forward the passage: "In brief... [and so on] ...of the dark side.

"Systematically" means by way of method. "Systematic attention" (*yoniso manasikāra*) is the initial attention directed toward [phenomena] such as impermanence (*anicca*). "Wisdom" (*paññā*) refers to that consisting of hearing and reflection (*sutamayī* and *cintāmayī*).

Wisdom (*paññā*), and the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Disenchantment (*nibbidā*) is the knowledge of penetration (*nibbedhañāṇa*). Mental pleasure associated with the factors of joy is the happiness accompanied by gladness and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "on the side of the wholesome" (*kusalapakkhe ca*), the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; it shows that the four directions are taken as a collective from both sides, not individually.
"Of these" (*tesam*) means of craving and so forth—that is, of craving and of those things belonging to the side of craving. Even though lust remains without remainder...

When [craving] is abandoned without remainder, ignorance is indeed abandoned as well; however, it is stated as "the fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāgā*) in order to show that the liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) is the direct antidote to lust.

The same principle applies here to the phrase "the fading away of ignorance" (*avijjāvirāgā*). Furthermore, this meaning is established by way of the commentary on the meaning of the canonical text (Pāḷi) as it has come down, beginning with:
"With the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom."

The former [term] refers to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala). For that is specifically called "the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāgā cetovimutti*) because it is the direct antidote to sensual lust and because of the perfection of concentration; this is stated here in the application of synonyms, beginning with:

"The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the fruit of the trainee (*sekkhaphala*); the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the fruit of the adept (*asekkhaphala*)," and so forth.

The last [term] refers to the fruit of arahantship; because of the complete abandonment of craving and ignorance, and because of the perfection of wisdom, it is called "liberation through wisdom by the fading away of ignorance" (*avijjāvirāgā paññāvimutti*).

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in the method of the Conversion of Delight (*nandiyāvaṭṭanaya*). "Among those" (*tesu*) refers to the four root terms mentioned as "the four terms," namely craving and the rest.

Here, "convergence" (*samosaraṇa*) is said to mean "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*). And since that [inclusion] occurs both by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and by way of commonality (*sabhāga*), after showing the four factors beginning with craving (*taṇhā*), it is stated:
"In these, eighteen root-terms converge. The intention is that they "partake of serenity" (*samathaṃ bhajanti*) both by way of intrinsic nature and by way of commonality.
The same method applies here as well for the phrase "they partake of insight" (*vipassanaṃ bhajanti*). [This concludes the section on] the bases of the methods (*naya-adhiṭṭhāna*).
He says, "The non-entry of methods into methods is indeed called the 'non-entry of methods into methods,'" thus stating: "The *Tipukkhalo*... [etc. ...

enter. Because there is no root-text for the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* or *Sīhavikkīḷita* that would cause it to be associated with the side of non-greed and non-delusion while being associated with the side of non-hatred, he says, "Non-hatred is simply non-hatred," showing that non-hatred is singular at one end of the sutta. Hatred...

"In this case too, the method is exactly the same as 'it is indeed a fault' (*doso eva*). They 'converge' (*samosaranti*) in the sense that they come together through similarity of class and similarity of nature.
He speaks with reference to the basic terms themselves as 'plane' (*bhūmi*) and 'domain' (*gocara*). It enters into each individual method because it enters into its respective basic term.

Or, when the wholesome is understood, the unwholesome is to be sought as its opposite; or when the unwholesome is understood, the wholesome is to be sought as its opposite, in accordance with the words of the sutta being commented upon."
It is to be investigated. Seeking and investigation is called "surveying the directions. That method must be demonstrated:
having thus sought, having defined the directions by means of those states, and having extracted that respective method, it should be applied.
Just as the inclusion of the root-terms within the root-texts was commented upon, in this very same manner, from the root-terms [to the subsequent] root-terms...
Showing that they should be understood as "selections" (*niddhāraṇā*), he said: "Just as in one... [etc. ...they are to be demonstrated.
The passage beginning with "In each one" is a statement of the reason. Therein, "in each" means in each method.

"When one state is known" means when one root-state, such as craving, is known either by its own nature or by way of selection. "All states are known" refers to those other states which constitute the remaining root-states.
All instances of greed and the like, when understood, become evident and manifest as being unfit for the practice of this method (*naya*).

The phrase beginning with “of these” constitutes the grasping of the peak of the three methods (*nayā*), which consists of those phenomena that represent the directions of the three methods; that is precisely according to the method explained below.
Furthermore, the phrase beginning with “in these” is the elucidation of the distinction between the two types of the action-method (*kamma-naya*); that is easily understood.
The commentary on the section on the origination of methods is finished.
Commentary on the section on the foundations of the Dispensation (Sāsanapaṭṭhāna): 89.
"In the sections on inclusion and so forth" means in the sections on inclusion, enumeration, and exposition. It has not been shown according to its literal form, but according to its meaning.

The intended meaning is that it has indeed already been shown. For the purpose of demonstrating that very same point in terms of its actual meaning, he sets it down as an illustration, just as the *Paṭṭhāna* is to be extracted by means of the root-terms (*mūlapada*).
The phrase "mutual inclusion" (*aññamaññasaṅgaha*) is a statement of the reason why the root-term *Paṭṭhānas* must be extracted from one another, according to the principle:
"If there is no entry [into the system], there would be an exit from it."

*Paṭṭhāna*: here, *pa-* is a prefix (*upasaggapada*). Showing that it indicates the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*), as in such passages as "They approached that which is best among the analyzed phenomena," he says "the standing (*ṭhāna*) by way of manners. *Idha* means in this *Nettippakaraṇa*.

“Of this”: of the teaching known as the *pariyatti-sāsana* (the scriptural dispensation). “Illumination of its suchness” (*tathābhāvadīpana*) means that because it proceeds in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, it must be illustrated by way of its established nature through various aspects such as the portion dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*);

thus, taking the sense of “it will be illuminated, therefore it is an illumination” (*dīpissati tasmā dīpanaṃ*). The training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and so forth are taken here in their collective form. By these [factors], such as the phenomena of defilement and so on—

The means for the occurrence of the factors of defilement and so forth, as well as the training in higher virtue and so forth, should be illustrated by the gradual discourse and the Dhamma teaching that is "exalted.
"Of these" refers to the factors of defilement and so forth. Again, "of these" is said with reference to the suttas.
"Herds" (goṭṭhā) means flocks (vajā). "Cows that have gone away" (paṭṭhitagāvo) means cows that have departed. "In the place where they came from" refers to the *Sīhanāda Sutta*.

The phrase "because it proceeds here" (*pavattagamanattā ettha*) is an elliptical expression (*vacanaseso*). Alternatively, it is called *paṭṭhāna* because it is a place where there is a proceeding (*gamanaṃ*);

that is to say, it is so named because it is the location where the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) proceeds without attachment. "Mixed" (*vomissā*) means mixed by way of dyads, triads, and tetrads, such as "that which pertains to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and that which pertains to purification (*vodānabhāgiya*)," and so forth.

The meaning is that it was taught having made its object the "occurrence" (pavatta) when the state of defilement (saṃkilesabhāva) is to be made known; this is a statement of the mere sense (atthamattavacana).
According to the method of grammatical derivation (saddanaya), the meaning should be understood as "that which exists in the portion of defilement. There is also a reading "saṃkilesabhāgika";
for that, the meaning is "that which has a portion of defilement" (saṃkilesabhāga), or "that which is connected to the portion of defilement," or [a term] belonging to the portion of defilement.
Or, that which has the nature of awakening [to] the side of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*); the meaning should be understood as "that very same thing belonging to the side of defilement.
"Crushing" (*padālana*) means cutting off; here, it should be seen that the state of being dependent upon crushing is included by the mention of "crushing" itself.
"In the Asekha" refers to the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkhadhamma*). "By way of their mixed method" refers to those [categories], such as the side of defilement and so forth.
By way of the fourfold method of negation, non-negation, and their mixture.

Having stated the definition and establishment of the terms beginning with “those six dyads,” he will himself show them in their specific form later, in the commentary on the meaning of the phrase “made common. [In the case of] “non-extraction...”
Having stated, "There is no cause," he then brought forward the canonical text beginning with "For he will say... in order to show the reason for its extraction.
What is called "purification" (*vodāna*) arises from defilement (*saṃkilesa*), because it is precisely the purification of that which is defiled that is intended.

Since purification is the cleansing from defilement by way of "purification through substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga-vodāna*) and so forth, therefore [the text says]: "But that, in terms of its meaning, consists of the portion dealing with the habitual tendencies (*vāsanābhāgiya*) and so on..."

Thus it was said. In this context, purification by means of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*) occurs by way of the portion dealing with purification (*vodānabhāgiya*) and so forth;
purification by means of eradication (*samuccheda*) and subsidence (*paṭippassaddhi*) occurs by way of the portion dealing with penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*);

and purification by way of subsidence alone should be understood as occurring by way of the portion dealing with the Adept (*asekkhabhāgiya*). That teaching which might deal with lust and the other [defilements] is the portion dealing with corruption (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*).
That teaching which partakes of generosity and so forth is one that partakes of purification through habituation (*vāsanā-bhāgiyā*).

However, that which cuts off offenses—whether with remainder or without remainder—is one that partakes of penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiyā*) and one that partakes of the state of one beyond training (*asekha-bhāgiyā*).

This is stated because the category of defilement (*saṃkilesa-bhāga*) was already shown at the very beginning by the passage beginning, "A discourse partaking of the defilement of craving" (*taṇhā-saṃkilesa-bhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ*).
“Defilement is threefold... [etc. ... undertaken for the purpose of showing the objects. Craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is the longing for existence. “Arises” means it does not disappear.
“In this or that state of existence” means either in the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*), or in the fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*), or in the immaterial existence (*arūpa-bhava*).
“By way of connecting with other words” means by way of connecting with another word according to the method of dyads (*duka-naya*) itself. They are mixed.
"Composed" means they have been composed by way of association.

Having taken only those terms that should be shown according to the single and fourfold [schemata], and having mixed them by way of showing the method of repetition, the remaining eight sections of the *Paṭṭhāna*—namely, the dyads, triads, and fourfold schemata—have been shown; thus he said.
“Those same eight suttas as previously mentioned,” and so forth. Four single [suttas] were shown at the beginning of the Pāḷi.
As for the groups of six, four are found in the Pāḷi and two in the Aṭṭhakathā. As for the groups of three, two are found in the Pāḷi and two in the Aṭṭhakathā.
However, the two groups of four are found only in the Aṭṭhakathā. “Not found in the Pāḷi.”
This was stated with reference to non-arrival by way of identity; however, the fact of their arrival by way of method has indeed been demonstrated.
As for those [suttas] not included here in the text, we shall provide examples of them later.
"By sixteen" means by sixteenfold ways; for it is not that there are only sixteen suttas, but rather that they are of sixteen types.

Setting aside the primary enumeration, the method of expansion for that corresponding detailed enumeration—which is obtained through the "womb of formations" (saṅkhāragabbha) according to the *Kāraṇa-sutta*—is the *Paṭṭhāna-naya*.

By this [phrase]... [omitted] ...it is shown that there exists no portion of the scriptural teaching (pariyatti-sāsana) apart from the aforementioned *Paṭṭhāna*, because it occurs as various respective *Paṭṭhānas* according to what is appropriate.

If the ninefold teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*), such as the discourses (*sutta*) and verses (*geyya*), proceeds precisely according to the aforementioned *Paṭṭhāna* method, then how is it that the nature of defilement and so forth for the unstated verses and other texts here should be understood? With reference to this question, the passage beginning with "How then...
was stated in order to show that the canonical text beginning with "A verse should be inferred by means of a verse" is set forth.

In this context, "this verse is like" means it is like the verse cited here, beginning with: "Blinded by desire, shrouded by a net... mental states are preceded by the mind... he whose mind is like a rock is liberated above, below, and everywhere.
As for "verses," these refer to other verses appearing in the Buddha’s word within the Tipiṭaka that have not been cited here; they become manifest at the time of the commentary.

Regarding the statement, “Whatever verse has been spoken as ‘this verse is such-and-such’ should be inferred as ‘partaking of defilement’ or ‘partaking of defilement, purification, penetration, and the state of one beyond training (asekha),’ and it should be made known by grasping the method,” this was said to show that it must be understood through the application of the guiding principle.
Here, the word *vā* has the sense of an unexpressed alternative. “In the remaining phrases” refers to the phrases within the discourses on grammar (*veyyākaraṇa*).

90. "The Dhamma of the Noble Ones" refers to the conduct consisting of the division of what is to be practiced (*cāritta*) and what is to be avoided (*vāritta*), namely virtue and proper behavior. Even the non-performance of that which must be performed unconditionally is indeed a transgression.
Wisdom is called "cleansing" (*dhonā*) because it shakes off defilements such as ignorance by means of "shaking off through substitution" (*tadaṅga*) and other methods.

However, the phrase "the wisdom of consuming after reflecting" is stated here because it is delimited by the context of the treatise. "One who acts having transgressed that" [refers to one who acts beyond that].

One who consumes requisites without reflecting upon them, failing to see the danger in such consumption, and consuming them as if under a debt, is not liberated from the suffering of hell and other realms, nor from the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
A "kukkujanaka" is the flowering stalk of a plantain tree. "For ruin" means for destruction. "In that way" means just as [the plantain] ends with the ripening of its fruit.

The word *tathā* (thus) has the sense of a conclusion, [indicating] that the plantain, as well as the bamboo and the reed, belong to the class of medicinal herbs (*osadhijātika*). Therefore he said: "the fruit of the bamboo, the fruit of the reed.

By the word *api* (even) in the phrase "even in a good field," he shows: "how much more so in fields corrupted by defects such as saltiness? By the phrase "chagaṇa... [etc. ...the purpose," he shows that it is corrupted by a defect in the seed due to the absence of the aforementioned preparation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*).
91. *Sajjitaṃ* means prepared. *Aparikkhate* means when one is unafflicted, not suppressed by opposing states.

That wisdom of the nourishment of the Dhamma (*dhammojapaññā*) by which a person endowed with it wanders seeking what is wholesome, thinking, "What have I heard, or what am I hearing?"—that is called *kissa*.
*Dubbhāsitaṃ* means badly spoken; or, it is spoken that is corrupted by the faults of envy, stinginess, and so forth.
92. *Vicināti* means he specifically gathers or produces [falsehood].
*Vigatabhūtā* means one from whom truth has departed. Therefore, he says, "a speaker of falsehood. *Avajātaputtā* means a base son.

He speaks with reference to one who, having gone forth in the Blessed One’s dispensation, leads a degraded life. *Nerayiko* means one destined for rebirth in hell. *Pāpakaṃminō* refers to those who perform evil deeds. *Papataṃ* means a precipice; it is hell (*naraka*), because they fall into it.

"By way of the distinction in the intrinsic nature of craving and the rest" means by way of the differentiation of their respective natures, namely: for craving (*taṇhā*), the state of yearning; for views (*diṭṭhi*), the state of distorted seeing; and for misconduct (*duccarita*), the state of corrupted conduct. "By way of the distinction in their states" refers to the specific states of these:

for craving, there are desire (*chanda*), affection (*pema*), greed (*lobha*), lust (*rāga*), delight (*nandī*), thirst (*pipāsā*), infatuation (*mucchā*), and so forth; for views, there are grasping (*gāha*), misapprehension (*parāmāsa*), wrong adherence (*micchābhinivesa*), vain agitation (*visukavipphandita*), distorted seeing (*viparītadassana*), and so forth;

and for misconduct, there are the particular states of leading to rebirth among animals, hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), or the realm of asuras, and so on. The word "and" (*ca*) [in the original compound] includes... [their]... [further distinctions].

It is comprised of various types such as craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*), and so forth; views regarding a self (*attānudiṭṭhā*); grasping at eternalism (*sassatagāha*);

bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*); and the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*). "Vast" (*vipula*) means sublime (*uḷāra*); the meaning is that it is a great accumulation of things such as oil and the like, as well as wealth and grain. "Confined space" (*sambādha*) refers to the crowding and collisions of people.

Regarding the phrase "he does not harm with a stick," the laying aside of the stick mentioned here pertains to both the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*). Demonstrating the fruit of both of these, he says, "That person," and so forth.
94. That which crushes one who possesses it is *kiñcana*; this refers to lust (*rāga*) and so forth.
That which binds and obstructs the arising of the wholesome is *palibodha*; this also refers to lust and so forth.

Thus, *kiñcanapalibodha* means "the bond of worldly things," where *kiñcana* itself is the *palibodha*. Alternatively, *kiñcanapalibodha* means both "worldly things" and "obstructions"; the sense is that it consists of both material trifles and the defilements such as lust.
“Visesitaṃ” means contrary or uneven; the meaning is that it is an irregular action. “Rājabhaṇḍaṃ” refers, they say, to the women of the harem.
“Yācayoga” means the practice of begging, so called because it fulfills the desires of beggars. Therefore he said, “connected with what is to be begged.
“Dānayutta” means one who is constantly engaged in the act of giving. Regarding “delighting in giving and sharing,” here “giving” (dāna) refers to [the giving] to those in need.
Generosity is the relinquishing of what has been prepared according to one's intention; sharing is the distributing of even a very small portion from what is to be enjoyed by oneself.
Regarding the phrase "By these... it comes to be," the word *hoti* (comes to be) should be connected with the term *samannāgato* (endowed), not with *sotāpanno* (stream-enterer).
Thus, it is said: "He is a stream-enterer... it comes to be," in order to show that he is endowed with those qualities. This is the possession of those states.

For here it is these [factors] that are prescribed, not the state of being a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*); thus he shows that these phenomena are the characteristics of a stream-enterer, not the characteristic of the state of being a stream-enterer.
For it is said: "It shows the state of being obtainable by one who is a stream-enterer...
95. That by which one speaks or talks is *lapanaṃ*, namely, the lip.
97. *Mudito* means delighted by divine success (*dibbasampatti*). 99.

Although the phrase "he has crossed over" (*udatāri*) expresses the act of crossing as something belonging to the past, he nevertheless says, "Because the function of the Noble Path is the crossing of the flood," taking the act of crossing itself [as the primary sense].
Similarly, regarding the terms *vippamutto* and *vimutto*, the act of being released (*muccana-kiriyā*) may also be predicated here.

100. Since the word *bhavanti* preceded by the word *pātu* may signify either arising (*uppāda*) or manifestation (*āvibhāva*), the meaning of the phrase “*pātubhavantī*” is stated as “they arise and they manifest.

“Of the dhamma that has become manifest” (*pātubhūta-dhammassa*) means of the dhammas conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) that have arisen, or of the dhamma of the Four Truths that has become evident (*vibhūta*). “Not fit” (*no kalla*) means not appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "phenomena with cause" (*sahetudhamma*): here, are only those phenomena produced by conditions (*paccayuppanna*) intended, and not the conditioning phenomena themselves?
This should not be viewed in that way, because even conditioning phenomena do not transcend the state of being produced by conditions.

Alternatively, "phenomena with cause" refers to phenomena produced by conditions as the primary factor, while the conditioning phenomena are mentioned as subordinate factors; thus it should be understood here.
The state of being established in both [the forest and the village] should be understood.

"Forest-dwelling" means endowed with the factors of forest-dwelling (*āraññaka-aṅga*). "Unknown" means not known by way of familiarity; the meaning is that one is unassociated. Therefore he said, "ever-new.
Through such phrases as "freedom from ill-will and cruelty," "absence of suspicion of enmity," and "being exempt from blame," [these qualities are shown].
Through these causes, by abandoning anger, one sleeps happily. However, because the absence of the fever of anger is more evident, he says: “...anger... one sleeps.
Regarding the phrase “of the poison-root,” here “poison” is intended to mean suffering because of its similarity to poison; thus he says: “of that which has suffering as its result.
“Happiness” refers to mental happiness. The construction is: “Having reviled one who is being reviled, and [the suffering] arises on account of that reviling.”
101. "Drawing out the arrow" means the extraction of the arrow.

Because sensual perception (*kāmasaññā*) has many divisions—both by way of the diversity of its objects and by way of the diversity of its modes of occurrence—it is said, "by whatever [perception] of the body.
"By way of giving" means by means of giving as the primary factor; the meaning is, "having made giving the foremost."

By the phrase “by way of bringing about the Noble Path,” he clarifies that compassion (*anukampā*) and sympathy (*anuddayā*) are exclusively blameless. The explanation of the meaning of the word “compassion” is “the act of feeling pity” (*karuṇāyanā*), and for the other [sympathy], it is “the act of feeling loving-kindness” (*mettāyanā*).

102. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “nature and so forth,” he includes such things as the atom (*aṇu*), the Lord (*issara*), Pajāpati, the Primordial Man (*purisa*), time (*kāla*), the Ordainer (*adhiṭṭhāyaka*), the Creator (*kārī*), and others.
“In sensual pleasures” (*kāmesu*) means in the strands of sense-pleasure, which are objects such as visible forms and the rest.

“Due to the abundance of defilements” means by way of the state of having many defilements. “Due to the weakness of prior causes” means because of not having performed wholesome deeds that serve as a supporting condition for turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya).
“Through the cultivation of mental tranquility” means through serenity and insight, which are the cultivations that bring about mental tranquility.

“Hindrances” refers specifically to the defilements that act as obstacles to the fulfillment of virtue and the other perfections. It is said, “with their heads cast down by the crest of knowledge,” because these ignoble ones are not even able to lift up the crest of wisdom.

103. It is said, “Having described the praise of Jetavana in the first verse,” because the Blessed One’s suitability as a dwelling place for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and the fact that he has resided there constitute its preeminent excellence. For it has been said:
“Whether in a village or in the forest, whether in a low-lying area or on high ground—wherever the Arahants dwell, that spot is delightful.”

Here, the word *dhamma* is used as a synonym for concentration (*samādhi*), as in such passages as "those Blessed Ones were of such a nature" (*evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto*). Thus he says, "Dhamma means concentration. The factors conducive to concentration are mindfulness and effort.
"He would not follow after" means he would not pursue. For pursuing by way of craving and views is precisely what is meant by "not following after.

"He would contemplate" refers to the discernment of insight (*vipassanā-sammasana*). For discernment is indeed insight, whether it be by way of pairs, by way of moments, or by way of successive order.

From thorough comprehension (*sammasana*) comes what is called "counter-insight" (*paṭivipassanā*). For this is a further cultivation that serves as a cause for the removal of views, the uprooting of conceit, and the exhaustion of craving;
specifically, it is a cultivation that acts as a cause which is unshakable and unshakeable by its opposite.
By the phrase "repeatedly... applying," he shows the cultivation of those phenomena that have Nibbāna as their object, just as it is said: "one who cultivates empty huts."
A "compact" (*saṅgara*) is the giving of a promise by making some pretext whatsoever.

That, moreover, may occur by making a pretext of one's own particular duty out of friendly intimacy, or by making a pretext of arriving at the appointed time, or by making a pretext of providing some small gift, or by making a pretext of acting as a guarantor through the pledging of a deposit;
it is with reference to these modes of establishing friendship and so forth that he said this.

“‘He binds together... and so on, up to ‘is called. Because he has practiced in this way”: because he has practiced with diligence through the medium of the perception of impermanence regarding the formations belonging to the three periods of time.
“The divine eye is well-purified”: since this is a teaching that leaves something remaining, he said, “that which he realizes. For here, the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) is intended.

104. "End" (*anta*) refers to that which constitutes the far limit of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "Of the Vedas" refers specifically to the Vedas of path-knowledge, because through the attainment of Arahantship, one has reached their end and conclusion.

"Excesses" (*ussada*) refers to lust and the other defilements, so called because they are "excessive" due to their intensity and accumulation within the cycle of kamma and its results, as well as the cycle of defilements.

They are "white" (*sukka*) because of their bright appearance; they are "seizers" (*gaha*) because they are particularly distinguished. Alternatively, all the forms of stars are "white. "He finds" (*vindati*) means he perceives; the sense is that he penetrates [them].
The statement, “There is an internal fixation on insight,” is said because the state of having gone beyond (pāragū) is specified as being “in regard to one’s own phenomena.
And that [state] is taught precisely by way of such fixation. It is said: “Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known.

And the state of having gone beyond those aggregates occurs through the clear comprehension and realization (abhisamaya) of them; and from that, [the knowledge extends] to their origin, which serves as their cause.

In cessation, which has the characteristic of the non-occurrence of that [suffering], and in the path leading to cessation, the state of having reached the further shore regarding the other truths is indeed stated by way of the fulfillment of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through abandoning, actualizing, and developing. For the clear realization of the Four Truths occurs even through the awakening to one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Indeed, this has been said: "In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, the world..."
“I proclaim [the Dhamma], as well as the origin of the world,” and so forth. Alternatively, “among one’s own states” means among one’s own qualities.
One’s own qualities (*attadhammā*) refer to the qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so on of a clansman who desires his welfare.

For the qualities of purification—virtue, concentration, wisdom, and so on—are called a person’s own qualities because they bring about absolute benefit and happiness; they are not the defiled qualities that lead to harm.
They are like the qualities of others. One who has gone to the further shore—the limit—through the fulfillment of those virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) is called a *pāragū*.

Regarding the expression “*akkula pakkula*”: this refers to a mode of conduct that causes harm. For at that time, the roar of the *yakkha*, which was produced by one wishing to terrify the Blessed One with a herd of goats, reached the range of hearing of beings in this manner: “*akkula pakkula*.”
Therefore, it is said that "it causes confusion and disorder.

"He does not rejoice" means he is not satisfied [thinking], "She has come to see me. However, since the word *abhinandati* also carries the sense of "accepting," as in such phrases as "he rejoiced in the Blessed One’s speech," it is therefore said: "with his mind..."
“He does not accept it. “He does not grieve” means he does not fall into mental distress [thinking], “She is departing without having greeted me.
“‘The victor in battle is freed from bonds’”—this is a statement of the reason for the absence of both delight and grief.
“By that” means by bathing in water. For this very reason it was said: “One is not made pure by water. Its meaning is as follows: [not] by emerging from water and so forth...

There is no such thing as the purification of beings from evil through water. For here, terms such as "emerging from water" (*udakummujjana*) and so forth are expressed simply as "water" (*udaka*) by means of eliding the latter member of the compound. Or rather, there is no purification of beings from evil—that is, no cleansing of sin—by means of water, which serves as the instrument for actions such as emerging from it.
Alternatively, [one might think] that one is purified from the stain of evil by means of the aforementioned "pure water."
“There is no being. If that were so, then all fishermen would achieve purification from evil. Therefore he said:

“Many people bathe here. For all those who commit evil deeds such as matricide, and others such as cow-slaughterers and buffalo-killers—even down to the fish and turtles—who descend into the water, there would be purification from evil for them all; it is not [the case].
But this is indeed so. Why? Because bathing is not an antidote to the causes of evil. For whatever destroys something is its antidote;
just as light is the antidote to darkness, and knowledge to ignorance, but bathing is not so for evil.
Therefore, one must reach the conclusion here: "One does not become pure by water. To show, however, that by which one becomes pure, [the Buddha said]:
“*Yamhi saccañca*,” and so forth, has been stated. Therein, *sacca* (truth) refers both to verbal truth (*vacīsacca*) and to the truth of abstinence (*viratisacca*).
Alternatively, *sacca* refers to the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*) and the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*). *Dhamma* refers to the remaining noble qualities (*ariyadhamma*).
The separate mention of *sacca* here is for the purpose of showing its manifold utility. The rest is easily understood.
"Refuting birth-based power" means refuting those who claim to be brahmins merely by birth, such as those who address others with the term "bho," or it means refuting the doctrine of birth;
for it is said: "One is not a brahmin by birth. This is stated because the Elder, by speaking in that manner, was as if subduing them even while not actually suppressing them.
105. "In liberation" means in the element of nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

"Together with the latent tendencies" (*sāsavāna*): here, even for one whose taints are destroyed, the cultivation of defilements within the continuum—which serves as the cause for bodily and verbal activities resembling those of one whose taints are not yet destroyed—is called "latent tendency" (*vāsanā*).
This is like the Venerable Pilindavaccha’s use of the term "outcaste" (*vasala*). Thus, it is "together with the latent tendencies."
This word "bhāvanā" is neuter when accompanied by its latent tendency (*savāsana*), as in such expressions as "the moon and sun move unevenly.
The meaning is: "having left no remainder of the aforementioned latent tendencies.

"The correct practice of the path by way of avoiding wrong paths" means that one who is skilled in the path is likewise skilled in what is not the path; however, the Blessed One, due to his omniscience, is skilled in all things whatsoever.
He said: "Skilled in both the path and what is not the path.

(106) "Possessing darkness" means one who has the aforementioned darkness; thus, "darkness" refers to the person. Alternatively, the aggregates themselves, existing in a state of non-illumination, are "darkness. "Become light" means the light of birth and qualities; the meaning is that his qualities are manifest.
They call the bond consisting of defilements "firm," because it is only Buddhas, penetrating the Truths, who sever it, and no others.

Although it is firm in its sense of causing deprivation, he said, "even the state of being a bond," and so forth, in order to demonstrate its lax mode of operation. By this, it is shown that it was said: "O monks, the bond of Māra is indeed more subtle.
(107) Although volition (cetanā) is common to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, here the formative action of demerit (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) is intended;
thus, demonstrating the meaning by way of that, he said, "one intends by way of unwholesome volition. Volition is the act of directing the mind toward an object.

The meaning is that it proceeds as a state of mental activity and engagement. However, since volition (cetanā), when it originates an intimation (viññatti), produces a manifest application (payoga) like a double effort or exertion, it is therefore said to "formulate" (pakappeti).
For here, "formulating" (pakappana) is intended in the sense of the formulation of a manifest application. Thus he says: "it formulates that very [intention]."
The meaning of "condition" (*paccaya*) here is stated to be the meaning of "object" (*ārammaṇa*), as it is said: "it is a condition for the process of existence.
