Just as the momentum found in the ocean of water by way of the arising of waves is called "consisting of waves," so too the momentum found in the ocean of the eye by way of the appearance of forms is called "consisting of forms. It is exactly the same.

The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "Drawing forth" (*āviñchana*) means dragging along; here, "dragging along" should be understood as the cause for the continuity of the stream of existence (*santāna*) becoming inclined toward that [object].

"Surging up" (*samudāna*) is the agitation of the defilements (*kilesa*); it should be understood as the state of being subject to their power, and the similarity of the defilements to waves and so forth, because they bring harm to beings through their constant tossing about.
It is [also] by the non-permission for one who has approached to rise again, due to the successive arising of forceful impulses.
And by the destruction of the essence of the virtues, the likeness of anger, enmity, and so forth to waves and the like should be understood.
"He delights facing it" means that he receives and accepts the pleasure and mental joy associated with that object.
"He speaks out" means that he speaks having become attached through the influence of craving. To illustrate that attachment of his, [the text says] "Oh, what happiness! and so forth.
It has been said. "Clinging" (*ajjhosāna*) means entering into and making exclusive the basis for craving through craving, which consists of the state of being resolved upon (*adhimuccana*).
Therefore, he said: "He remains clinging, having swallowed and finalized.
(109) By the words beginning with "Why," he states that the suffering of torment is difficult to remedy. "In whatever manner" (*yena vā pakārena*); "by which" (*yena*)...
Or rather, by means of that mode of wrong adherence consisting of attachment to sensual pleasures and attachment to views;
householders and renunciants, having performed such [deeds], imagine it to be their own prosperity.
But it is actually only non-prosperity, because that mode is a non-means for prosperity and a means for non-prosperity. "Even so" refers to the frustration of one's desires here and there.

Even though they do not attain it: because those outside this [teaching], not understanding the escape from existence in its entirety, regard a certain form of existence—which has dull defilements, long life, and much happiness—as "Nirvana" precisely due to its state of having dull defilements and so forth;
therefore, they speak of liberation from existence by means of existence itself.

Craving accompanied by the view of becoming (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) is called "craving for becoming" (*bhavataṇhā*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound in the first phrase; thus he says, "as in the case of 'craving for becoming' and so forth.
"In which" means in which becoming.

"Precisely from that" means precisely from the delight in existence. For the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) of sentient beings toward one another is powerful. "Without remainder" means without remainder, leaving nothing behind.

It is called "going with the stream" (*anusotagāmī*) because it proceeds in accordance with the current of *saṃsāra*. It is called "going against the stream" (*paṭisotagāmī*) because it proceeds by way of opposition to that very same [stream] through such practices as the contemplation of disenchantment; the meaning is that its intrinsic nature is established through the possession of unwavering confidence and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "one of noble birth" (*abhijātiko*), he says "births" (*jātiyo*) because the prefix is merely for the purpose of lengthening the word, as in the expressions "is found" (*palabbhati*) or "is buried" (*nikhajjati*).
Alternatively, one is "dark" (*kaṇho*) due to being endowed with dark qualities (*kaṇhadhamma*); that is, one who possesses evil even in the first stage of life or the middle stage of life.
"Having sacrificed and remained [in that state], one is reborn into dark states; the meaning is that even afterwards one produces evil.
Alternatively, "bright" (*sukka*) should be understood here by the very opposite of what was stated above. 111.
"In the former" means in the preceding word; it is the locative case used for the object, because therein the thing to be given is established.
In the second case regarding the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), that very legal issue is indeed *nibbāna*.

Alternatively, it is a description of the equal sweetness of the state of being worthy of receiving requisites and of arhatship, for the purpose of showing the distinguished Dhamma within the duties of both householders and those who have gone forth. Or else, "by whatever basis" refers to the basis of craving, such as the cessation of form and the formless;
and by the phrase "the basis of the Eel-Wriggler's evasion, etc.," the word "etc. includes the bases for false adherence, such as beauty and pleasure.

It includes [them]. Or, just as there is a classification of a sutta dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) by way of craving, views, and misconduct, so too, in order to show the classification of suttas dealing with the cleansing of craving (taṇhāvodānabhāgiya) and so forth by way of serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and good conduct (sucarita), it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Craving... [and so on]... should be demonstrated."

"This occurs thus": Just as a person becomes a fool by means of ill-considered thoughts and so forth, so too this discourse—occurring by way of the cultivation of such ill-considered thinking—is called "pertaining to defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*).
Having previously explained it through the classification of defiled phenomena, he now speaks of it by grouping them together in general.
Or, regarding "this discourse pertaining to purification" (*vāsanābhāgiya*), the meaning here should also be understood according to this same method.

“By way of the bases for defilements” means by way of the locations where defilements arise. “By way of the manifestations of defilements” means by way of the specific modes of the arising of defilements.
One is bound by sensual lust and so forth; that is, by way of karma, its result, and so on, which have sensual lust and the rest as their cause.
Even though these [factors] persist only for a certain duration, one is said to be “bound,” which is why sensual lust and the others are called “fetters” (*saṃyojana*). “Grasps” means firmly.
It grasps and sets it in motion. The remainder has been commented upon because it follows the method already stated and is self-evident.
112. "By way of illustration" means by way of example; the sense is "by way of showing a single part.
For the entire teaching of the Piṭaka (Pariyatti-sāsana) is encompassed by the sixteen sections of the Paṭṭhāna. Just as [the nature] of those sixteen parts...

The inclusion of the sections on the *paṭṭhāna* (conditional relations) is merely by way of illustration; for what more need be said here regarding the fact that the citation of even a single portion of those sixteen [sections] serves as an example?
Therefore it was said: "the meaning is 'by way of showing a single part'.
But why is only a single part of the *paṭṭhāna* cited in the Pāḷi here, and not the remainder? It is for the purpose of demonstrating the method (*naya*). By this method...
The remaining state of the *paṭṭhāna* (conditional relations) should also be understood.

In this context, the passage beginning, “Even if one speaks but little that is connected [to the goal]... he partakes of the fruit of recluseship,” refers both to the category of the *vāsana-bhāgiya* (conducive to purification) and the *asekha-bhāgiya* (pertaining to the Adept).
For here, the phrase “even if one speaks but little that is connected” belongs to the *vāsana-bhāgiya*.
“He partakes of the state of one who is worthy” (sa bhāgavā sāmaññassa hoti)—this pertains to the stage of one beyond training (asekkha).
Likewise is the Maghadeva Sutta. For therein it is said:

“Once upon a time, Ānanda, in this very Mithilā there was a king named Maghadeva, righteous, a king of righteousness, established in righteousness, a great king of righteousness; he practiced righteousness toward brahmins and householders.”
“Among the Negamas and in the countryside, he observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight”—
this is the portion dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*). “But this, Ānanda,
is the noble practice that I have now brought forth for the sake of complete disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, and full enlightenment.”
“...it leads to Nibbāna”—this pertains to the state of one beyond training (*asekkha*). “When the wise man dispels negligence with diligence”—this pertains to penetration (*nibbedha*).
“The palace of wisdom... [he] looks down upon”—this pertains both to the state of one beyond training and to penetration.
Likewise, there is the sutta beginning: “Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties. Therein, the passage: “Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties. Which three?
The faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known”—this pertains to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). The passage:
“the faculty of one who has already known” (*aññātāvindriya*)—this pertains to the state of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).
The Raṭṭhapāla Sutta deals with the portion concerning defilement, the portion concerning purification, and the portion concerning the state of one beyond training (*asekkha*).
For therein, defilement is analyzed by such passages as, "The world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving"; the qualities of one beyond training by such passages as, "Alone, withdrawn";
and the qualities of purification by the remainder.
“Those who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones are unsurpassed in word, thought, and deed;
established in peace, gentleness, and concentration, they have attained the essence of learning and wisdom.

This [verse] pertains to the stage of purification by habituation (*vāsanā-bhāgiya*), the stage of penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*), and the stage of the one beyond training (*asekha-bhāgiya*). For herein, “those who... the Dhamma... [is explained].
“Delighting in what is proclaimed by the Noble Ones”—this is *vāsanā* (habitual perfuming). “Unsurpassed... established”—this is *nibbedha* (penetration).
“They have attained the essence through learning and wisdom”—these are the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkhadhammā*).
Likewise, there is the verse: “The faithful one, learned, seeing the fixed course. For therein, “the faithful one, learned” is *vāsanā*, and “seeing the fixed course” [is *nibbedha*].
“The wise one does not side with the faction among those who have gone over to factions; having overcome greed, hatred, and resentment”—this is penetration (*nibbedha*).
“He would wander rightly in the world”—this refers to the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkhadhammā*).

The restraint from all taints (*sabbāsavasaṃvara*) should be understood as pertaining to all aspects by way of the dangers (*parissaya*) and so forth. For therein are the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhammā*).
The mundane wholesome states, the states of training (*sekkhadhammā*), and the states beyond training (*asekkhadhammā*) have been analyzed.
Furthermore, the "unshared portion" (*asabbabhāgiya*) should be understood as figurative expressions concerning water and so forth, such as "seeing sees.

Thus, within this sixteenfold *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*, there are these three portions of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāga*) by way of craving and so on, and three portions of purification (*vodānabhāga*) by way of cleansing and so on.

There are three sections pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāga*) by way of the aggregates of virtue and so forth of those in training (*sekkha*), and three sections pertaining to the adept (*asekkhabhāga*) by way of the very same aggregates of virtue and so forth of those beyond training (*asekha*). By way of these, there are twelve root matrices (*mūlapaṭṭhāna*).
However, when these are analyzed according to the method of detailed exposition, they amount to four thousand and ninety-six. As for the demonstration:

These [factors] are to be extracted. Now, as for those [factors], they consist of eight portions of defilement: three portions of the defilement of craving by way of the craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*) and so forth;
two portions of the defilement of views by way of eternalism and annihilationism; and three portions of the defilement of misconduct by way of bodily misconduct and so forth.
Furthermore, there are three bases for meritorious action consisting of giving, by way of the gift of the Dhamma, material goods, and protection from fear.

There are eight portions of the category of perfuming (*vāsanābhāga*): the three bases for meritorious action consisting of virtue, by way of good conduct of body and so forth; and the two bases for meritorious action consisting of development, by way of serenity and insight.
[These pertain to] the five trainees: the follower by faith, the one liberated by faith, the follower of Dhamma, the one attained to view, and the body-witness.
There are fifteen factors conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāga*), consisting of three aggregates beginning with virtue (*sīla*) for each [of the five stages].

There are three dhammas of the highest fruit (*aggaphala*) for those liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*), distinguished as emptiness (*suññatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and desirelessness (*appaṇihita*); in these, there are likewise three aggregates beginning with virtue for each, making eighteen.
By including the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) on the common ground of being that which is not to be trained in, [there are nineteen].

There are nineteen factors pertaining to those beyond training (*asekkha*); thus, the previous thirty-one and these nineteen together constitute fifty dhammas pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth.
Therefore, by way of these fifty dhammas pertaining to defilement and so forth, there are fifty suttas.

And because those liberated by wisdom—without making a distinction between those liberated in both ways and those liberated by wisdom alone, and without including the unconditioned element—do not possess the status of "adept" (asekkha) in the literal sense, and thus constitute only nine types of adepts, there are forty [factors] in total; therefore, it is said in the *Peṭaka*:
"It should be sought through forty modes; the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna* is demonstrated through fifty modes."

And it has been said. However, by way of grouping according to the method of detailed exposition previously stated, there are sixteen; again, by way of the threefold division beginning with "partaking of defilement" (saṃkilesabhāgiya), there are twelve;
again, by way of the defilements of craving (taṇhā), views (diṭṭhi), and misconduct (duccarita), and the purification (vodāna) from those same craving, views, and misconduct, there are six;

and again, [those six] are further divided into: partaking of defilement, partaking of purification (vāsanābhāgiya), partaking of vision (dassanabhāgiya), partaking of purification, and partaking of the Adept (asekkhabhāgiya).

There are five; again, by way of the *Mūla-paṭṭhāna*, there are four; by way of being shared by worldlings (*puthujjana-bhāgiya*), shared by those in training (*sekkha-bhāgiya*), and shared by those beyond training (*asekkha-bhāgiya*), there are three;
and again, by way of being shared in defilement (*saṃkilesa-bhāgiya*) and shared in purification (*vodāna-bhāgiya*), there are exactly two.

However, by way of the *Paṭṭhāna* itself, it is of only one kind; thus, although it is of one kind by way of the *Paṭṭhāna*, [it is further divided] by way of being shared in defilement and shared in purification.
"Twofold" means that, according to its divisions, it should be understood as extending up to four thousand and ninety-six types.
Thus this *Paṭṭhāna* is to be known both by way of its summary and its detailed analysis.
The intention is that this refers not only to the previous [summary], but also to this detailed division of the *Paṭṭhāna*. It is "worldly" (*lokika*) because it is associated with the world.
Or "worldly" (*lokiya*); "by way of a portion" (*padesena*) means by way of a single part. "In all portions" (*sabbapadesu*) refers to the third sections of their respective chapters.

"Of the Buddha and others" (*buddhādīnaṃ*) refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha. Furthermore, in this context, "Dhamma" should be understood through the mention of the "Buddha and others," or by means of the word "others" (*ādi*).
"Parinamati" means it ripens. "Dharanti" means they proceed by way of continuity. "Taṃ" refers to the evil karma. "Te" refers to the aggregates produced by wholesome [karma].
"They protect" means they do not give an opportunity for [the evil karma] to ripen by yielding its result; this is the meaning.
And while this meaning applies to [karma] to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), it is also appropriately applicable to the other [types of karma] as well. Therefore, he said:
“In a second or third existence.

Regarding this, he says “one who desires his own welfare” because one who undertakes a practice that brings blameless happiness to oneself is, in the ultimate sense, called “one who desires his own welfare. Furthermore, one who desires happiness that is followed by further happiness is said to be “one who desires happiness.
“In the sense of being extensive” means in the sense of extensiveness, which is defined as the state of being the locus for the occurrence of views that are widely diffused.

114. In the phrase *diṭṭhe dukkhādidhamme*, the locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state by means of a state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe*); the meaning is: "when the phenomena of suffering and so forth have been seen and known.

Regarding the words "above" (*uddha*) and so on, he says "above is the future, and also what is higher," etc., because this exhausts time and space without remainder. By "going" (*gamanena*), he means by the going of death and rebirth (*cutūpapāta*). 115.
"For the purpose of making the city gates firm" means for the purpose of making the doorposts of the city firm. By "having deep rims" (*gambhīranematāya*).
“Nema” refers to the portion of a pillar or similar object that has entered into the earth and remains fixed there;
that which has a deep *nema* is called *gambhīranema*. The state of being such is *gambhīranematā*, and [the earth shakes] by means of that.

“Shaking” (*kampana*) is the moving back and forth of what is already standing; “trembling” (*cālana*) is the displacement from its standing place. “Having plunged into” means by way of the realization of the unerring nature [of reality].
"Having entered," means "having become as if one has entered.
He shows this by supplying the remainder of the verse's statement: "by way of abandoning the fetters.

Alternatively, since the accomplishment of development does not occur without the abandoning of that which is to be abandoned, the abandoning of what is to be abandoned is established by implication as being both internal and external.

Having joined [the two] with the two phrases, in order to show that one is "separated from the fetters pertaining to the lower and the higher" (*orambhāgiya-uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), and to support this meaning by means of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it was said: "Therefore he said, 'in the whole world'.
"With non-greed as the head" means preceded by non-greed; for this reason, the practitioner of yoga is called "one who has the desire for renunciation" (*nekkhammacchanda*).
The perception of foulness (asubhasaññā) is said to be "predominantly characterized by non-greed" because it is the direct antidote to lust, or else because it consists of the ten types of foulness.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "meditative absorptions (jhāna), etc.," insight (vipassanā) and other such qualities are included.

Because all four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) have non-ill-will as their primary factor—since they counteract the lust for cruelty and the lust for pleasure which are rooted in ill-will—it is said: "The four... [non-ill-will] is the path of Dhamma."

The construction is: "the jhānas and so forth have been attained. Regarding the ten recollections... [and so on]... the intention is that right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) is the "footing of the Dhamma" (*dhammapada*) because they are to be attained by means of that mindfulness.
In the development of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānabhāvanā*), concentration (*samādhi*) is also predominant, not mindfulness alone;

it is for the purpose of showing this that it is said: "the ten kasiṇas... [and so on]... right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) is the footing of the Dhamma. By way of the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*)...
The inclusion of those things already understood should also be seen as occurring right here.
116. "Characteristics" (upalakkhaṇakāraṇāni) means signs for recognition.

Regarding the phrase "evil itself is worse," he said "it becomes evil"; and "worse" (pāpiyo) is stated by way of a change in grammatical gender. "Singular number" (ekavacana) [refers to] "plural number" (bahuvacana): where the singular should have been used, the plural was stated.
117. "By way of adherence through clinging that settles down" means by way of craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) and views regarding existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*).
For these cause sentient beings to settle down (*allīyāpenti*) in states of existence. "By way of adherence through over-leaping" means by way of the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*).

For this is called "adherence through over-leaping" because it adheres by making the cutting off of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭupaccheda*) out of the mere cutting off of what is appropriate (*avaṭṭupaccheda*). "They settle down" means from right practice.
They fall into contraction. "They run away" means they overstep right practice (*sammāpaṭipatti*).
"And of those" refers to both of those forms of dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) and all other conceivings (*maññita*) besides them. 118.
"This is a desirable ripening, this is an undesirable ripening" refers to the fruit designated as a desirable ripening and the fruit designated as an undesirable ripening.
By the phrase “*akaṅkhato na jāneyyun*,” he demonstrates the meaning of the word “*na jaññā*” by way of showing its connection with the word “*ākaṅkhato*.
“*Na upalabbhati*” means “it is not found,” which is to say, “it does not exist. 120.

“*Tāni*” refers to the kamma, the sign of the kamma, and the sign of the destination. For this is merely a manner of spreading out, namely, the hanging down of shadows. “*Evaṃ hotī*” means that remorse arises in such a manner as: “Alas, I have not done what is wholesome! and so forth.
"By those seeking" means by those who strive within their own and others' continuums to accomplish [the goal]. "Bearing the fruit of suffering" means having suffering as its result.
"By three causes" means by way of body, speech, and mind; for these are called causes because they serve as the doors for their respective restraints (saṃvara).
Alternatively, "by three bases" means by three points of origin. "Closed" means that which covers.
“Designated as the place of arising”: this is said by taking the commonality of being stone.
123. “Mixed with dust”: mixed with flower-dust. “Of him”: of that Sage, both in training and beyond training.

For those dwelling in the village, there is no loss of faith or loss of wealth due to his wandering in the village—as there would be for those who are full of great desires and so forth; rather, [there is an increase].
Showing that there is indeed an increase from stage to stage, he said, "it becomes as it was originally.
"Internal meditation subject" refers to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.
By "by that," he means by wholesome bodily and verbal action. Showing the meaning of "firmness" as being called "strength," he said, "thāmavā means one who possesses stability."

Regarding the statement, "There is no love equal to self-love," he said this because it is taught that "one who has grasped [the self] as 'self' [develops] love based on that self" and thus speaks of "love equal to the self.
However, referring to the manifestation of the radiance of the Blessed One’s insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), he said, "But wisdom...
is able to... Indeed, the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) and the super-knowledges (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) illuminate infinite and immeasurable world-systems.
124. "Afraid of what? means for what reason afraid.

"Having established" means having set forth. The construction is "he should be addressed by the supplicants," which means he is fit to be requested. "Requisites for sacrifice" means the equipment for sacrifice.
To define the tetrad mentioned in the phrase "standing firm in these four qualities," it says: "Faithful..."
"One factor," and so forth, is what was stated.
In the verse, the method of pairs (*dukanaya*) consists of treating each pair of the phenomena mentioned as a single factor.
He speaks with reference to "the nature of birth" (*jātidhamma*), meaning the nature of occurrence (*pavattidhamma*).

125. Showing that the collection of truths is distinguished from a single instance of truth by way of its exhaustive inclusion of all [truths], he said, "Whether it be ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*).
"Four terms" (*caturo padā*) means four terms; this is stated with a shift in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), meaning four constituent parts of the Dhamma.
The mention of "four terms" is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the division into seven categories, not because it conforms to the specific nature of the Dhamma already attained.
“Nimmadāti na madā.
There is also a reading: “Saccavādī jino romo. In that context, *romo* refers to those heretics who are stained by the passion of wrong views and to the founders of those sects;

it is terrifying because he teaches the Dhamma as the opposite of passion to those who preach what is not the Dhamma, or because he reveals the danger therein to those who preach what is not the Dhamma.
It is to be feared; or, because it is difficult to approach for those who have not abandoned the lack of restraint, its meaning is that it is "hard to encounter.
It is both true and a Dhamma, thus it is "the True Dhamma" (*saccadhamma*). Therefore he said: "By way of being exclusively an escape," and so forth.
"The state of being the one-way path" means the state of being the single path; the meaning is the state of being no other path.

He says, "by means of the four terms beginning with 'conducive to defilement' (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*)," because it is stated that the category conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) alone is divided into two:
that which pertains to seeing (*dassanabhāgiya*) and that which pertains to development (*bhāvanābhāgiya*).

"Of the remaining triads" refers to the eight triads beginning with the triad based on the seven [types of] persons (*satta*). And "of the remaining terms" refers to the mixed terms such as "conducive to defilement" and "conducive to purification through habituation" (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
By the word "ca" (and), the terms beginning with "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) are also included.
For this demonstration of the method (*nayadassana*) occurs through the combination of the mixed terms—referred to as "the remaining terms"—with the mundane triad (*lokiyattika*) itself;

whereas for the other triads, this demonstration of the method occurs through the combination of both the terms beginning with "partaking of defilement" and the "remaining terms. Thus, it is said: "It is easy to understand by following the stated method."

It has been stated. "Overcoming" means abandoning. Although the factors pertaining to the residual impression (vāsanā) and the factors pertaining to defilement (saṃkilesa) are both mundane, nevertheless, the latter are to be abandoned by the former through the method of specific counteraction (tadaṅga-vasena) and through suppression (vikkhambhana-vasena). Because it possesses such capacity for abandoning, it is called "abandoning";
thus it is said: "The discourse pertaining to the residual impression serves for the overcoming of that which pertains to defilement."

The construction is as follows: "The states of purification are to be attained by means of transcending the states of defilement. Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is threefold: cultivation of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), cultivation of insight (*vipassanā*), and cultivation of the path (*magga*).

Since the cultivation of the path is already included [in the preceding context], the cultivation of insight is likewise already included; therefore, without mentioning that, only the other two are taken here.

Nevertheless, considering the objection that if it is stated, "for the sake of relinquishing the discourse pertaining to development," then has even the development of jhāna by one beyond training (*asekha*) been entirely relinquished, the commentary shows that the Pāḷi states, "the discourse pertaining to those beyond training is for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life. Thus it says:
"When the qualities of one beyond training have arisen, the task of developing the path..."
Having said, "There is no such thing," he stated, "The cultivation of jhāna is also for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life.

"Single-seeded" (*ekabījī*) means that the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*), which is the sole seed of existence, is his single seed; one who possesses that is a "single-seeded" person.
"Having run on and wandered about" means having approached by way of rebirth; "having transmigrated" (*saṃsaritvā*) is a synonym for that. "Family" (*kulaṃ*)...
"One who goes from family to family" (*kolaṅkolo*) means he goes to a family (*kulaṃ gacchati*). This designation is made without eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) in the first word.

"Of those stream-enterers" refers to their classification, namely the division into the "one-seeder" (*ekabījī*) and so forth. The merit-activity that serves as a support for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya-puññakamma*), established in a previous existence, is here called the "prior cause.
That which is called "having performed merit" (*katapuññatā*) exists because, once the first path has been accomplished, one abides in the state of having practiced [the path].

He says, "It would entail... [it] does not reach the higher paths," with the intention that karma which has already ripened its result cannot serve as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the higher paths.
It would follow that the three [higher] paths are purposeless, because the function to be performed by them has already been accomplished by the first path alone.
He says, "It would entail... [it] does not reach the first path," because it is impossible for a task to be performed by what has not yet arisen. Thus...
Having shown the lack of logical consistency in the first three positions, he says, “Vipassanā...
is appropriate,” demonstrating that only the fourth position is logical here. He clarifies that logic with the words beginning, “For if...”.
The strength of insight (vipassanā) should be understood as arising from the ripening of the states conducive to liberation, the sharpness of the faculties, and the clarity of knowledge.
For it is the transmigrator by way of a mixed method that is intended here, because it is said, "having run on among gods and humans.
One who stands here in the sensual existence is "one standing here" (*idhaṭṭhaka*). Because of being reborn in the worlds of humans and gods, he is "intermingled by way of place" (*okārena vokiṇṇa*).
For a noble disciple, rebirth in various classes of beings is like a purification for him, in that it removes the evils such as the stains of the defilements.
He said: "Having purified the six deva-worlds. By the phrase "having stood in Akaniṭṭha," it should be understood that the purification of the lower Brahma-worlds has already been stated.
"Making faith the yoke" means making faith the burden, the foremost, and the leader. [This refers to] the recollection of faith.
One who follows by way of practice, or who has faith as a preliminary recollection, or whose nature is to follow through faith, is a *saddhānusārī* (faith-follower).
The same method applies here for the term *dhammānusārī* (Dhamma-follower); however, in this context, "Dhamma" should be understood as wisdom (*paññā*).
One who is liberated while having faith is a *saddhāvimutta* (liberated-by-faith); even if he is not liberated in every respect, the meaning is that he is liberated by means of mere faith.

"One liberated by resolution through faith" (*saddhā-vimutta*) means one who is resolved through faith (*saddhāya adhimutta*). "By the method stated" refers to the degree of strength or weakness of the insight (*vipassanā*) regarding the higher paths.
"One who has attained through vision" (*diṭṭhippatto*) means one who has reached cessation through the vision consisting of the realization of the Four Noble Truths;

or, one who has reached the end of vision (*diṭṭhanta*) is "one who has attained through vision," referring to the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*), which is termed "vision."
"Immediately preceding" is what is meant. For it refers to the period starting from the first fruit up to the supreme path, [the stage] of those who have attained vision (*diṭṭhippatta*).
"This" refers to the statement concerning the state of being liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*) and having attained vision among the stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) as previously described.

"Of the eight liberations": there are eight liberations, namely the four fine-material-sphere attainments (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*) and the four immaterial-sphere attainments (*arūpāvacara-samāpatti*); [it means] "of these."

"One who realizes the limit of what has been touched" (*phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikaroti*) is a body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*). "The limit of what has been touched" (*phuṭṭhanta*) means the end of those things touched;
the intended meaning is the time immediately following the immaterial jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*). This is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*);
thus it is said that he realizes that which is to be realized precisely at the moment immediately following the touch, as in such expressions as "the moon and sun revolve unevenly."

Or rather, this should be understood as a gerundive neuter (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*). For one who is liberated from the material body and from a portion of the mental body by means of formless jhāna through the liberation of suppression, by him the liberation termed "cessation" is as if perceived or revealed;
yet it is not realized by the body itself. However, when certain taints have been exhausted by taking cessation as the object, [that liberation is attained].

Therefore, that [cessation] has been realized by him. Consequently, because he realizes with the mental body (*nāmakāya*) the cessation to be realized exactly as it was contemplated, he is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*);
yet he is not "liberated" because some of his taints (*āsava*) have not yet been fully exhausted.

"Without distinction" means without the distinctions such as "one who attains Nibbāna in the interval" (*antarāparinibbāyin*), and so forth. And this term "without distinction" refers to those who are "liberated through faith," "attained to vision," and "body-witnesses."

Here too, it should be applied by bringing [the terms] together. For just as there is one non-returner (anāgāmin) by means of the mere touching of the various distinctions such as those who attain parinibbāna in the interval and so forth, even so, by means of the touching of the aforementioned distinctions, there are three types of non-returners: the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta), the one attained to view (diṭṭhippatto), and the body-witness (kāyasakkhī).
And it should be understood that this counting of non-returners is performed by taking such a classification of states.
“Among the Avihas, etc. and so forth is easy to understand.
One who is liberated by wisdom alone, and not also by the preeminent concentration that constitutes liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*), is one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*).
One who is “liberated in both ways” (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) is liberated from both parts; [that is,] by means of the suppression and the eradication of the defilements.
Showing the meaning of "liberated from the material body and the mental body," he said: "Liberated... [as above] ...is called liberated.
One is liberated from the material body by means of the formless attainments, and from the mental body by means of the supreme path. As it is said:
"Here, monks, a certain person, with his own body, attains those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms..."
“Having touched [the cessation of perception and feeling] with the body, he dwells therein; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This person, monks, is called one liberated in both ways.
Now, after the eight liberations have been taught in the Mahānidāna Sutta—beginning with “one possessing form sees forms” and ending with the attainment of cessation—it says:
“Ānanda, when a bhikkhu enters upon these eight liberations in forward order...
[as before] ...this, Ānanda, is called a bhikkhu liberated both ways. And, Ānanda, there is no liberation both ways other than this that is higher or more sublime.”
That which was stated was said with reference to the foremost of those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*).

In this context, since even a single formless attainment (*āruppasamāpatti*) is said to have suppressed the body, five types of those liberated in both ways should be understood as those who have attained the four formless attainments and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This same method applies to the "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhin*) as well.
For even when only a portion of the eight liberations (aṭṭhavimokkha) is present, the designation "eight liberations" is used, just as one says "beings in the world.

Among the thirteen headings (sīsa), the headings of impediments (palibodha-sīsa) and so forth, as well as the heading of occurrence (pavatta-sīsa), are what must be abandoned; the headings of resolve (adhimokkha-sīsa) and so forth are the abandoners;
and the heading of the objective field (gocara-sīsa) is the fruit of abandonment. For that is the fruit which has the internal state of the object as its nature; it is liberation (vimokkha).
The object of the path that brings about exhaustion and of its fruit is cessation, which is the summit of formations and consists in seclusion from formations.

In order to show the state of being "of equal summit" (samasīsibhāva)—that is, the simultaneous accomplishment of the objective domain for both those things to be exhausted and the fruits that effect their exhaustion—thirteen summits are mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. Here, however, for whichever person...

Since it is stated in the *Puggalapaññatti* that "the exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after one another," he says "the head of the defilements" and so forth,
applying the explanation specifically to those who have the heads of the active defilements. In that context, even regarding the head of the active [defilements],
the Path, having been set in motion, emerges from it by ensuring that they do not recur beyond the point of death.

Even though it is exhausted [by the path], it is said that "the life-faculty, which is the head of the process, is exhausted by the death-consciousness" because the process continues until the moment of death.
The tasks of reviewing must be accomplished immediately after oneself through the exhaustion of the defilements; and the reviewing stages belong to the exhaustion of the defilements itself.

They deserve to be called "times" (vāra). For, according to the statement, "When there is liberation, the knowledge 'it is liberated' arises," the exhaustion of the defilements is said to be completed by the conclusion of the reviewing consciousness.
Now, if that completion occurs through the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), then the life-force is also completed by that very same [consciousness].
Thus, due to this equality of the time of death, there is an equality between the exhaustion of the defilements and the exhaustion of the life-force.

It is said, “by way of equality of turns,” because there is no priority or posteriority. Regarding the phrase “having descended into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), he attains final nibbāna,” it should be understood that here the consciousness of final nibbāna itself is spoken of by virtue of its state of transcending dissolution.
“Conduct” (carita) refers to the activity of body, speech, and mind. And herein, a person is called “one of lustful temperament” (rāgacarita) by reason of the predominance of lust.
It is characterized; thus, this is a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*). Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'one whose underlying tendency is lust' or 'one who has an excess of lust.

By that, it should be understood that the state of power of lust—which has become firmly established in the continuum through its unabandoned nature—is what is characterized. This same method applies to the others as well.

Showing that the description was made by eliding the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) from "by those possessing virtue and so forth," he said: "By those possessing virtue and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of donors and others should be understood.
"Known as objects" means that only those things which have become objects are what is known.

"In the planes of the worldlings and so forth" refers to the planes of the worldlings (puthujjana), the trainees (sekha), and the non-trainees (asekha). Among these, restraint occurs by way of the plane of the worldlings; abandoning and development occur by way of the plane of the trainees;
realization occurs by way of the plane of the non-trainees; and [the remaining factors] occur by way of both the plane of the worldlings and the plane of the trainees.

Or, restraint and the development of abandoning [defilements] are as appropriate. For the development of restraint and the development of abandoning are possible for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) in their preliminary stages;
the other [development] belongs to one in training (*sekkha*), while realization occurs by way of the stage of one beyond training (*asekkha*). This has been shown by way of method:
"Monks, that which has not been prohibited by me with the words 'this is not allowable,' if it conforms to what is allowable..."
It is explained by way of showing the method through such passages as, "He rejects what is improper; that is allowable for you. "Leading to the state of one with lust, etc.
means leading toward the condition of being possessed of lust and so forth.
"From their mutual association" refers to the [categories] beginning with "the portion dealing with defilement and the portion dealing with purification," and so on.
"From the mutual conjunction of the factors. "Of many kinds" means twelvefold, or even up to four thousand and ninety-two kinds; thus it is of manifold varieties.

"From the conjunction of mundane beings, the mundane basis, and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," [it includes] mundane knowledge, supramundane knowledge, both mundane and supramundane knowledge, the mundane object of knowledge, the supramundane object of knowledge, and both mundane and...

The possible divisions of the *Paṭṭhāna* are included here, such as: the supramundane is both the object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) and mundane knowledge is both the object of knowledge and knowledge; supramundane knowledge is both the object of knowledge and knowledge; and mundane and supramundane knowledge are both the objects of knowledge and knowledge—and so forth.

"In both cases" refers to those beginning with the "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and those beginning with the "mundane" (*lokiya*). "As appropriate" means whichever [division] is fit to be joined by way of association (*saṃsagga*).

"Each respective state" (*so so dhammo*). For the connection is made precisely through compatibility and non-contradiction. Indeed, a connection such as "worldly [states] partaking of penetration" (*lokiyaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ*) and so forth is not possible.
"Found in the three Piṭakas" means found and existing within the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) as recorded in the three councils (*tisso saṅgītiyo*), that is, in the Tipiṭaka.
By this, it is indicated that there is not merely a compilation (*saṅgaha*) of those aforementioned categories of the *Paṭṭhāna* sections, but rather their definitive determination (*niddhāraṇā*).
It is not the cause; rather, it clarifies that there is "seeing" as well in the text. Therefore he said: "That which is seen in those various planes.
With the words "For by that very reason," etc., he demonstrates the conformity of the reading with the meaning already stated.
The commentary on the section on the *Paṭṭhāna* of the Teaching is finished.
Commentary on the Conclusion:

Regarding the phrase "in a place for entering the True Dhamma," this is said with reference to a dwelling place where, having come from other regions, there is an abundance of hearing, retaining, mastering, inquiring about, and attending to the True Dhamma;
or else, it refers to being a place for the introduction of the True Dhamma of the scriptures into one's own mental continuum.
Thus it has been said. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthavaṇṇanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā* is finished.
The *Nettippakaraṇa-ṭīkā* is finished.
